2. Add a matching scheme and build configuration per flavor in Xcode
3. Give each flavor a Dart entry point (`lib/main_dev.dart`), or drive everything from `--dart-define`
4. Build with `flutter build apk --flavor dev --target lib/main_dev.dart`

Two things worth knowing. `--dart-define-from-file=config/dev.json` feeds a whole config file in at compile time, which beats a wall of individual `--dart-define` flags and keeps keys out of the repo. And `flutter_flavorizr` generates the Android and iOS boilerplate for you if you would rather not hand-edit Gradle and the Xcode project.

questions.question: How do you sign Android and iOS builds in CI without leaking the keys?
questions.answer:
Signing is the single highest-stakes secret in mobile CI. Lose the upload key and you can't publish updates; leak the .p12 and someone can ship a malicious update under your identity. The discipline is: keys stay encrypted at rest, decoded at build time into a temporary file, and shredded when the job ends.

Android:
• Generate a release keystore (.jks) once, store it Base64-encoded in GitHub Secrets / your CI's secret store
• A keystore.properties file holds storeFile, storePassword, keyAlias, keyPassword — generated on the fly in CI from secrets
• `signingConfigs.release` in build.gradle reads from keystore.properties
• Use Play App Signing — let Google hold the upload key. You sign with an upload key, Google re-signs with the actual app signing key. Lose the upload key and you can recover via Play Console.

iOS:
• Two artifacts: a Distribution Certificate (.p12) and a Provisioning Profile (.mobileprovision)
• fastlane match is the standard — store both, encrypted, in a private git repo; CI calls `fastlane match appstore --readonly`
• Alternative: store .p12 + profile as Base64 in CI secrets, decode in a temp keychain that's deleted after build
• Xcode Cloud sidesteps the whole dance — Apple holds the signing assets and signs the archive for you; the tradeoff is that your build lives in Apple's system, not next to the rest of your CI

Always:
• Mark the secrets as masked in CI output
• Restrict who can read or rotate them; keep an audit log
• Rotate after any team member with access leaves
• Do not commit keystore.properties or .p12 — put them in .gitignore explicitly
questions.code_example:
# .github/workflows/release.yml — Android signing
jobs:
  build-android:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v5
      - uses: subosito/flutter-action@v2
        with: { flutter-version-file: pubspec.yaml, cache: true }

      - name: Decode keystore
        run: echo "${{ secrets.KEYSTORE_BASE64 }}" | base64 --decode > android/app/release.jks

      - name: Write keystore.properties
        run: |
          cat > android/key.properties <<EOF
          storeFile=release.jks
          storePassword=${{ secrets.KEYSTORE_PASSWORD }}
          keyAlias=${{ secrets.KEY_ALIAS }}
          keyPassword=${{ secrets.KEY_PASSWORD }}
          EOF

      - name: Build app bundle
        run: flutter build appbundle --release --obfuscate --split-debug-info=symbols/

      - name: Cleanup
        if: always()
        run: |
          rm -f android/app/release.jks android/key.properties

# build.gradle reads the properties
# def keystoreProps = new Properties()
# keystoreProps.load(new FileInputStream(rootProject.file("key.properties")))
# signingConfigs { release { storeFile file(keystoreProps['storeFile']); ... } }

# ── iOS: fastlane match — recommended ────────────
# Fastfile
# lane :ci_release do
#   setup_ci   # creates a temporary keychain
#   match(type: 'appstore', readonly: true,
#         git_url: 'git@github.com:acme/match-certs.git')
#   build_app(scheme: 'Runner', export_method: 'app-store')
# end

# CI step:
#   - run: bundle exec fastlane ios ci_release
#     env:
#       MATCH_PASSWORD: ${{ secrets.MATCH_PASSWORD }}
#       APP_STORE_CONNECT_API_KEY_KEY: ${{ secrets.APP_STORE_API_KEY }}
#       MATCH_KEYCHAIN_PASSWORD: ${{ secrets.KEYCHAIN_PASSWORD }}

questions.question: How do you manage app versioning in Flutter — version, build number, semver?
questions.answer:
Three numbers travel together in every build: the public version, the build number, and the semantic intent of the change. They serve different audiences.

pubspec.yaml `version` field — `1.4.2+87`:
• `1.4.2` is the public version (semver-style: major.minor.patch). Visible in stores, in About screens.
• `+87` is the build number — strictly increasing integer. Stores require it to be higher than any previously uploaded build.
• Flutter expands this into Android `versionName`/`versionCode` and iOS `CFBundleShortVersionString`/`CFBundleVersion`

Rules to live by:
• Build number must always go up. The cleanest source is the CI build counter (GitHub Actions `${{ github.run_number }}`) or a monotonic timestamp
• Don't let two CI runs produce the same build number — even on a re-run
• Public version follows semver intent: bump patch for fixes, minor for additive features, major for breaking UX/API changes that users care about
• On hotfixes branched from a tagged release, bump only the patch and the build number — don't accidentally release `1.5.0+old` ahead of `1.4.2`

Driving it from one source:
• Manual: edit pubspec.yaml on every release. Simple, fragile.
• `flutter build --build-name=1.4.2 --build-number=$RUN_NUMBER` overrides pubspec at build time. Recommended for CI.
• Generated build-info file in code so the running app can show its own version (`PackageInfo.fromPlatform()`).
questions.code_example:
# pubspec.yaml
version: 1.4.2+87
# major.minor.patch+build_number
#  ↓             ↓
#  Android versionName     versionCode = 87
#  iOS CFBundleShortVer    CFBundleVersion

# .github/workflows/release.yml
name: Release
on:
  push:
    tags: ['v*']      # e.g. v1.4.2 triggers a release build

jobs:
  build:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v5
      - uses: subosito/flutter-action@v2
        with: { flutter-version-file: pubspec.yaml, cache: true }

      - name: Derive version
        id: ver
        run: |
          # Strip leading 'v' from the tag
          VERSION="${GITHUB_REF_NAME#v}"
          BUILD="${{ github.run_number }}"
          echo "version=$VERSION"   >> "$GITHUB_OUTPUT"
          echo "build=$BUILD"       >> "$GITHUB_OUTPUT"

      - name: Build (override pubspec values)
        run: |
          flutter build appbundle --release \
            --build-name=${{ steps.ver.outputs.version }} \
            --build-number=${{ steps.ver.outputs.build }} \
            --obfuscate --split-debug-info=symbols/

# ── Read version inside the app at runtime ──────────
# import 'package:package_info_plus/package_info_plus.dart';
#
# final info = await PackageInfo.fromPlatform();
# print('${info.version}+${info.buildNumber}');  // 1.4.2+87

questions.question: How do you automate Play Store and App Store releases from CI?
questions.answer:
Both stores expose APIs for unattended uploads. Reaching them safely from CI is the standard final step of a release pipeline.

Google Play:
• Generate a service account in Google Cloud, grant it Play Console access
• Download its JSON key — store as a CI secret
• Use `fastlane supply` or the Gradle `play-publisher` plugin to upload an .aab and bump tracks (internal → alpha → beta → production)
• Tracks let you stage rollouts: upload to internal first, promote when smoke tests pass, then ramp production from 1% → 10% → 100%

Apple App Store:
• Generate an App Store Connect API Key (.p8 + key id + issuer id) — replaces username/password / 2FA pain
• Use `fastlane pilot` to upload to TestFlight, `deliver` to push metadata + binary to App Store, `submit_to_app_review` to start review
• TestFlight build availability typically takes 5–30 minutes after upload
• App Store metadata (screenshots, descriptions, what's new) can be checked into the repo (fastlane metadata) so each release ships with version-controlled copy

Guardrails:
• Always upload to internal/TestFlight first; gate prod promotion on a manual approval step or a green smoke job
• On a build pulled from review, your CI should be able to re-promote a previous artifact rather than rebuild — keep .aab/.ipa artifacts retained for at least 90 days
• Never let a CI matrix accidentally upload the same build to production twice; idempotency check on the build number is cheap insurance
questions.code_example:
# fastlane/Fastfile
default_platform(:android)

platform :android do
  desc 'Upload AAB to Play Console internal track'
  lane :internal do
    upload_to_play_store(
      track: 'internal',
      aab: '../build/app/outputs/bundle/release/app-release.aab',
      json_key_data: ENV['PLAY_SERVICE_ACCOUNT_JSON'],
      release_status: 'completed',
    )
  end

  desc 'Promote internal → production with staged rollout'
  lane :promote do |options|
    upload_to_play_store(
      track: 'internal', track_promote_to: 'production',
      rollout: options[:rollout] || '0.1',  # 10%
      json_key_data: ENV['PLAY_SERVICE_ACCOUNT_JSON'],
    )
  end
end

platform :ios do
  desc 'Upload IPA to TestFlight'
  lane :beta do
    api_key = app_store_connect_api_key(
      key_id: ENV['ASC_KEY_ID'],
      issuer_id: ENV['ASC_ISSUER_ID'],
      key_content: ENV['ASC_API_KEY_P8'],
    )
    upload_to_testflight(
      api_key: api_key,
      ipa: '../build/ios/ipa/Runner.ipa',
      skip_waiting_for_build_processing: true,
    )
  end
end

# .github/workflows/release.yml — release stage
# - run: bundle exec fastlane android internal
# - run: bundle exec fastlane ios beta
# - name: Manual approval for prod ramp
#   uses: trstringer/manual-approval@v1
#   with: { approvers: alice,bob }
# - run: bundle exec fastlane android promote rollout:0.1

questions.question: How do you set up beta distribution with Firebase App Distribution and TestFlight?
questions.answer:
Beta channels are how you get a build into the hands of real users without going through the public store review and ramp. Each platform has a different best-practice channel.

iOS — TestFlight (Apple-only, no alternative):
• Internal testers: up to 100, no review needed, instant access — invite by Apple ID
• External testers: up to 10,000, requires Apple's beta review (~24h on first build, automatic on subsequent ones in the same group)
• Build expires after 90 days, so testers always have a fresh artifact
• Crash reports flow into Xcode Organizer / your APM

Android — Firebase App Distribution OR Play Console internal/closed testing:
• Firebase App Distribution: by-email invitations, OTA updates, supports APKs (faster turnaround for ad-hoc testing)
• Play Console internal track: tied to the store identity — closer to what users actually get; required if you want Play Integrity attestations to work in beta
• Many teams run both — Firebase for engineering smoke tests, Play internal for product/QA

Process hygiene:
• Auto-publish every main-branch build to a private internal channel — catches build issues before they touch a tester
• Promote tagged release builds to a wider beta group; keep release notes per build
• Wire crash reports / analytics back to a build_id so you can correlate beta crashes to commits
• Have a recovery path: if a beta is broken, you can roll back testers to an older artifact without going through a full release
questions.code_example:
# .github/workflows/beta.yml
name: Beta
on:
  push:
    branches: [main]

jobs:
  android-beta:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v5
      - uses: subosito/flutter-action@v2
        with: { flutter-version-file: pubspec.yaml, cache: true }
      - run: flutter build apk --release --obfuscate --split-debug-info=symbols/
      - name: Distribute to Firebase
        uses: wzieba/Firebase-Distribution-Github-Action@v1
        with:
          appId: ${{ secrets.FIREBASE_ANDROID_APP_ID }}
          serviceCredentialsFileContent: ${{ secrets.FIREBASE_SA_JSON }}
          groups: engineering-smoke
          file: build/app/outputs/flutter-apk/app-release.apk
          releaseNotes: |
            Build: ${{ github.sha }}
            Branch: ${{ github.ref_name }}

  ios-testflight:
    runs-on: macos-latest      # Apple silicon since macos-14
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v5
      - uses: maxim-lobanov/setup-xcode@v1
        with: { xcode-version: latest-stable }   # never trust the image default
      - uses: subosito/flutter-action@v2
        with: { flutter-version-file: pubspec.yaml, cache: true }
      - name: Build IPA
        run: flutter build ipa --release --obfuscate --split-debug-info=symbols/
      - name: Upload to TestFlight
        run: bundle exec fastlane ios beta
        env:
          ASC_ISSUER_ID: ${{ secrets.ASC_ISSUER_ID }}
          ASC_KEY_ID: ${{ secrets.ASC_KEY_ID }}
          ASC_API_KEY_P8: ${{ secrets.ASC_API_KEY_P8 }}

# ── fastlane/Fastfile — the Firebase lane, for local runs ────────
# platform :android do
#   lane :smoke do
#     firebase_app_distribution(
#       app: ENV['FIREBASE_ANDROID_APP_ID'],          # 1:NNN:android:xxx
#       service_credentials_file: 'firebase-cd.json',
#       android_artifact_path: '../build/app/outputs/flutter-apk/app-release.apk',
#       android_artifact_type: 'APK',
#       groups: 'engineering-smoke',
#       release_notes_file: 'release_notes.txt',
#     )
#   end
# end

questions.question: How do you avoid flaky integration tests in Flutter CI?
questions.answer:
Integration tests on emulators in CI are notorious for flakes that block green builds for reasons unrelated to your code. The solution is a mix of test design (eliminate timing assumptions) and infra design (eliminate environment surprises).

Design the tests:
• Never `Future.delayed` to wait for UI — use `await tester.pumpAndSettle()` for animations, or pump until a finder appears with a polling helper. Sleeps are the #1 source of flake.
• Replace network with deterministic test doubles. The test should not depend on a real backend, ever. Use a recorded fixture or an in-process fake server (`shelf` works well).
• Stub time. If your code reads `DateTime.now()` or starts timers, expose a Clock abstraction and inject a fake; otherwise tests behave differently at midnight.
• Make IDs stable. Use Keys for finder-by-id rather than text. Translations and rebuilds break text-based finders.
• Reset state between tests. Wipe localStorage/secure storage in setUp; set a fresh ProviderScope (Riverpod) or recreate the Cubits.

Design the infra:
• Use one device per test, not parallel devices on the same emulator — emulators sharing GPU on CI runners stutter
• Boot the emulator with `-no-snapshot-save -no-window -no-boot-anim -gpu swiftshader_indirect` for headless reliability
• Pre-warm: open a dummy Flutter app once before running the suite to avoid first-build cold-start variance
• Quarantine flakes: tag a test `@Tags(['flaky'])` and run it nightly with retries instead of blocking PRs
• Capture screenshots and logs on failure — re-running blindly hides flake patterns

questions.question: What is fastlane and what does it actually buy you over a hand-rolled CI script?
questions.answer:
fastlane is a Ruby tool that turns the long, error-prone sequences of cert/profile/build/upload commands into named lanes. You write a Fastfile once, then `fastlane release` does the right thing on any machine — local, CI, or a teammate's laptop.

What lanes wrap:
• `match` — synchronizes signing certs and provisioning profiles across the team via an encrypted git repo
• `gym` — builds an iOS .ipa with the right scheme, configuration, export options
• `pilot` / `upload_to_testflight` — uploads to TestFlight and waits for processing
• `supply` / `upload_to_play_store` — uploads .aab/.apk to Play and manages tracks
• `deliver` — manages App Store metadata, screenshots, what's new
• `screengrab` / `snapshot` — automated localized screenshots

What you actually buy:
• Reproducibility: any clean machine with the right secrets can produce the same artifact
• Auditability: lanes are checked into the repo, code-reviewed like any other code
• Smaller-blast-radius secrets: fastlane can use App Store Connect API keys (no human 2FA), match (read-only mode in CI)
• Recovery patterns: lanes that re-promote already-built artifacts, lanes that roll back, lanes that bisect a regression by version

When NOT to bother:
• A solo project shipping monthly — bash + `flutter build` + a couple of GitHub actions is enough
• If you're already on Bitrise or Codemagic, which abstract this — adding fastlane doubles the layers without much benefit
• On Xcode Cloud, signing, archiving and TestFlight upload are built in; fastlane still earns its place for Play uploads and metadata, but not for the iOS build itself
questions.code_example:
# fastlane/Fastfile
default_platform(:ios)

before_all do
  ensure_git_status_clean
  ensure_git_branch(branch: 'main')
end

platform :ios do
  desc 'Sync signing — read-only in CI'
  lane :certs do
    match(type: 'appstore', readonly: ENV['CI'] == 'true')
  end

  desc 'Build, archive, upload to TestFlight'
  lane :beta do
    certs
    increment_build_number(build_number: ENV['CI_BUILD_NUMBER'] || latest_testflight_build_number + 1)
    build_app(
      scheme: 'Runner',
      export_method: 'app-store',
      output_directory: 'build/ios/ipa',
    )
    upload_to_testflight(
      skip_waiting_for_build_processing: true,
    )
  end

  desc 'Promote latest TestFlight build to App Store, with phased release'
  lane :release do
    deliver(
      submit_for_review: true,
      automatic_release: false,
      phased_release: true,                 # 1% / 2% / 5% / 10% / 20% / 50% / 100%
      force: true,                          # skip metadata HTML preview
      precheck_include_in_app_purchases: true,
      submission_information: { add_id_info_uses_idfa: false },
    )
  end
end

# Usage
# bundle exec fastlane ios beta             # nightly
# bundle exec fastlane ios release          # tagged release
# Override env: ASC_KEY_ID / ASC_ISSUER_ID / ASC_API_KEY_P8 set in CI

questions.question: How do you do staged rollouts and quick rollbacks safely?
questions.answer:
Mobile releases ship to thousands of devices in minutes once you push the button. A staged rollout caps the blast radius if something is broken; a clean rollback path lets you stop bleeding fast.

Staged rollouts:
• Play Console — production track supports percentage rollouts (1% → 5% → 20% → 50% → 100%). Bake at each stage for at least 24h while watching crashlytics + key metrics.
• App Store — Phased Release ramps 1/2/5/10/20/50/100% over 7 days. You can pause from App Store Connect at any stage.
• Both let you halt and resume. Use the pause button when in doubt — the cost of a 12h delay is negligible.

What to monitor during a rollout:
• Crash-free user rate vs. previous version (set a guardrail: <0.5% drop is fine, >1% drop pause)
• Critical funnel metrics: sign-in success, checkout completion, push opt-in
• Backend errors that spiked with the rollout
• Reviews / support tickets in real time

Rollback options (in order of preference):
• Halt the staged rollout — Play Console immediately stops new users from getting the bad build; Phased Release pauses the ramp
• Server-side feature flag — hide the bad feature without an app update. Always ship risky features behind a remote flag.
• Re-release the previous build with a new version number — slow (review queue), but works. Keep the previous artifact warm in CI for 30+ days.
• Force-update screen — the app calls a config endpoint that says "please update". The current build still runs but a soft block escalates to hard if needed.

Guardrail: ship every release behind at least one feature flag for the new code paths. "Roll back" by toggling the flag is 1000x faster and safer than re-releasing.
questions.code_example:
# Play Console — staged rollout via fastlane
lane :promote do |opts|
  rollout = opts[:rollout] || '0.05'   # 5% by default
  upload_to_play_store(
    track: 'production',
    track_promote_to: nil,             # already on production from internal
    release_status: 'inProgress',      # required for staged rollouts
    rollout: rollout,
    json_key_data: ENV['PLAY_SERVICE_ACCOUNT_JSON'],
  )
end

# Halt a staged rollout immediately
lane :halt do
  upload_to_play_store(
    track: 'production',
    release_status: 'halted',
    json_key_data: ENV['PLAY_SERVICE_ACCOUNT_JSON'],
  )
end

# ── Server-side feature flag — the fastest "rollback" ──────────
# Firebase Remote Config / GrowthBook / LaunchDarkly. In Dart:
#
#   class FeatureFlags {
#     static Future<bool> get newCheckoutEnabled async {
#       final remote = FirebaseRemoteConfig.instance;
#       await remote.fetchAndActivate();
#       return remote.getBool('checkout_v2_enabled');  // toggle = instant kill
#     }
#   }
#
#   FutureBuilder<bool>(
#     future: FeatureFlags.newCheckoutEnabled,
#     builder: (_, snap) => snap.data == true
#         ? const NewCheckoutFlow()
#         : const LegacyCheckoutFlow(),
#   )

# ── Force-update gate (last resort) ─────────────────────────────
# Server returns: { "min_supported_build": 90 }
# App on build 87 < 90 -> show a blocking screen with a store link.
# Prefer fixing the bug; force-update is an emergency button you rarely press.

questions.question: Explain Flutter's three trees: Widget, Element, and RenderObject.
questions.answer:
Flutter keeps three parallel trees so that cheap descriptions can be thrown away and rebuilt constantly while the expensive layout objects survive.

• Widget tree — immutable blueprints, the thing you write inside `build()`. Recreated from scratch on every build; lightweight value objects; describes WHAT to show.
• Element tree — mutable and long-lived. An Element holds its current widget, owns the State for a StatefulWidget, knows its position in the tree, and performs reconciliation between the old and the new widget subtree. `BuildContext` IS the Element.
• RenderObject tree — layout, painting and hit testing. Expensive to allocate, so the framework tries hard to update one in place rather than replace it.

Reconciliation rule: at the same position, if the new widget has the same `runtimeType` and the same key, the Element is reused and simply given the new widget (the fast path, and the reason `const` widgets are free). A different type or a different key unmounts the old Element and mounts a new one, which also builds a new RenderObject and drops any State it held.

Keys exist for the cases where matching by position is wrong — reordering, inserting or removing items in a list of stateful children. A `ValueKey` tied to your model id makes Flutter match by identity instead of index, so state, scroll position and animations follow the right item.

questions.question: How does Flutter's rendering pipeline work? Explain the frame lifecycle.
questions.answer:
Every frame runs the same fixed sequence, and the whole sequence has to fit inside one display refresh — roughly 16 ms at 60 Hz, and only 8 ms on a 120 Hz ProMotion screen.

1. Vsync — the display asks for a frame and the Scheduler wakes up
2. Animation tick — tickers and AnimationControllers advance, then post-frame callbacks are queued
3. Build — dirty Elements run `build()` and the new widget subtrees are reconciled
4. Layout — RenderObjects compute sizes: constraints go down, sizes come back up, the parent sets each child's position
5. Compositing bits — the framework works out which subtrees need their own layer
6. Paint — RenderObjects record paint commands into layers; this produces a display list, not pixels
7. Compositing — the layer tree is flattened into a scene and handed to the engine
8. Rasterization — the raster thread turns the scene into pixels

Two threads, two kinds of jank:
• UI thread (Dart) — steps 2 to 7. A red bar here means build or layout is too expensive: too many rebuilds, an unbounded `ListView`, heavy work in `build()`.
• Raster thread — step 8. A red bar here means painting is too expensive: shader warm-up, oversized images, too many `saveLayer` calls from `Opacity` and clips.

Impeller is the default rasterizer on iOS and Android and precompiles its shaders, which is what removed the old first-run shader jank; Skia lives on behind the web renderers. DevTools shows the two threads as separate bars, and that split is how you tell "my build is slow" from "my painting is slow".

questions.question: What are slivers in Flutter and how do you build custom scroll effects?
questions.answer:
Slivers are scroll-aware render objects — they know their scroll offset and can change size/appearance as the user scrolls. They're the building blocks of CustomScrollView.

Why slivers?
• Mix different scroll behaviors (collapsing header + list + grid) in one scroll view
• Efficient — only render what's visible
• Enable advanced effects: parallax, sticky headers, collapsing toolbars

Built-in slivers:
• SliverAppBar — collapsing/floating/pinned app bar
• SliverList / SliverFixedExtentList — lazy list
• SliverGrid — lazy grid
• SliverToBoxAdapter — embed any widget
• SliverPadding, SliverFillRemaining, SliverPersistentHeader

Custom slivers with SliverPersistentHeader for sticky section headers.

questions.question: What is BuildContext and what does it actually hold?
questions.answer:
BuildContext is a handle to a location in the Element tree. Each Element implements BuildContext — when you receive `BuildContext context` in `build()`, it IS the Element. The framework hides the cast so you can't accidentally call lifecycle methods, but the identity is real.

What it knows:
• Its position in the tree — parent, ancestor types, depth
• How to walk up to find inherited widgets (`dependOnInheritedWidgetOfExactType`)
• Whether the widget is still mounted
• Theme.of, MediaQuery.of, Scaffold.of, Navigator.of all use it for ancestor lookup

What it does NOT know:
• Anything about descendants by default (no `findChild`)
• Anything about other branches of the tree
• Its own future — you cannot pre-compute results that depend on a context that doesn't exist yet

Lifecycle pitfalls:
• A context is valid only while the widget is mounted. After an `await`, you must check `if (!context.mounted)` before using it (or capture what you need from context BEFORE the await).
• Storing a context in a long-lived field is almost always a bug — the underlying Element may be unmounted before you use the context again.
• Using the wrong context for `showDialog` (e.g. capturing context from outside the navigator subtree) leads to dialogs appearing in the wrong route.

questions.question: What are BuildOwner and PipelineOwner, and why split them?
questions.answer:
Flutter splits every frame into two stages with two different owners, because reconciling widgets and laying out render objects have completely different cost profiles and ordering rules.

BuildOwner — owns the Element tree. Responsibilities:
• Track "dirty" elements (those whose widget changed or whose State called setState)
• During the build phase, run buildScope: walk dirty elements in tree order, call build(), reconcile children
• Handle GlobalKey reservations and re-parenting

PipelineOwner — owns the RenderObject tree. Responsibilities:
• Track the "needs-layout", "needs-compositing-bits", "needs-paint" and "needs-semantics" sets
• Each frame, flush each phase in order: flushLayout → flushCompositingBits → flushPaint → flushSemantics
• Enforce the invariants between phases (you cannot paint until layout has settled)

Why split:
• Build is a diff stage — nearly free when nothing changed, and it recurses deeply
• Layout and paint touch heavy native objects with strict ordering rules
• Decoupling lets the framework reuse the Element/Render protocol in other contexts (golden tests, headless rendering, custom embedders)

Most developers never touch these directly — but knowing them explains why setState marks an Element dirty (BuildOwner.scheduleBuildFor) while a RenderObject change like `markNeedsLayout` takes an independent path (PipelineOwner.requestVisualUpdate). Both end up calling scheduleFrame on the Scheduler, which runs both owners on the next vsync.

questions.question: How does compositing work? When does Flutter create a new layer?
questions.answer:
After paint, RenderObjects produce a Layer tree — not a flat bitmap. The compositor (Impeller on iOS and Android, Skia behind the web renderers) walks the layer tree and produces the final scene. Layers exist so that scrolling/animating subtrees can be re-composited without being re-painted.

What creates a new layer:
• `RepaintBoundary` — explicit. Always creates an OffsetLayer; everything inside is composed as a single layer.
• `Opacity` (with values strictly between 0 and 1) — saveLayer + alpha-blend → expensive new layer
• `BackdropFilter` — needs to read the framebuffer behind it → ImageFilterLayer
• `ShaderMask`, `Transform` (3D only), some `ColorFilter` cases
• Animations using `FadeTransition` / `SlideTransition` — they wrap the child in lightweight layers internally
• ClipPath / ClipRRect with antialiasing in some cases

What does NOT create a layer:
• Plain `Container`, `Padding`, `Align`, `SizedBox` — they paint directly into the parent's layer
• An alpha colour on a paint (`Colors.black.withValues(alpha: 0.6)`, which replaced the deprecated `withOpacity`) — shader-level alpha, no extra layer
• `Transform.translate(Offset)` — purely 2D, often a single Matrix4 applied at composite time

Why it matters:
• Each layer is a memory allocation; too many small layers cost RAM and indirection
• A repainted layer doesn't force re-paint of siblings; an unwrapped expensive widget under a sibling that animates DOES
• `RepaintBoundary` is the lever you reach for when DevTools shows a static subtree being repainted because of a neighbor's animation

Debug visibility: `debugPaintLayerBordersEnabled = true;` outlines every layer; `debugRepaintRainbowEnabled = true;` flashes layers on repaint — use both when diagnosing.

questions.question: How does hit testing work in Flutter?
questions.answer:
When the user taps the screen, Flutter walks the RenderObject tree to figure out who consumes the event. That walk is called hit testing.

The protocol:
1. Pointer event lands at coordinates (x, y) in screen space
2. The framework calls `RenderView.hitTest(result, position)` — the root render object
3. Each RenderObject in the path implements `hitTest(BoxHitTestResult result, {Offset position})`:
   • It first asks each child whether they were hit (`hitTestChildren`)
   • Then decides whether IT was hit (`hitTestSelf`)
   • If yes, it adds itself to the result list
4. The result is an ordered list from leaf (deepest, hit-tested first) to root
5. The framework dispatches the event to listeners on each entry — the closest one usually wins (handled events bubble up by convention, but Flutter doesn't auto-bubble — gestures cooperate via the gesture arena)

Key quirks:
• Render boxes outside their parent's bounds are NOT hit-tested — `Stack` with overflow visible can render but not receive events past parent edges. Wrap in `MouseRegion`/`Listener` only inside the parent's clipped area, or restructure.
• Transparent areas of widgets normally don't catch hits. `IgnorePointer` blocks all hits below it; `AbsorbPointer` catches them but doesn't dispatch.
• `GestureDetector` with `behavior: HitTestBehavior.translucent` makes a transparent area still hit-testable — useful for tap-on-empty-space.
• `HitTestBehavior.opaque` blocks descendants from being hit-tested in the same area.
• `Stack(fit: StackFit.expand)` sizes children to its size — children outside the stack's clip won't be hit-tested.

Gesture arena:
• Multiple gestures can compete for the same pointer (tap vs. drag vs. long-press)
• They join the arena; whichever "wins" (declares first) gets the pointer
• That's how a ListView can scroll while ignoring a competing tap on a child

questions.question: What is the Semantics tree and how does Flutter implement accessibility?
questions.answer:
Beside the Widget/Element/RenderObject trees, Flutter maintains a Semantics tree. It's the bridge to platform accessibility services: TalkBack on Android, VoiceOver on iOS, screen readers on desktop, browser ARIA on web.

How it's built:
• Each RenderObject can describe itself with `describeSemanticsConfiguration(SemanticsConfiguration)`
• Default widgets fill in obvious info (Text → label, Button → label + button role + tap action, Image → label from semanticLabel)
• You can add or override with the `Semantics` widget — explicit label, hint, role, value, actions
• The framework merges descendants into a flat node when they would be reported as one (a Card wrapping a label and a button collapses sensibly)

What reaches the OS:
• Each enabled user (TalkBack/VoiceOver active) triggers Flutter to compile the SemanticsTree and ship it to the platform via the engine; it updates incrementally as the tree changes
• Tap actions on a Semantics node become accessibility actions on iOS/Android — "double-tap to activate", "swipe up for more", etc.
• Live regions (`liveRegion: true`) cause the screen reader to announce changes (think error toasts)

Things to get right:
• Use semantic widgets (`Tooltip`, `MergeSemantics`, `ExcludeSemantics`, `Semantics`)
• Provide semanticLabel on icons that aren't decorative — `Icon(Icons.search, semanticLabel: 'Search')`
• Mark decorative images with `excludeFromSemantics: true`
• Don't put button-ish behavior on a `GestureDetector` without wrapping it in `Semantics(button: true, ...)` — VoiceOver will not call it a button
• Test with the OS screen reader, not just the inspector — many issues only show up in real use

Debug overlay: wrap your app in `SemanticsDebugger(child: ...)` to see the semantics nodes the OS sees.

questions.question: What is the Flutter engine, and how does the embedder boot a Flutter app on each platform?
questions.answer:
Flutter ships as three layers — a Dart framework, a C++ engine, and a per-platform embedder that hosts the engine inside an otherwise normal native app.

• Framework (Dart) — the part you write. Widgets, rendering, gestures, animation. Pure Dart on top of dart:ui.

• Engine (C++) — `libflutter.so` / `Flutter.framework`. Runs the Dart VM, owns the rasterizer (Impeller on mobile, Skia behind the web renderers) and exposes dart:ui, the lowest-level Dart bindings: Canvas, Path, ParagraphBuilder, the scheduler.

• Embedder — the platform-specific glue that hosts the engine in a native app:
• Android: FlutterActivity / FlutterFragment (Kotlin) loads libflutter.so and creates a FlutterEngine; FlutterView is the SurfaceView/TextureView the engine renders into.
• iOS: FlutterViewController embeds Flutter.framework and renders into a Metal-backed layer.
• macOS / Linux / Windows: each has its own embedder that integrates FlutterEngine with the platform's window and event loop.
• Web: the engine is compiled to JavaScript or WebAssembly and paints through CanvasKit or Skwasm; the old HTML renderer was removed, so `--web-renderer html` no longer exists.

Boot sequence:
1. The native entry point starts (Application.onCreate / AppDelegate didFinishLaunching)
2. Native code creates a FlutterEngine, which starts the Dart VM and loads the AOT snapshot (or the kernel file in debug)
3. The engine calls the Dart entry point — `main()` — wiring up the platform messenger for channels
4. main() calls runApp(), the framework boots, schedules the first frame, and paints through dart:ui into the engine

Why this matters:
• One app can host several FlutterEngines (add-to-app): each gets its own isolate but they can share assets, and FlutterEngineGroup makes the extra ones cheap
• Pre-warming an engine at launch makes the first navigation into Flutter instant instead of showing a blank frame
• Custom embedders exist for kiosks, embedded Linux and car head units — Flutter is a portable rendering kernel, not a UI library tied to one OS

For most app developers the embedder is invisible. But it explains why platform-channel calls hop to the platform thread, why hot reload is engine-driven, and why "upgrade the engine" is sometimes the real answer to a platform-only bug.

questions.question: What is the difference between let and var in Swift?
questions.answer:
A `let` binding can be assigned exactly once; a `var` binding can be reassigned as often as you like.

• let — the binding is fixed after initialization. Initialization can still be deferred, so `let x: Int; if c { x = 1 } else { x = 2 }` is legal.
• var — the binding can be pointed at a new value at any time.

The interesting part is how this interacts with value and reference semantics:
• For a value type (struct, enum) `let` freezes the whole value — you cannot mutate its stored properties or call a `mutating` method on it.
• For a reference type (class) `let` freezes only the reference — the object's own `var` properties are still settable through it.

Idiomatic Swift is `let` by default; the compiler emits a warning when a `var` is never mutated. It is not only style: a final class whose stored properties are all `let` of Sendable type gets `Sendable` conformance for free, which matters as soon as the value crosses an actor boundary.

questions.question: What are optionals in Swift and how do you safely unwrap them?
questions.answer:
An optional makes "this value might be missing" part of the type instead of a runtime surprise.

Under the hood `Optional<T>` is an enum with two cases, `.some(T)` and `.none`, which you write in source as `T?`.

Safe unwrapping options:
• `if let` / `guard let` — bind only when non-nil; the shorthand `guard let name else` reuses the same name
• `??` — nil-coalescing default
• `?.` — optional chaining, propagates nil through the whole expression
• `map` / `flatMap` — transform the wrapped value without unwrapping
• `switch` on `.some` / `.none` when you want both branches explicit

Force-unwrapping with `!` traps on nil. Reserve it for cases that are genuinely unreachable — a hardcoded URL literal, an outlet the storyboard guarantees — and write a real error path everywhere else. `try!` and implicitly unwrapped optionals (`String!`) carry the same risk.

questions.question: Explain value types vs reference types in Swift.
questions.answer:
Swift divides every type into value types, which are copied when you assign or pass them, and reference types, which are shared.

• Value types — struct, enum, tuple. Each variable owns its own copy, so nobody else can mutate it behind your back. That is what makes them the safe default under strict concurrency.
• Reference types — class, actor, closure. Many variables can point at one instance, and a mutation through any of them is visible to all.

Apple's guidance is to reach for `struct` first and use `class` only when you need something a value cannot give you: stable identity (`===`), inheritance, `deinit`, or Objective-C bridging.

The standard library collections — Array, Dictionary, Set, String — are all value types with copy-on-write. The buffer is shared until someone writes to it, so a copy costs a retain, not a memcpy. `isKnownUniquelyReferenced` is how you implement the same trick in your own types.

questions.question: What are closures in Swift and how do capture lists work?
questions.answer:
Closures are self-contained blocks of functionality (named or anonymous) that can be passed around. They capture variables from their surrounding scope by reference (for reference types) or by copying (for value types).

A capture list `[weak self]` / `[unowned self]` lets you opt into different memory semantics — required to avoid retain cycles when a closure outlives its owner (e.g. stored on a view, networking layer, or NotificationCenter).

Trailing-closure syntax + shorthand parameters ($0, $1) make Swift closures concise.

questions.question: What is the difference between Array, Set, and Dictionary in Swift?
questions.answer:
Array, Set and Dictionary are the three standard-library collections, and choosing between them is really a choice about ordering and lookup cost.

• `Array<Element>` — ordered and index-addressed, duplicates allowed. O(1) random access, amortised O(1) append, but O(n) for `contains`.
• `Set<Element>` — unordered and unique; `Element` must be `Hashable`. O(1) average insert and `contains`, plus union/intersection/subtracting.
• `Dictionary<Key, Value>` — unordered key-to-value pairs with unique `Hashable` keys. O(1) average lookup.

All three are value types with copy-on-write, so passing one around is cheap until somebody mutates it.

All three also conform to Sequence and Collection, so `map`, `filter`, `reduce`, `sorted` and `first(where:)` work identically on each — which is why the right answer to "my `contains` is slow in a loop" is usually "turn the Array into a Set first".

questions.question: Explain Swift error handling: throws, try, do/catch, Result.
questions.answer:
Swift makes failure part of a function's signature: a function that can fail is marked `throws` and every caller must write `try`.

Errors are ordinary values conforming to the `Error` protocol, and an enum with associated values is the usual shape — it lets the caller `switch` on the exact failure and pull out a retry delay or a field name.

Forms of try:
• `try` — propagate the error to the caller
• `try?` — collapse to an Optional, discarding the error
• `try!` — trap on error; same risk profile as force-unwrapping

`do` / `catch` handles the error locally, and `catch` patterns can match specific cases. When you need to store an outcome rather than handle it immediately — caching, passing across a boundary, testing — use `Result<Success, Failure>`.

Typed throws (`func f() throws(AuthError)`) landed in Swift 6: the compiler then knows the exact error type, so `catch` is exhaustive and no `as?` cast is needed. Untyped `throws` is still the default and still right for most APIs, because adding a new error case to a typed throws function is a source-breaking change.

questions.question: Swift has tuples, ranges and `guard` — what problem does each one solve?
questions.answer:
Tuples, ranges and `guard` are three small features that turn up in almost every Swift file, and each one replaces something heavier.

• Tuple — a fixed-size group of typed, optionally named values. It buys you a multi-value return without declaring a struct: `func minMax(_ xs: [Int]) -> (min: Int, max: Int)?`. The moment the tuple escapes the function it was made in, or needs a method, promote it to a struct.
• Range — `0..<10` is half-open, `1...10` is closed, and one-sided forms like `2...` and `...2` slice collections. Ranges conform to Sequence, so you iterate them directly and use them as subscripts into arrays and strings.
• guard — an early exit that the compiler forces you to honour: the `else` block must leave the current scope. Unlike `if let`, the bound value stays in scope for the rest of the function, so the happy path stays flat and unindented instead of drifting right with every nested check.

The rule of thumb for `guard` versus `if let`: use `guard` when the nil case means "we're done here", and `if let` when the nil case is just another branch you want to handle.

questions.question: What is the difference between struct and class in Swift?
questions.answer:
A struct is a value type and a class is a reference type; almost every other difference follows from that one.

• struct — copied on assignment and on every function call. No inheritance. Free memberwise initializer. Methods that change stored properties must be marked `mutating`. Small ones live on the stack or inline in their container.
• class — shared by reference and counted by ARC. Supports inheritance, `deinit`, and identity comparison with `===`. Always heap-allocated.

Use struct by default. Reach for class only when you need something a value cannot provide: identity that many owners must share, inheritance, `deinit` for cleanup, or `AnyObject` conformance for Objective-C interop and `weak` references.

Concurrency has sharpened the rule. A struct of Sendable properties is Sendable for free, while a class with `var` properties is not — sharing one across tasks is a compile error under the Swift 6 language mode unless you make it an actor, make it immutable, or take a lock and claim `@unchecked Sendable`.

questions.question: What are protocols in Swift and how are they different from interfaces?
questions.answer:
A protocol declares a contract — methods, properties, associated types, initializers — that conforming types must implement.

Differences vs Java/C# interfaces:
• Both classes AND value types (struct, enum) can conform.
• Protocols can have associated types — generic-like type parameters (`associatedtype Item`).
• Protocol extensions can provide default implementations and add methods to all conformers without modifying their source.
• Existentials (`any Protocol`) are runtime-erased boxes; opaque types (`some Protocol`) are compile-time concrete.

Protocol-oriented programming (POP) is Swift's idiomatic answer to inheritance.

questions.question: Explain enums with associated values and raw values in Swift.
questions.answer:
A Swift enum is a full type that can carry data, which is why it models a closed set of alternatives far better than a set of integer constants.

• Raw values — every case maps to the same underlying primitive (Int, String, Character). The compiler synthesises `RawRepresentable`, giving you `HTTPStatus(rawValue: 404)` and `.ok.rawValue`. Note the initializer is failable, because an unknown raw value has no case.
• Associated values — each case carries its own typed payload, and different cases can carry different payloads. That is what makes an enum an algebraic data type, and it is the right shape for screen state, parser tokens, and anything with a "loading / loaded / failed" life.

A case can have raw values or associated values, never both.

Enums are value types and can carry methods, computed properties, static members and protocol conformances just like a struct. Pair them with `switch`, which the compiler checks for exhaustiveness — add a case and every switch that forgot it fails to compile, which is the whole point.

`indirect` allows recursive cases (a tree, a linked list) by boxing the payload behind a pointer.

questions.question: What are extensions in Swift and what can/can't they do?
questions.answer:
Extensions add functionality to an existing type — your own types, standard library types, even types imported from a framework — without subclassing and without touching the original source.

Can add:
• Computed properties (instance and static)
• Methods (instance, static, and `mutating`)
• Initializers (convenience initializers for classes)
• Subscripts
• Protocol conformance, including conditional conformance
• Nested types

Cannot add:
• Stored properties — there is no room for them in the original type's memory layout
• Overrides of existing methods — an extension adds, it never replaces
• A designated initializer on a class you do not own

One Swift 6 wrinkle: conforming an imported type to an imported protocol (`extension URL: Identifiable`) is a retroactive conformance, and the compiler now warns about it, because the owning module could add the same conformance later and the two would collide. Spell it `extension URL: @retroactive Identifiable` to acknowledge the risk, or wrap the type instead.

Idiomatic uses: split a large type into feature-sized chunks, conform a type you do not own to a protocol you do own, add helpers to Array and String, and keep protocol default implementations out of the protocol declaration.

questions.question: What is protocol-oriented programming and how is it different from class inheritance?
questions.answer:
Protocol-oriented programming (POP) — a Swift idiom championed at WWDC 2015 — composes behavior via small protocols and default implementations rather than deep class hierarchies.

Why POP over class inheritance:
• Works with structs and enums, not just classes
• Multiple conformance — a type can adopt many protocols, sidestepping single-inheritance
• Composition over inheritance — features added in tiny chunks (Equatable, Hashable, Identifiable) and mixed at will
• Better testability — protocols become natural mock boundaries
• No fragile-base-class problem

When to keep inheritance: deep frameworks (UIView/NSObject), Cocoa/UIKit interop, override-based template methods.

questions.question: Explain access control levels in Swift.
questions.answer:
Swift has six access levels, and a member is always capped by the visibility of the type that contains it.

From most to least visible:
• open — visible everywhere AND subclassable/overridable from another module. Classes and their members only.
• public — visible from any module, but subclassing and overriding are limited to the defining module.
• package — visible from any target in the same Swift package. Fills the gap between `internal` and `public` for multi-module packages.
• internal (the default) — visible inside the current module only.
• fileprivate — visible inside the same source file.
• private — visible inside the enclosing declaration and its extensions in the same file.

The containment rule catches people out: a `public` method on an `internal` type is effectively internal, and a `public` function cannot expose an `internal` type in its signature. Initializers default to `internal`, which is why a `public struct` from a package is not constructible from outside until you write `public init`.

Start closed and widen deliberately. `private` by default keeps the invariants of a type inside the type, and a small `public` surface is the only thing that makes a module's API reviewable.

questions.question: What are property observers and lazy properties?
questions.answer:
Swift lets a stored property carry behaviour in two ways: observers that fire around a change, and `lazy`, which defers the initializer until the first read.

• willSet / didSet — run just before and just after the value changes. `willSet` sees `newValue`, `didSet` sees `oldValue`. They only apply to stored properties, and they do NOT fire when you assign from inside the type's own initializer.
• lazy — the initializer runs on first access, not at init time. It must be a `var` (the storage is written on first read), it can refer to `self`, and it is not thread-safe: two concurrent first-reads can run the initializer twice.
• Computed property — no storage at all; the getter runs on every access and an optional setter runs on every assignment.

Pick by intent: observers for side effects on change (invalidate a layout, fire analytics), `lazy` for an expensive default you may never need, computed for a value that is always derivable from other state.

Two traps worth remembering. Observers fire on every assignment, even when the new value equals the old one, so guard with `oldValue` when the work is expensive. And a `lazy` property is a mutation, so reading one on a `let` struct instance will not compile.

questions.question: What are generics in Swift? How do where clauses work?
questions.answer:
Generics let you write one implementation that works for many types while keeping full type safety — no `Any`, no casting, no boxing.

• Generic functions — `func clamp<T: Comparable>(_ v: T, to r: ClosedRange<T>) -> T`
• Generic types — `struct Stack<Element> { private var storage: [Element] }`
• Constraints — `<T: Equatable>` requires a conformance; multiple constraints are allowed
• Parameter packs — `func log<each T>(_ values: repeat each T)` takes a variadic list of DIFFERENT types, which is what made `SwiftUI`'s `TupleView` and `Regex` output types expressible

A `where` clause is where the complicated constraints go, and it can say things the angle brackets cannot:
• Constrain an associated type: `where C.Element: Comparable`
• Require two associated types to be identical: `where C1.Element == C2.Element`
• Scope a whole extension: `extension Stack where Element: Equatable` adds `contains` only to stacks whose element is equatable — this is how conditional conformance works

Performance is the reason to prefer generics over existentials. The optimiser specialises a generic function for each concrete type it is called with, so the result is close to hand-written code; an `any Protocol` parameter dispatches through a witness table instead.

questions.question: What are opaque types (some) vs existentials (any) in Swift?
questions.answer:
Both `some` and `any` let you refer to a protocol, but `some` names one hidden concrete type while `any` is a box that can hold a different type each time.

• `some Protocol` — an opaque type. The compiler knows exactly one concrete type is behind it and just refuses to tell the caller which. Static dispatch, no boxing, no allocation. A function returning `some Shape` must return the same concrete type on every path.
• `any Protocol` — an existential. A box holding any conforming value (heap-allocated when the value does not fit inline), carrying a witness table for dynamic dispatch. Two `any Shape` values can wrap different types, which is exactly what an array of mixed shapes needs.

Rule of thumb: use `some` for return types and for parameters where the concrete type is fixed at each call site, and reach for `any` only when you genuinely need heterogeneous storage, such as `[any Shape]`.

Two things that changed and are worth knowing. Existentials gained primary associated types, so `any Collection<Int>` is expressible and useful. And in the Swift 6 language mode a bare protocol name used as a type is an error — you must write `any Shape` explicitly, which was the whole point of the syntax: the cost is now visible in the source.

questions.question: What are property wrappers in Swift?
questions.answer:
Property wrappers package storage + behavior into a reusable annotation. The compiler synthesizes the underlying storage and rewrites property access to call wrapper methods. Behind every SwiftUI `@State`, `@Published`, and `@AppStorage` is a property wrapper.

A wrapper is a struct/class/enum marked `@propertyWrapper` exposing `wrappedValue` (and optionally `projectedValue` exposed via `$`).

Use cases: persistence (@AppStorage), validation (@Clamped), lazy thread-safe init, dependency injection, debouncing, instrumentation.

One caveat on the SwiftUI examples: `@Published` and `ObservableObject` are property wrappers, but the Observation framework that replaced them for new code uses the `@Observable` MACRO instead, which rewrites the whole type rather than wrapping one property. Macros have largely taken over the jobs property wrappers were being stretched to cover.

questions.question: What are result builders (DSLs) in Swift?
questions.answer:
Result builders (originally function builders) let you write declarative DSLs in Swift. The compiler transforms a series of expressions inside a builder-tagged closure into a single composed value via `buildBlock`, `buildOptional`, `buildEither`, `buildArray`.

SwiftUI's `@ViewBuilder`, RegexBuilder, and SwiftPM's package builder are all built this way.

Benefits: readable, declarative client code; static type checking of every clause; easy authoring of testing/UI/parser DSLs.

questions.question: What are key paths in Swift?
questions.answer:
A key path is a typed, storable reference to a property that you write with a backslash and pass around like any other value.

Three forms, ordered by what they let you do:
• `KeyPath<Root, Value>` — read only
• `WritableKeyPath<Root, Value>` — read and write, on a `var` of a value type
• `ReferenceWritableKeyPath<Root, Value>` — write through a class reference, so the root can be a `let`

What they buy you:
• Generic accessors — one `sorted(by:)` or `grouped(by:)` that takes `\.age` instead of a closure per call site
• Terser call sites — `users.map(\.name)` is the same thing as `users.map { $0.name }`
• SwiftUI and Combine plumbing — `\.self` for `ForEach` identity, `.assign(to: \.value, on: object)` in Combine, and `@Environment(\.colorScheme)` all take key paths
• `@dynamicMemberLookup` with a key path subscript, which is how a wrapper type forwards `wrapper.name` to `wrapper.value.name` with full type checking

Unlike string-based KVC from Objective-C, a key path is checked at compile time: rename the property and the key path stops compiling instead of failing at runtime.

questions.question: Explain Codable in Swift and how to customize JSON encoding/decoding.
questions.answer:
Codable is just `Encodable & Decodable`, and conforming makes the compiler synthesise a symmetric encoder and decoder over your stored properties.

Customization, from cheapest to most invasive:
• A `CodingKeys` enum — rename fields, or drop one by leaving its case out
• `keyDecodingStrategy = .convertFromSnakeCase` — handle a whole snake_case payload at once
• `dateDecodingStrategy` / `dataDecodingStrategy` — pick the wire format
• A property wrapper — for a pattern that repeats across many types
• Hand-written `init(from:)` and `encode(to:)` — full control, including tagged unions with a discriminator key
• `userInfo` on the encoder or decoder — pass context such as an API version into a custom implementation

Gotchas that show up in interviews:
• `JSONEncoder`'s default date strategy is `.deferredToDate`, which writes a bare `Double` of seconds since 2001 — not ISO 8601. Set `.iso8601` explicitly on BOTH the encoder and the decoder.
• `.convertFromSnakeCase` converts incoming keys before matching, so a `CodingKeys` case whose raw value is still snake_case will never match. Use one mechanism or the other, not both.
• A missing key throws `keyNotFound` unless the property is Optional; JSON `null` for a non-optional throws `valueNotFound`. There is no implicit default — synthesise one with a custom `init(from:)`.
• Writing your own `init(from:)` switches synthesis off entirely; you then owe every property by hand.

questions.question: Explain async/await in Swift. How does it differ from completion-handler callbacks?
questions.answer:
An `async` function is one that can suspend in the middle and resume later, and `await` marks every point where that is allowed to happen.

• `async` on the declaration means the function may suspend; every caller must be async too, or start a `Task`.
• At an `await` the function gives up its thread — the runtime is free to run other work, and your code may resume on a different thread than it started on.
• `async throws` propagates errors exactly like synchronous `throws`, with the same `try` / `do` / `catch`.

Versus completion handlers:
• Linear control flow — sequential steps read as sequential code, with no nesting per step.
• Errors go through `try` / `catch` instead of a `Result` switch inside every callback.
• The compiler guarantees the continuation resumes exactly once. Forgetting to call a completion handler, or calling it twice, is a whole class of bug that stops existing.
• Cancellation, structured concurrency and actor isolation all compose with it. A callback API gets none of that.

Swift Concurrency shipped in Swift 5.5 and back-deploys to iOS 13. The part that matters today is the Swift 6 language mode, where the same suspension points are also checked for data races: values crossing an `await` must be Sendable, and the compiler proves it rather than trusting you.

questions.question: What is structured concurrency? How does Task work?
questions.answer:
Structured concurrency means every piece of concurrent work has a scope: a child task cannot outlive the function that started it, cancellation flows down the tree automatically, and the parent cannot return until all its children have finished.

• `async let x = ...` — a child task bound to the enclosing scope. It starts immediately and must be awaited (or explicitly cancelled) before the function returns.
• `withTaskGroup(of:)` / `withThrowingTaskGroup(of:)` — a dynamic number of children, consumed as they complete. Use it when the fan-out width is only known at runtime.
• `withDiscardingTaskGroup` — the same, for children whose results you throw away; it reclaims each child as it finishes instead of holding them all.

`Task { ... }` is the unstructured escape hatch: it is not a child of anything, so it survives the function that created it and you own its lifetime through the returned handle. It does inherit the actor isolation, priority and task-local values of the context that created it — `Task.detached` inherits none of those and is almost never what you want.

Cancellation is cooperative in every case. Cancelling a task sets a flag on it and its children; nothing is interrupted. Your code has to notice, either by calling `try Task.checkCancellation()`, by testing `Task.isCancelled`, or by awaiting something that checks for you — `Task.sleep` and URLSession both throw on cancellation.

questions.question: What problem do actors solve in Swift, and what is actor reentrancy?
questions.answer:
An actor is a reference type whose mutable state is isolated: only one task executes inside it at a time, so data races on that state are impossible by construction rather than by discipline.

The compiler enforces it. From outside, every access to actor state goes through `await`, because the call may have to wait for the actor to become free. Inside the actor, code runs synchronously and can touch the state directly.

Key points:
• Members are isolated by default; mark a member `nonisolated` when it touches no mutable state (a computed `id`, a `description`).
• Reading a property from outside is asynchronous too — `await counter.value`, not `counter.value`.
• `@MainActor` is a global actor that pins work to the main thread. Annotate the whole view model or view type rather than sprinkling `MainActor.run` at call sites.
• Recent toolchains ship an approachable-concurrency mode that makes MainActor the default isolation for a module, so you annotate what leaves the main actor instead of what stays on it.

Reentrancy is the sharp edge. An actor is reentrant: while one task is suspended at an `await` inside an actor method, the actor is free to start another task's call. Actor isolation protects each individual statement, not the whole method — so any invariant you established before an `await` may be false after it. The fix is to re-check state after every suspension point, or to keep an in-flight `Task` in a dictionary so a second caller joins the first request instead of starting a duplicate.

questions.question: What is AsyncSequence and AsyncStream?
questions.answer:
AsyncSequence is the asynchronous counterpart of Sequence: elements arrive over time and you consume them with `for await element in sequence`, or `for try await` when the sequence can fail.

`AsyncStream<T>` and `AsyncThrowingStream<T, Error>` are the concrete implementations you use to turn a push-based API into one. You get a continuation, hold onto it, and `yield` from wherever the values actually come from — a delegate callback, a NotificationCenter observer, a timer, a C callback.

`AsyncStream.makeStream(of:)` returns the stream and its continuation as a tuple, which is the modern way to build one; the older trailing-closure initializer forces an implicitly-unwrapped optional dance to get the continuation out.

Things to get right:
• Call `continuation.finish()` when the source is done, or the consuming `for await` never ends.
• Set `onTermination` to tear down the underlying source when the consumer goes away or the task is cancelled.
• Choose a buffering policy. The default is unbounded, which quietly grows without limit if the producer outruns the consumer; `.bufferingNewest(1)` is usually what you want for UI state.
• An AsyncStream has a single consumer. If two places need the values, hand out a broadcast type or an `AsyncChannel`, do not iterate the same stream twice.

Compared with Combine: AsyncSequence covers the emit-over-time case with less machinery and composes with cancellation and actors for free, but Combine still has the richer operator set for merging and combining many publishers.

questions.question: What is Sendable, and how does Swift enforce data-race safety?
questions.answer:
`Sendable` is a marker protocol that says a value is safe to hand from one concurrency domain to another, and the compiler checks it at every boundary crossing.

Sendable is inferred for free:
• Value types whose stored properties are all Sendable (struct, enum)
• Final classes with only `let` stored properties of Sendable type
• Actors, whose state is isolated by definition

Not Sendable:
• A class with `var` stored properties — unless you serialise access yourself and declare `@unchecked Sendable`
• Closures, unless marked `@Sendable`; a closure passed to `Task.detached` must be one

How the enforcement actually works today:
• The Swift 6 language mode makes these diagnostics errors rather than warnings, so data-race safety is a compile-time property of the module, not a review checklist.
• Region-based isolation softens the rule usefully: a non-Sendable value CAN be passed to another actor as long as the compiler can prove the sender never touches it again. The `sending` parameter modifier is how an API spells that promise.
• Global `var`s are the most common first error when you turn the mode on. The fixes, in order of preference: make it a `let`, move it into an actor, or mark it `nonisolated(unsafe)` if you have audited the synchronisation yourself.
• For state that must be shared and mutable, prefer `Mutex` from the Synchronization module over `NSLock` plus `@unchecked Sendable` — it is Sendable on its own and keeps the value it guards genuinely unreachable without the lock.

questions.question: How do you cancel async work in Swift?
questions.answer:
Cancellation in Swift Concurrency is cooperative — the task you cancel is asked to stop, and the code inside has to honor the request.

Mechanisms:
• `task.cancel()` — sets `Task.isCancelled = true` for the task tree.
• `try Task.checkCancellation()` — throws CancellationError if cancelled.
• `if Task.isCancelled { return }` — silent bail.
• Built-in awaitables (URLSession.data, sleep, TaskGroup) honor cancellation automatically.
• `withTaskCancellationHandler { … } onCancel: { … }` — register a synchronous cleanup hook.

A common pattern is store the current task in your view model, then `cancel()` it when the user types a new query / leaves the screen.

questions.question: What is SwiftUI and how does it differ from UIKit?
questions.answer:
SwiftUI is Apple's declarative UI framework, introduced in iOS 13 (2019). You describe what the UI should look like for a given state; the framework diffs and applies changes.

Key differences vs UIKit:
• Declarative — `var body: some View` returns a view tree; UIKit was imperative (build, then mutate UIViews).
• Single source of truth — state drives rendering; SwiftUI invalidates and re-runs `body` when state changes.
• Composition — small views combine into bigger ones; modifiers are values that transform a view.
• Cross-platform — same code runs on iOS, iPadOS, macOS, watchOS, tvOS, visionOS.
• View is a value type (struct), recreated cheaply on every body invocation. UIView was a reference type.

questions.question: Explain stack containers in SwiftUI: VStack, HStack, ZStack, LazyVStack/HStack.
questions.answer:
Stacks are how SwiftUI lays out children along an axis, and picking one is mostly a question of direction plus whether the content is long enough to need laziness.

• VStack — children top to bottom. Takes `alignment` (horizontal) and `spacing`.
• HStack — children left to right. Takes `alignment` (vertical) and `spacing`.
• ZStack — children back to front along the Z axis, aligned to a single `alignment` point.
• LazyVStack / LazyHStack — same layout, but children are only created as they approach the viewport. They belong inside a ScrollView; on their own they have no scrolling.
• Grid — a real two-dimensional layout with `GridRow`, where columns line up across rows. LazyVGrid and LazyHGrid are the scrolling, item-count-driven alternatives.

A non-lazy stack sizes itself by asking every child, so a VStack of 10,000 rows builds 10,000 views before the first one appears. That is the whole reason the lazy variants exist — and also why a LazyVStack cannot centre its content, since it does not know its own height yet.

`Spacer()` is a low-priority flexible view that pushes siblings apart, and layout priority breaks ties when the parent cannot satisfy everyone. When stacks stop being enough, the `Layout` protocol lets you write a custom container, and `ViewThatFits` picks the first child that fits.

questions.question: How do view modifiers work in SwiftUI?
questions.answer:
A modifier is a method on View that returns a new view wrapping the original with extra behavior (padding, background, foreground, gesture). Modifiers compose left-to-right; order matters.

Key points:
• Each modifier returns `some View` — the result is a new struct, not a mutated view.
• Order changes layout: `.padding().background(.red)` differs from `.background(.red).padding()` — the former adds red around content+padding, the latter pads then puts red behind only content.
• Custom modifiers via `ViewModifier` protocol or extension on View.
• Some modifiers are environment-aware (e.g. `.font` reads from environment).

questions.question: How does navigation work in SwiftUI? NavigationStack and NavigationSplitView.
questions.answer:
SwiftUI navigation is state-driven: you push by appending a value to a path, not by calling a method on a navigation controller.

• NavigationStack — push and pop navigation. `NavigationStack(path: $path)` binds either a typed array of route values or a `NavigationPath` for heterogeneous routes. Appending pushes, removing pops, `path.removeAll()` pops to root.
• NavigationSplitView — two- or three-column sidebar / content / detail layout for iPad, Mac and visionOS, which collapses to a plain stack automatically on iPhone.
• `.navigationDestination(for:)` registers a route type, and `NavigationLink(value:)` supplies a value of that type. The two are matched by type, which is what decouples the link from the destination.

`NavigationView` and `NavigationLink(destination:)` have been deprecated since iOS 16 and should not appear in new code.

Two things that bite people:
• `.navigationDestination` must be inside the stack's content and must not be inside a lazy container — put it on the List, not on a row, or the modifier is never registered and the push silently does nothing.
• Because the path is just data, deep linking and state restoration are ordinary array operations. Decode a URL into `[Route]`, assign it, and the whole stack appears — no imperative sequence of pushes, and no timing bugs.

questions.question: How do you build a List in SwiftUI, and why does row identity matter?
questions.answer:
A List gives you a scrolling, platform-styled container with separators, selection, swipe actions and pull-to-refresh for the cost of one view, and `ForEach` fills it from a collection.

The pieces:
• List — the container. `.listStyle(.plain / .insetGrouped / .sidebar)` picks the look.
• ForEach — generates one view per element. Works inside List, VStack and LazyVStack alike.
• Section — groups rows under an optional header and footer.
• Row-level modifiers — `.swipeActions(edge:)`, `.listRowSeparator`, `.listRowBackground`, `.contextMenu`.
• List-level modifiers — `.searchable(text:)`, `.refreshable { await ... }`, `.moveDisabled`, and `List(selection:)` for single or multiple selection.

Identity is the part people get wrong. SwiftUI diffs the old and new element lists by identity, and that identity decides which view keeps its state, which row animates from where, and whether the scroll position survives a reload. Conform your model to `Identifiable` with a stable id from your data — a database id or a UUID stored on the model.

The classic bug is `ForEach(items, id: \.self)` on a value type, or an `id` derived from the array index. Both make identity change whenever the content or the order changes, so rows lose their state, animations jump, and in-flight edits get reattached to the wrong row.

For a very long list, prefer `List` over `ScrollView` + `LazyVStack`: List already reuses rows, whereas a LazyVStack creates every row it has scrolled past and keeps it.

questions.question: How do you write SwiftUI previews for a view with several states or a service dependency?
questions.answer:
Previews render a view inside Xcode without launching the app, which turns the iteration loop from a build-and-navigate into a couple of seconds.

The API is the `#Preview` macro; `PreviewProvider` is the older form you will still meet in existing code. Add `@Previewable` to a `@State` declaration inside a `#Preview` when the view needs a live binding to drive.

How to make previews earn their keep:
• One preview per state that has its own layout risk — loading, empty, error, one item, many items, longest realistic string.
• Cover the environment axes that break layouts: `.preferredColorScheme(.dark)`, `.environment(\.dynamicTypeSize, .accessibility1)`, `.environment(\.layoutDirection, .rightToLeft)`.
• Keep sample data in a factory next to the model (`User.preview`) rather than inlining a fixture in every preview.
• Inject a fake service so the preview never touches the network. For an `@Observable` dependency that means `.environment(MockService())`; for a legacy `ObservableObject` it is still `.environmentObject(...)`.
• Give each preview a name (`#Preview("Empty state")`) — the names are how you navigate the canvas once there are six of them.

A preview that cannot be created without a network call, a database, or a logged-in session is telling you the view knows too much. Push the dependency out behind a protocol and the preview becomes trivial — which is why previews are a design pressure, not just a viewer.

questions.question: Explain @State and @Binding in SwiftUI.
@StateObject vs @ObservedObject: what breaks if you pick the wrong one?
questions.answer:
Both wrappers observe an `ObservableObject`, and the difference is ownership: @StateObject keeps the object alive across body re-evaluations, @ObservedObject does not.

• @StateObject — the view OWNS the object. SwiftUI instantiates it once and keeps it alive for the whole lifetime of that view. Use it in the view that creates the model.
• @ObservedObject — the view OBSERVES an object owned elsewhere. SwiftUI does not keep it alive, so if you instantiate the object inline it is recreated on every re-render.

That recreation is the bug interviewers are fishing for, and it is silent: a spinner that never stops, a form that clears itself mid-typing, a counter that snaps back to zero whenever an unrelated parent redraws.

For new code this pair is largely historical. With the Observation framework you mark the model `@Observable`, own it with a plain `@State`, and pass it to children as an ordinary `let` — no wrapper on the child at all. Know @StateObject and @ObservedObject anyway: they are everywhere in existing code and in anything that back-deploys below iOS 17.

questions.question: How do you pass shared state down a SwiftUI tree without prop-drilling?
questions.answer:
SwiftUI's environment is a dependency-injection channel scoped to a view subtree: you inject once near the root and any descendant reads it directly.

• Observation era — `.environment(session)` injects an `@Observable` object and the descendant reads it with `@Environment(AppSession.self) private var session`. This is the form for new code.
• ObservableObject era — `.environmentObject(session)` plus `@EnvironmentObject private var session: AppSession`. Still everywhere in existing codebases.
• Value types — declare the key on `EnvironmentValues` (the `@Entry` macro writes the boilerplate for you), then inject with `.environment(\.theme, .dark)` and read with `@Environment(\.theme)`.

Reach for it for genuinely cross-cutting state: the signed-in user, theme, feature flags, a navigation router. When only one child needs a value, pass it through the initializer instead — the environment hides the dependency from the type's signature, so it also hides it from whoever refactors next.

Both object forms trap at runtime if you forget to inject, and the crash happens deep in the descendant, far from the mistake.

questions.question: What does the @Observable macro change compared with ObservableObject and @Published?
questions.answer:
The Observation framework makes every stored property of a class observable and narrows re-rendering to the properties a view actually read.

• Mark the class `@Observable` — the macro rewrites its stored properties into tracked ones. No `@Published`, no `objectWillChange`, no conformance to write.
• The owning view holds it with a plain `@State var vm = FeedVM()`; child views take it as an ordinary `let`, with no wrapper of their own.
• Tracking is per-property: a view that reads only `vm.title` does not re-render when `vm.items` changes. With ObservableObject, any `@Published` write refreshed every observing view.
• `@Bindable` projects a two-way Binding out of an Observable's property when a TextField or Toggle needs one.
• It is not SwiftUI-only — `withObservationTracking(_:onChange:)` gives the same tracking in plain Swift, which is how UIKit code can observe the same models.

It shipped in iOS 17 and is the default for new SwiftUI code; ObservableObject stays only for targets that back-deploy further.

questions.question: What makes SwiftUI re-run a view's body, and when does its @State get thrown away?
questions.answer:
SwiftUI re-runs `body` when a dependency that view read has changed, and it throws the view's state away when the view's identity changes.

• Identity — how SwiftUI tells views apart across body re-evaluations. Two flavours: structural (position in the view tree) and explicit (`.id(...)`, `Identifiable` in a ForEach). Same identity means the same view; a different identity means teardown plus a brand-new lifetime.

• Lifetime — the span from a view's creation to its removal. @State, @StateObject and running `.task` work are all bound to lifetime, so a change of identity resets state and restarts tasks.

• Dependencies — everything the view read while producing `body`: state, bindings, environment values, observed properties. Changing one invalidates exactly the views that read it, which is why `@Observable` re-renders less than ObservableObject did.

The gotcha: moving a view structurally — wrapping it in an `if`, reordering a stack, switching branches of a conditional — changes its identity and silently resets its state. Use `.id(stableValue)` when you want that reset, and keep the id stable when you do not.

questions.question: Which SwiftUI modifiers run async work in a view, and what happens to that work when the view disappears?
questions.answer:
Two modifiers tie a SwiftUI view to Swift Concurrency, and both scope the async work to the view's lifetime instead of to a Task you manage by hand.

• `.task { await ... }` — starts when the view appears and is cancelled automatically when it disappears. `.task(id: value)` cancels and restarts whenever `value` changes, which is how you reload for a new item id.
• `.refreshable { await ... }` — wires pull-to-refresh into a List or ScrollView; the system keeps the spinner up until your async closure returns.
• `.onAppear` takes a synchronous closure, so a bare `Task { }` started there is unstructured and nothing cancels it when the view goes away.
