Cancellation is cooperative. URLSession's async methods, `Task.sleep` and task groups all honour it, but a tight compute loop has to check `Task.isCancelled` itself.

Keep the work on an `@Observable` model with async methods and let the view bind to its loading and error state; the logic then stays testable without instantiating a view.

questions.question: What is UIKit? How does it relate to SwiftUI in modern iOS apps?
questions.answer:
UIKit is Apple's imperative UI framework for iOS, iPadOS, tvOS and Catalyst — it has powered every iOS app since 2008. Core types include UIView, UIViewController, UIWindow, UINavigationController, UITableView, UICollectionView.

In modern apps:
• Greenfield iOS apps often start with SwiftUI; UIKit is reached for when SwiftUI lacks features (custom transitions, certain gestures, complex collections).
• You can mix the two: UIHostingController hosts SwiftUI inside UIKit; UIViewRepresentable / UIViewControllerRepresentable hosts UIKit inside SwiftUI.
• UIKit still backs all third-party iOS code shipped before iOS 13 and remains the default in many enterprise codebases.

questions.question: Walk through the UIViewController lifecycle: which callbacks fire once and which fire on every appearance?
questions.answer:
Only `viewDidLoad` fires once per controller instance; the appear and disappear callbacks fire again every single time the screen comes back.

• `init(nibName:bundle:)` / `init(coder:)` — the controller exists, its view does not. Touching `view` here forces it to load early.
• `loadView()` — the root view is being created. Override only when you build the hierarchy in code and want to replace the root view outright; never call `super` there if you assign your own.
• `viewDidLoad()` — the view is in memory. One-time setup: subviews, constraints, cell registration, delegates.
• `viewWillAppear(_:)` — about to become visible, on every appearance. Refresh data that may have changed while you were away, add observers.
• `viewDidAppear(_:)` — on screen and the transition is finished. Start animations, fire the screen-view analytics event, kick off work you deferred.
• `viewWillDisappear(_:)` / `viewDidDisappear(_:)` — leaving. Save drafts, pause timers and video, remove observers you added on appear.
• `viewWillLayoutSubviews()` / `viewDidLayoutSubviews()` — the layout pass. These run many times per appearance, so keep them cheap and idempotent.
• `deinit` — deallocated. Invalidate timers and cancel long-running tasks.

The follow-up interviewers reach for: heavy work in `viewWillAppear` stutters the push animation, because the transition has not started yet. Move it to `viewDidAppear` or into a cancellable task.

questions.question: What is the difference between frame and bounds in UIView?
questions.answer:
A view's frame is measured in its superview's coordinate system, its bounds is the view's own coordinate system, and that difference is exactly what makes scrolling work.

• `frame` — where I sit inside my superview and how big I am.
• `bounds` — my internal coordinate space. The origin is normally (0,0) and the size matches the view. Moving `bounds.origin` changes which part of myself is on screen, which is how UIScrollView scrolls: `contentOffset` is `bounds.origin`.
• `center` — my midpoint in superview coordinates. Setting it moves the frame and leaves bounds untouched.

Once the view carries a non-identity `transform` — rotation, scale — `frame` is only the axis-aligned bounding box of the transformed view, so setting it is meaningless. Position with `center`, size with `bounds`, and rotate or scale with `transform`.

A subview's frame is expressed in its parent's bounds, so changing the parent's `bounds.origin` moves every child on screen without touching a single child frame.

questions.question: When the user taps the screen, how does UIKit decide which view receives the touch?
questions.answer:
Every touch is resolved in two passes: UIKit first hit-tests to find the view under the finger, then delivers the event up the responder chain starting from that view.

1. Hit-testing — beginning at the window, UIKit calls `hitTest(_:with:)` recursively; each view answers `point(inside:with:)` and the deepest subview containing the point wins. Views that are hidden, have an alpha below 0.01, or have `isUserInteractionEnabled == false` are skipped entirely, and hit-testing never escapes a superview's bounds — which is why a button poking outside its parent is untappable.
2. Delivery — `touchesBegan/Moved/Ended/Cancelled` is sent to the hit view. If it does not implement them, or implements them and calls `super`, the event walks up the responder chain: view → superview → … → view controller → its parent controller → window → application.

Gesture recognizers attached to the hit view or to any ancestor see the touches first and can cancel delivery to the view, which is why adding a plain tap recognizer to a container quietly breaks a table view's row selection underneath.

`UIResponder` is the shared superclass of UIView, UIViewController, UIWindow and UIApplication, so the same chain also carries motion events, key commands and target-less `sendAction` calls. First responder status is a separate idea: it names the responder that receives keyboard input, not the one that received the touch.

questions.question: How do UITableView and UICollectionView work? What is reuse?
questions.answer:
Both are scroll-based containers backed by a data source and a delegate.

• Data source supplies cells (and, for collections, supplementary views) for index paths.
• Delegate notifies about selection, sizing, scroll, etc.
• Cell reuse — instead of creating thousands of cells, the view recycles offscreen cells via `dequeueReusableCell(withIdentifier:for:)`. Cells must implement `prepareForReuse()` to wipe state.
• Modern API: UITableViewDiffableDataSource / UICollectionViewDiffableDataSource — declare snapshots of (Section, Item), the framework computes the diff and animates inserts/deletes/moves automatically.
• Compositional layout (UICollectionViewCompositionalLayout) — describe complex grids/lists as composable sections.

questions.question: What is the difference between Storyboards, XIBs, and programmatic UIs?
questions.answer:
Storyboards, XIBs and code are three ways to build the same UIKit screen, and they differ mainly in how well they survive a team, a merge and a refactor.

• Storyboards — a visual editor for whole flows, with segues between scenes. Fast to prototype and easy to show a designer; painful to merge because the XML is machine-generated, slow to open once large, and a lot of behaviour hides in inspector checkboxes that no code review will ever catch.
• XIBs — one view or one screen per nib. The same visual benefit with a much smaller blast radius, and a reasonable fit for reusable custom views.
• Programmatic — the view tree built in Swift. Reviewable diffs, easy to parameterise and refactor, no runtime string identifiers; more typing, and no canvas unless you wrap the view in a SwiftUI `#Preview`.

Teams of any size have largely converged on programmatic UIKit or SwiftUI for new screens. Storyboards survive mostly as the launch screen, and even that is now better expressed as the `UILaunchScreen` dictionary in Info.plist.

The signal an interviewer is listening for is the merge argument, not a stylistic preference.

questions.question: What is Auto Layout? How is it different from frame-based layout?
questions.answer:
Auto Layout is a constraint-based layout engine. You declare relationships between views (e.g. "top of A is 16pt below bottom of B") and the system solves them every layout pass to compute concrete frames.

Vs frame-based:
• Adapts to size classes, dynamic type, rotation, multitasking, RTL.
• Same code works across devices — no per-screen frame math.
• Slower than raw frames at extreme scale (10k+ views), but plenty fast for normal apps.

Three constraint APIs from Apple:
• NSLayoutConstraint(item:...) — verbose, original.
• NSLayoutAnchor — fluent, type-safe (modern recommended).
• UIStackView — composes flow layouts without explicit constraints.

Third-party DSLs (SnapKit, PinLayout) add more sugar but anchors usually suffice.

questions.question: What is intrinsic content size? How does it relate to compression resistance and hugging?
questions.answer:
A view's intrinsic content size is the size it wants to be based on its own content — a label sized to its text, a button to its title plus insets.

Auto Layout treats it as a pair of default width and height constraints, and two priorities decide who yields when the row is too narrow:

• Content hugging — resistance to growing larger than the intrinsic size. Higher means the view stays small.
• Compression resistance — resistance to shrinking below the intrinsic size. Higher means the view stays large.

Defaults are 250 for hugging and 750 for compression resistance, identical on every view, which is why two labels sharing a row produce an ambiguous layout until you break the tie. Give the title a lower compression resistance than the badge and the title truncates while the badge keeps its full width.

A custom view joins in by overriding `intrinsicContentSize`, and it must call `invalidateIntrinsicContentSize()` whenever its content changes — otherwise Auto Layout keeps solving against the stale measurement.

questions.question: Why reach for UIStackView instead of writing constraints between siblings?
questions.answer:
UIStackView generates the constraints between its arranged subviews for you: you set an axis, a distribution and an alignment, then constrain only the stack itself.

Key properties:
• axis — .horizontal / .vertical
• distribution — .fill, .fillEqually, .fillProportionally, .equalSpacing, .equalCentering
• alignment — .leading, .center, .trailing, .fill (the perpendicular axis)
• spacing — a fixed gap, or `setCustomSpacing(_:after:)` for one child

The property that earns its keep is `isHidden` on a child: the stack removes the slot and closes the gap, with no constraint of your own to activate or deactivate. Doing that by hand means toggling constraints and is where most "unable to satisfy" logs come from.

Nesting stacks models most screens cleanly — it is the same idea as flexbox in CSS or Column/Row in Compose. The cost is a deeper view hierarchy, so for very large scrolling grids a compositional collection view layout beats stacks inside cells.

questions.question: What is the safe area? How do you handle it in UIKit?
questions.answer:
Safe area is the region of the screen NOT covered by system UI: status bar, navigation bar, tab bar, home indicator, and notches/cutouts on modern iPhones. Anchoring content to the safe area keeps it visible regardless of device.

• `view.safeAreaLayoutGuide` — UILayoutGuide whose anchors describe the safe area for that view.
• `view.safeAreaInsets` — the inset values (top/leading/bottom/trailing).
• Override `safeAreaInsetsDidChange()` to react.
• Use `additionalSafeAreaInsets` on a UIViewController to push your content past a custom overlay (e.g. a floating banner).

questions.question: How do you debug Auto Layout issues like 'unable to satisfy constraints'?
questions.answer:
When Auto Layout can't find a valid solution it prints a long diagnostic and breaks one constraint. To investigate:

• Read the diagnostic — it lists every involved constraint, with addresses; pause the running app and `po` each constraint to find the offender.
• Identifier — set `constraint.identifier = "contentBottom"` so the log names them.
• Symbolic breakpoint on `UIViewAlertForUnsatisfiableConstraints` — the debugger pauses at the very moment the conflict is detected.
• View Debugger (Xcode → Debug → View Debugging → Capture View Hierarchy) — visualize the tree, inspect constraints, see ambiguous frames in red.
• `view.hasAmbiguousLayout` and `view.exerciseAmbiguityInLayout()` — toggle ambiguous views to spot which one floats.
• Set lower priority (e.g. 999) on optional constraints to mark which one is allowed to break.

questions.question: What is the difference between layoutIfNeeded, setNeedsLayout, and layoutSubviews?
questions.answer:
`setNeedsLayout` schedules a layout pass, `layoutIfNeeded` runs one immediately, and `layoutSubviews` is the callback UIKit invokes during that pass — you call the first two and override the third.

• `setNeedsLayout()` — marks the view dirty and returns straight away; UIKit lays it out before the next frame is drawn. Cheap, and safe to call repeatedly.
• `layoutIfNeeded()` — forces the pending layout to happen now, synchronously, for the view and its subtree. Use it only when you need the new frames in this turn of the run loop.
• `layoutSubviews()` — never call it directly. Override it for what Auto Layout cannot express: a CAGradientLayer's frame, a mask path, a corner radius derived from the final height.

The standard animation recipe: change the constraint constants, then call `layoutIfNeeded()` inside a `UIView.animate` block so UIKit interpolates between the old and new layouts instead of snapping to the new one.

The matching pair for drawing is `setNeedsDisplay()` and `draw(_:)`; layout and drawing are separate passes, and calling the layout methods will not redraw anything.

questions.question: Compare MVC, MVVM, VIPER, and TCA on iOS.
questions.answer:
Every iOS architecture is a different answer to one question: where does the logic that is not view code live?

• MVC — Apple's default, and in practice Massive View Controller. The UIViewController owns the views, the state and the business logic. Fine for one screen, untestable at scale.
• MVVM — presentation logic moves into a ViewModel that publishes observable state, and the view binds to it. Today's SwiftUI pairing is an `@Observable` model owned by `@State`. Testable, but it says nothing about navigation.
• VIPER — View, Interactor, Presenter, Entity, Router. Maximum separation, maximum boilerplate; still alive in large UIKit enterprise codebases.
• Clean Swift (VIP) — a unidirectional View → Interactor → Presenter cycle inspired by Clean Architecture. Same trade-off as VIPER, less common now.
• Coordinators — not a whole architecture but a bolt-on: navigation moves out of view controllers into Coordinator objects, so screens stay reusable and deep links have one owner.
• TCA (The Composable Architecture) — Point-Free's Redux-flavoured library: State, Action, Reducer, Effect, Store. Composable features, exhaustive tests, controlled dependencies; a real learning curve and a hard dependency on someone else's library.

There is no winner. Choose on team size, on how much of the logic you need under test, and on whether the codebase is SwiftUI or UIKit. The answer an interviewer wants names the trade-off rather than a favourite.

questions.question: How do you avoid 'Massive View Controller' in UIKit?
questions.answer:
A view controller should orchestrate, not implement: everything that is not wiring — presentation logic, data sources, navigation, networking — belongs in a collaborator you can test on its own.

• ViewModel — presentation logic and screen state. The controller binds to it and forwards user events, nothing more.
• Separate data source objects — move the `UITableViewDataSource` or diffable data source configuration into its own type.
• Coordinators — take navigation and presentation out, so the controller never knows what screen comes next.
• Service layer — networking and persistence behind injected protocols instead of singletons called inline.
• Child view controllers — compose a big screen from small ones with `addChild` / `view.addSubview` / `didMove(toParent:)`.
• Constructor injection — pass collaborators through `init` so tests can substitute fakes without a framework.

Rule of thumb: a 200-line view controller is fine, a 2000-line one is a smell. The reliable give-away is a controller that imports your networking module.

The point is not line count, it is that the interesting logic should be reachable from a unit test without instantiating a view.

questions.question: What is the Coordinator pattern? When is it worth using?
questions.answer:
A Coordinator is an object responsible for navigation. View controllers (or SwiftUI views) ask the coordinator to navigate; they never push/present each other directly.

Benefits:
• VC reuse — same VC can be used in different flows because flow lives in the coordinator.
• Easier deep linking — coordinator owns the full path.
• Easier testing — VC tests don't have to mock UINavigationController.
• Clear flow boundaries — login flow, onboarding flow, checkout flow each have their own coordinator.

Worth it for medium+ apps with multiple flows. Overkill for small 2-screen apps. SwiftUI alternatives: NavigationStack with typed routes serves the same role.

questions.question: How would you inject dependencies into a view model so it can be unit-tested?
questions.answer:
Constructor injection is the default answer on iOS: declare collaborators as protocols, take them in `init`, and let a composition root at the app entry point decide which implementations are used.

• Constructor injection — the most explicit and the most testable; a test passes fakes with no framework involved.
• Property injection — set after `init`. The escape hatch for objects you do not construct yourself, such as storyboard-instantiated view controllers.
• Method injection — hand the dependency to the single call that needs it.
• Environment (SwiftUI) — `.environment(...)` injects down the view tree. Convenient for cross-cutting services, but the dependency vanishes from the type's signature.
• DI containers such as Swinject, Factory or Needle — register and resolve by type. They hide the wiring, which is both the point and the risk: a missing registration becomes a runtime crash instead of a compile error.

Prefer constructor injection plus a small composition root in `App` or `AppDelegate`. Reach for a container only when the wiring itself becomes the pain — many services, deep graphs, per-feature scopes.

Whatever you choose, depend on a protocol rather than a concrete type, and never let a view model call a singleton directly; that is the thing that makes it untestable.

questions.question: What is The Composable Architecture (TCA) and what problems does it solve?
questions.answer:
TCA is a Redux-style library from Point-Free that models a feature as data: state in a struct, every event in an Action enum, and a pure reducer that turns one into the other.

• State — a single `Equatable` struct describing everything the screen shows.
• Action — an enum of every event, from user taps to responses coming back.
• Reducer — a pure function that mutates state and returns an `Effect`; no networking happens inside it.
• Effect — async work, wrapped so it can be cancelled and, in tests, replaced.
• Store — holds the state, receives actions, runs the effects.

What it buys you:
• One source of truth per feature, and features compose into larger features through reducer combinators.
• `TestStore` replays every action and fails the test if any state change or in-flight effect is unaccounted for — the strictest testing story of any iOS architecture.
• Dependencies are declared with `@Dependency` and overridden per test, so there is no ambient singleton to reset between cases.

The cost is real: a sizeable library to learn and keep updated, more indirection than MVVM for a simple screen, and boilerplate that the `@Reducer` and `@ObservableState` macros reduce without removing.

questions.question: How do you organize a large iOS codebase? Modules, frameworks, SPM packages.
questions.answer:
Split the app into local Swift Package modules and keep the app target a thin shell that only wires them together.

• Local SPM packages — a `Package.swift` per feature, referenced by path. Each module builds independently, so incremental builds parallelise and `public` becomes a real API boundary. This is the default today.
• Xcode frameworks — the pre-SPM way. Still everywhere in older projects; slower to build and clumsier to depend on.
• XCFrameworks — prebuilt binaries, for distributing an SDK or vending code you cannot ship as source.

A layout that scales:
• `App/` — entry point and composition root, and nothing else.
• `Features/Feed`, `Features/Profile`, `Features/Search` — one module per feature, each with its own tests.
• `Core/Networking`, `Core/Persistence`, `Core/Logging` — cross-cutting infrastructure.
• `DesignSystem` — shared components, colours, typography.

Two rules keep it healthy: features depend on Core and DesignSystem but never on each other, and anything two features need moves down into Core rather than sideways. Cross-feature imports are how a modular project quietly turns back into one module.

The payoff is build time and blast radius — a change inside a feature recompiles that feature, and a module you can build alone is a module you can test alone.

questions.question: What is URLSession and how do you make a GET request with async/await?
questions.answer:
URLSession is Apple's HTTP stack, and since Swift Concurrency arrived the everyday API is a pair of async methods that return `(Data, URLResponse)` and throw on failure.

• `data(from: url)` — a plain GET.
• `data(for: request)` — full control over method, headers and body.
• A session you configure yourself when you need timeouts, a cache policy, default headers or a delegate; `URLSession.shared` is fine for simple cases.

Two things the API deliberately does not do for you. A 404 or a 500 is a successful request, not a thrown error, so you have to cast the response to `HTTPURLResponse` and check `statusCode` yourself. And decoding is a separate step with `JSONDecoder`, which throws its own errors you should not merge with transport errors.

The old `dataTask(with:completionHandler:)` callbacks still exist and still work, but new code should not use them: they sit outside structured concurrency, so task cancellation never reaches them and every call site turns back into a completion-handler pyramid.

questions.question: How do you build a typed APIClient layer in Swift?
questions.answer:
A reusable APIClient handles common concerns once: base URL, auth headers, retries, decoding, error mapping. Typical building blocks:

• Endpoint type — describes path, method, query, body. Often a protocol or struct.
• Client — takes Endpoint, executes URLRequest, decodes response.
• Request modifiers — interceptors (auth token, request id, log).
• Error type — typed `APIError` enum (network, decoding, status, server-message).

Keep the client untyped on body/response (Data) and let strongly-typed wrappers decode. Test by injecting a `protocol Networking` so you can swap a fake.

questions.question: How do you cancel network requests and handle timeouts in Swift?
questions.answer:
Cancellation and timeouts are separate mechanisms in Swift, and a solid client uses both: cancellation stops work you no longer want, timeouts stop work that is never coming back.

• Task cancellation — `task.cancel()` propagates into the underlying URLSessionTask; the async methods throw `CancellationError` or `URLError(.cancelled)` and the transfer stops. Structured children are cancelled with their parent, and `.task` on a SwiftUI view cancels when the view disappears.
• Per-request timeout — `URLRequest.timeoutInterval`, or on the session configuration `timeoutIntervalForRequest` (the gap allowed between bytes) and `timeoutIntervalForResource` (the ceiling for the whole transfer).
• A manual deadline — race the work against a sleeping task inside `withThrowingTaskGroup` when the API you are calling has no timeout of its own.

Two things that catch people out. Cancellation is cooperative, so a tight compute loop has to check `Task.isCancelled` itself. And a cancelled request is not a failure the user should see, which is why the catch block must separate `CancellationError` from real errors before showing an alert.

Debounce plus cancel-previous is the standard typeahead pattern: every keystroke cancels the in-flight task and starts a new one after a short sleep, so only the last query reaches the network.

questions.question: How do you handle authentication tokens and automatic refresh?
questions.answer:
One auth interceptor in the API client attaches the bearer token to every request and, on a 401, refreshes once and retries — no call site should ever know that tokens exist.

• Store the access and refresh tokens in the Keychain, never in UserDefaults.
• The refresh call itself must bypass the interceptor, or a failing refresh will 401 and trigger another refresh forever.
• Refresh must be concurrency-safe: five requests failing at once should share one refresh, not fire five. An `actor` holding the in-flight refresh `Task` is the idiomatic Swift answer, and it is usually the point of the question.
• Retry exactly once. If the refresh itself fails, clear the Keychain and route to login.
• Do not blindly replay non-idempotent requests — a POST that already reached the server should not be sent twice.

URLSession's authentication challenge delegate covers HTTP Basic and Digest, but for bearer-token APIs an interceptor in your own client is simpler, easier to test, and the only place that can coordinate a shared refresh.

questions.question: How do you upload a file as multipart/form-data with URLSession?
questions.answer:
URLSession has no multipart builder, so you assemble the body yourself: a unique boundary string, one part per field carrying its own Content-Disposition header, and a closing boundary that ends in two extra dashes.

• `upload(for:from:)` — the async method for a body you already hold in memory; it returns `(Data, URLResponse)` just like `data(for:)`.
• `upload(for:fromFile:)` — streams from disk instead of loading the file into memory, which is what you want for anything camera-sized.
• Set the request's Content-Type to `multipart/form-data; boundary=<your boundary>`, and use CRLF line endings inside the body — a bare newline is rejected by many servers.
• For progress, pass a `URLSessionTaskDelegate` to the async upload call and implement `didSendBodyData`.
• For an upload that must survive the app being suspended, build the session from `URLSessionConfiguration.background(withIdentifier:)`. Background sessions accept file-based uploads only, never in-memory Data, and completion arrives through the delegate after relaunch.

Hand-built bodies fail in exactly two places: a missing CRLF before the closing boundary, and holding a large file in Data on a memory-tight device.

questions.question: How do you implement certificate pinning in iOS?
questions.answer:
Certificate pinning hardens TLS by trusting only specific server certificates / public keys, defending against MITM with rogue CAs.

• Pin the leaf or intermediate certificate (rotate when server rotates).
• Pin the public key (rotation-friendly — only when the team rotates the keypair).
• App Transport Security (ATS) provides pinning via `NSPinnedDomains` plist (iOS 14+).
• Manual: implement `urlSession(_:didReceive:completionHandler:)` and validate the server trust against a bundled certificate hash.
• Always plan for rotation — bundle multiple pins, ship a kill-switch, keep an out-of-band update path.

questions.question: What are the persistence options on iOS and when do you choose each?
questions.answer:
iOS gives you a ladder of storage options and the answer is always the lightest one that fits: preferences in UserDefaults, secrets in the Keychain, an object graph in SwiftData or Core Data.

• UserDefaults — small key-value preferences: last selected tab, onboarding seen, a local toggle. A plain plist inside your container, unencrypted and loaded into memory, so keep it small.
• Keychain — the only correct home for tokens, passwords and anything biometry-gated. Encrypted by the system, and by default it survives deleting the app.
• FileManager — Codable JSON or binary blobs in Documents (backed up) or Caches (the system may purge it). Right for downloaded content, exports and anything large.
• SwiftData — the Swift-first object graph, schema declared with `@Model` and queried from SwiftUI with `@Query`. The default choice for a new app with relational data.
• Core Data — the same engine underneath, driven by a visual model and NSManagedObject. Still the answer for existing projects and for the corners SwiftData does not reach.
• SQLite directly, usually through GRDB — full SQL, full control over indices, joins and transactions.
• CloudKit — Apple's sync backend, standalone or as the sync layer under SwiftData or Core Data.

Two mistakes worth naming out loud: secrets in UserDefaults, because it is a readable plist that ends up in backups; and a whole Core Data stack for what is really three settings.

questions.question: What is Core Data and what are its core concepts?
questions.answer:
Core Data is Apple's object graph + persistence framework (since iOS 3). It's NOT just an ORM — it tracks object relationships, undo/redo, change notifications, and only uses SQLite as a backing store.

Key concepts:
• NSManagedObjectModel — the schema (entities, attributes, relationships). Often defined in the .xcdatamodeld editor.
• NSPersistentContainer — owns the model, the store coordinator, and the contexts. Convenience entry point.
• NSManagedObjectContext — workspace for objects. You fetch/insert/update on a context and call `save()` to persist. Each context is bound to a queue.
• NSManagedObject — base class of generated entity classes.
• NSFetchRequest / NSPredicate — query API.

Common pitfalls: thread-confined contexts (don't pass NSManagedObject across queues), heavy main-context fetches, missing batch operations for large updates.

questions.question: What is SwiftData and how does it differ from Core Data?
questions.answer:
SwiftData is Apple's Swift-first persistence framework, and it is the same Core Data engine underneath with the schema written as Swift code instead of drawn in a model editor.

• `@Model` on a plain class declares the entity: stored properties become attributes and references to other models become relationships.
• Macros carry the details — `@Attribute(.unique)`, `@Relationship(deleteRule: .cascade)`, `@Transient`.
• `ModelContainer` maps to NSPersistentContainer and `ModelContext` to NSManagedObjectContext; `@ModelActor` gives you a background context that Swift Concurrency understands, instead of `perform` blocks.
• In SwiftUI, `.modelContainer(for:)` installs the container and `@Query` fetches with a `#Predicate` and sort descriptors, re-running by itself whenever the store changes.
• Sync is one argument: `ModelConfiguration(cloudKitDatabase:)`.

Choose SwiftData for a new app that can target iOS 17 and later. Choose Core Data when you are maintaining an existing store, when a migration needs a custom mapping model, or when you depend on APIs SwiftData still does not surface. The two can share one store, so an existing Core Data app can adopt SwiftData incrementally rather than in one rewrite.

The honest caveat: SwiftData is younger, so predicate and migration edge cases are still where you will hit its limits first.

questions.question: How do you securely store secrets on iOS using Keychain?
questions.answer:
The Keychain is the system's encrypted store for small secrets, and the two attributes that matter on every item are its accessibility class and its access control.

• Accessibility — when the system is willing to decrypt the item. `kSecAttrAccessibleWhenUnlocked` for things you only touch in the foreground, `kSecAttrAccessibleAfterFirstUnlock` for anything a background task needs. The `…ThisDeviceOnly` variants stay out of iCloud Keychain and out of device backups.
• Access control — to require biometrics or a passcode, build a `SecAccessControl` with `SecAccessControlCreateWithFlags` using flags such as `.biometryCurrentSet` or `.userPresence`, and pass it as `kSecAttrAccessControl`. `.biometryCurrentSet` invalidates the item as soon as the user enrolls a new face or fingerprint, which is the point.
• Items belong to your app's keychain access group; share between the app and its extensions with a keychain-sharing entitlement.

The SecItem C API is verbose enough that most teams wrap it in a small helper or use a library such as KeychainAccess or Valet.

Gotchas:
• Keychain items outlive deleting the app, so a reinstall can find the previous install's token. Clear them on first launch if you want a clean state.
• `SecItemAdd` returns `errSecDuplicateItem` instead of overwriting; delete first, or use `SecItemUpdate`.
• It is for short secrets. Encrypt a large blob to a file and keep only the key in the Keychain.

questions.question: How do you handle Core Data / SwiftData migrations safely?
questions.answer:
When the schema changes between releases you need a migration strategy, or the app crashes on launch against an incompatible store.

• Lightweight migration — adding or removing attributes, adding entities, simple renames with a renaming identifier. Core Data infers it automatically once `shouldMigrateStoreAutomatically` and `shouldInferMappingModelAutomatically` are set.
• Custom mapping models — for anything it cannot infer: splitting an entity, merging attributes, deriving a value. Author a `.xcmappingmodel` and an `NSEntityMigrationPolicy` subclass.
• SwiftData `VersionedSchema` — declare each schema version and chain them in a `SchemaMigrationPlan`. A stage is either `.lightweight`, or `.custom` with `willMigrate` and `didMigrate` closures for fixing data up around the change.

Always:
• Test the migration against a store captured from production, not a fresh one. The bugs live in the data you did not expect.
• Keep a debug escape hatch that deletes and recreates the store, so a support case is not a reinstall.
• Migrate from every shipped version, not just the previous one — users skip releases, and a chain of N versions must still work end to end.
• Do not stack several slow migrations on the launch path; collapse them into one in-place transformation, or run the expensive part in the background after the first frame.

questions.question: When would you choose a third-party SQLite layer (GRDB) over Core Data / SwiftData?
questions.answer:
Go to SQLite directly when the database is the interesting part of the app and Core Data's object graph is overhead rather than help.

Signs you want GRDB or raw SQLite:
• You need SQL that Core Data cannot express: window functions, recursive CTEs, full-text search with FTS5, non-trivial aggregate reporting.
• The workload is large or write-heavy and you want to choose the indices, the joins and the transaction boundaries yourself.
• You want plain value types, with no faulting, no managed object context and no thread-confinement rules to remember.
• You share a schema or migration scripts with a server or with cross-platform code such as a KMP module.

What you give up: faulting, the undo manager, automatic change notification into SwiftUI, model-level validation, and the almost-free CloudKit sync that Core Data and SwiftData offer. GRDB answers part of that with `ValueObservation` and its own migrator, but the layer is now yours to maintain.

For most apps SwiftData is the right default, and reaching for SQLite should be a decision you can justify with a specific query or a benchmark rather than a preference.

questions.question: How does ARC (Automatic Reference Counting) work in Swift?
questions.answer:
ARC is a compile-time mechanism: the compiler inserts the retain and release calls, so an object is deallocated the instant its last strong reference goes away, with no collector and no pause.

• Strong (the default) — holds the object alive.
• `weak` — does not hold it, and the reference becomes nil automatically when the object is freed, which is why it must be a `var` Optional.
• `unowned` — does not hold it and is not Optional; reading it after the object is gone traps. Use it only when the referenced object is guaranteed to outlive this one.
• Closures capture strongly by default, and that is where most leaks come from. `[weak self]` in the capture list is the fix.
• Structs and enums are copied rather than reference-counted, so ARC does not apply to them — though a struct holding a class reference still participates through that property.

Because deallocation is deterministic, `deinit` is a reliable place to invalidate timers and cancel work, and a `print` in `deinit` is the cheapest leak test you have. The trade-off against a tracing collector is the mirror image: no pauses, but cycles are never collected, so you have to break them yourself.

questions.question: What is a retain cycle? How do you detect and prevent them?
questions.answer:
A retain cycle is two (or more) reference-counted objects holding strong references to each other so refcount never hits zero. The objects leak.

Common sources:
• Closures captured strongly by their owner (delegates, completion handlers, Combine sinks, NotificationCenter blocks).
• Bidirectional class relationships (parent ↔ child) without weak/unowned.
• Repeated NSTimer / DispatchSourceTimer holding `target = self`.

Detect:
• Xcode's Memory Graph Debugger — pause, click the icon, look for cycles (purple icons indicate leaks).
• Instruments → Leaks template.
• `deinit print` smoke test — does the object's `deinit` ever fire?

Fix: `[weak self]` capture lists, `weak` properties, invalidate timers in deinit.

questions.question: How do you profile an iOS app with Instruments?
questions.answer:
Instruments is Apple's profiler suite, attached to a running app from Xcode with Product → Profile.

Templates worth knowing:
• Time Profiler — sampled CPU stacks. Invert the call tree or filter to the main thread to find the method that is actually costing you.
• Allocations — memory over time. Find growth that never comes back down, and abandoned memory after a screen is dismissed.
• Leaks — objects with no path from a root, which in practice means retain cycles.
• Hangs — main-thread stalls over 250ms, reported with the stack that caused them.
• Animation Hitches — frames that missed their deadline, for UIKit and SwiftUI scrolling.
• Network and Energy Log — request timings and payload sizes, battery cost.
• App Launch — pre-main and post-main phases on one timeline.

Instrument your own code with `OSSignposter`, the Swift API that replaced the `os_signpost` C functions: your phases then appear as intervals alongside the system's tracks in any template.

Two rules that decide whether the numbers mean anything: profile a Release build on a real device, because the Simulator has your Mac's CPU and none of its thermal limits; and use MetricKit for real-user data, since `MXMetricPayload` reports launch time, hang rate, disk writes and battery from devices you will never hold.

questions.question: How do you keep the main thread responsive in iOS apps?
questions.answer:
The main thread draws every frame and handles every touch, so anything slow there is visible: over roughly 16ms you drop a frame, and over 250ms the system calls it a hang.

• Move work off with structured concurrency — `async let`, task groups, or an actor that owns the expensive state. Fan out independent requests instead of awaiting them one after another.
• Parse and decode off-main: a large JSON payload, image decoding, sorting or diffing a big collection. Hand only the finished value back to the UI.
• Never call synchronous I/O on the main thread: `Data(contentsOf:)`, directory enumeration, a Core Data fetch against a large store, or a `DispatchQueue.sync` onto a busy queue.
• Defer non-critical work until after the first frame — `viewDidAppear` or a `.task` — rather than doing it in `viewDidLoad`.
• Update the UI on the main actor only: annotate the type or the method `@MainActor` instead of sprinkling `DispatchQueue.main.async` calls.
• Since Swift 6.2 a module can default to main-actor isolation, which makes accidental main-thread work easier to write than before. Mark the functions that should leave the main actor `@concurrent`, or isolate them to an actor of their own.

Find the offenders with Instruments: the Hangs instrument surfaces the stalls directly, Time Profiler filtered to the main thread shows what was running, and the Main Thread Checker catches UIKit calls made off-main, which is the same bug in the other direction.

questions.question: How do you optimize UITableView / UICollectionView scrolling performance?
questions.answer:
Smooth scrolling means every frame's work fits in the frame budget: about 16ms at 60Hz, 8ms on a 120Hz ProMotion display.

• Cell reuse — dequeue, never construct per visible row, and cancel the in-flight image request in `prepareForReuse`.
• Prefetching — implement `UITableViewDataSourcePrefetching` / `UICollectionViewDataSourcePrefetching` so images and pages are fetched before the row is on screen, and cancel that work in the `cancelPrefetchingForRowsAt` callback.
• Pre-decode images off the main thread with `CGImageSourceCreateImageAtIndex` and `kCGImageSourceShouldCacheImmediately`, and downsample to the size you actually display instead of holding a full-resolution bitmap.
• Diffable data sources instead of `reloadData`, so only the changed rows are touched.
• Give a fast `estimatedRowHeight` (or `.estimated` in a compositional layout) so UIKit does not measure every row up front.
• Content configurations (`UIListContentConfiguration`) are cheaper than a custom cell carrying a dozen subviews.
• Avoid offscreen rendering: `cornerRadius` plus `clipsToBounds` on an opaque image view is cheap, a mask layer or a shadow without an explicit `shadowPath` is not.
• Do not call `layoutIfNeeded()` inside `cellForRowAt` — let the layout pass run once after configuration.

Profile before and after with Animation Hitches and Time Profiler; scrolling problems are usually one expensive call in cell configuration, not a hundred small ones.

questions.question: How do you analyze and improve app launch time?
questions.answer:
App launch splits into two measurable phases with different fixes: pre-main work done by dyld and the runtime, and everything from main until your first useful frame.

• Pre-main — dyld loading and linking your dylibs, Objective-C runtime setup, `+load` methods and static initialisers. Shrink it by cutting dynamic frameworks (each one costs dyld time), removing `+load`, and avoiding global values whose initialiser does real work.
• Post-main to first frame — `application(_:didFinishLaunchingWithOptions:)`, scene setup, and building the first screen. This is where most of the avoidable time hides: SDK initialisation, a synchronous Keychain or Core Data hit, reading a config file, warming a cache.

Measure before you cut:
• Instruments' App Launch template shows both phases on one timeline.
• MetricKit's `MXAppLaunchMetric` gives a histogram of real users' cold launches, which is the only number that matters.
• `OSSignposter` intervals around your own startup phases show up alongside the system's tracks.

The reliable wins: defer every SDK that is not needed to draw the first screen, make services lazy so nothing initialises until first use, move cache warming into a background task started after the first frame, and merge small dynamic frameworks into fewer or into static ones.

Cold launch is the number to optimise — a warm launch reuses pages that are already resident and will flatter you.

questions.question: What is Combine? How do Publishers, Subscribers, and Operators relate?
questions.answer:
Combine models asynchronous work as a typed pipeline built from four roles.

• Publisher — emits a stream of values and one completion (finished or failure). Carries Output and Failure associated types.
• Subscriber — receives values, completion and demand signals. You rarely write one by hand; `sink` and `assign` cover almost everything.
• Operator — a method on Publisher returning a new publisher (map, filter, flatMap, debounce). Lazy: nothing flows until someone subscribes.
• Subscription — the link between publisher and subscriber, torn down through `AnyCancellable`.

Positioning matters in a 2026 interview. Combine shipped with iOS 13 and Apple has added essentially nothing to it since, steering new code to async/await, AsyncSequence and the Observation framework. It is still the right tool inside an existing Combine code base, for `ObservableObject`/`@Published` plumbing, and where you need declarative multi-stream composition (debounce plus combineLatest) with cancellation for free.

questions.question: What are Subjects in Combine? PassthroughSubject vs CurrentValueSubject.
questions.answer:
Subjects are publishers you can imperatively send values into — the bridge between non-Combine code and a Combine pipeline.

• PassthroughSubject<Output, Failure> — broadcasts values to current subscribers as they arrive. It holds no value, so a subscriber that arrives late sees nothing that happened before.
• CurrentValueSubject<Output, Failure> — holds a current value, set in the initializer and readable through `.value`. A new subscriber gets that value immediately, then every later update.

Use PassthroughSubject for events (button taps, gestures) and CurrentValueSubject for state (a loading flag, the current user).

In new code the equivalents usually live outside Combine: `@Observable` for view state, and `AsyncStream` with its continuation for wrapping a delegate or callback API. Reach for a Subject when the surrounding pipeline is already Combine, or when you need to hand callers an `AnyPublisher` because that is what the existing API vends.

questions.question: Which Combine operators cover transformation, combining streams, rate limiting and scheduling?
questions.answer:
Combine operators group into five jobs: transform, filter, combine, rate-limit and schedule.

• map / tryMap / compactMap — transform values; tryMap can throw.
• filter / removeDuplicates — drop values you do not want.
• flatMap — chain into another publisher; the tool for dependent requests.
• combineLatest / merge / zip — join several streams.
• debounce / throttle — control firing rate (typeahead, scroll).
• retry / catch / replaceError — error handling.
• receive(on:) / subscribe(on:) — choose the scheduler for downstream and upstream work respectively.
• assign(to:on:) / assign(to:) — bind output to a property without writing a `sink`.
• share / multicast — share one subscription's work across several subscribers.
• eraseToAnyPublisher() — type-erase at API boundaries.

Be deliberate about scheduling: by default work runs on whichever queue the publisher chose, so UI updates need `.receive(on: DispatchQueue.main)`.

Currency note worth saying out loud: Swift Async Algorithms now offers the same combinators — debounce, throttle, combineLatest, merge, zip, removeDuplicates — over AsyncSequence, so a greenfield target can get this composition without Combine at all.

questions.question: How does SwiftUI observe an ObservableObject, and what has replaced that pattern?
questions.answer:
SwiftUI observes a Combine-based view model through `ObservableObject` and `@Published`.

• ObservableObject — a reference type with a built-in `objectWillChange` publisher.
• @Published — a property wrapper that routes every mutation into `objectWillChange`, so views observing the object re-render.
• @StateObject when the view owns the object, @ObservedObject when someone else owns it, @EnvironmentObject for shared state injected down the tree.
• Custom pipelines feeding the UI must keep their cancellables alive in a `Set<AnyCancellable>`.

The caveat that makes this a modern question: `objectWillChange` invalidates the WHOLE view, so a change to any property re-renders every observer. The Observation framework (`@Observable`, held in a plain `@State`, iOS 17 and later) tracks individual property reads instead and is the default for new SwiftUI code — an `@Observable` class needs no Combine at all.

Keep Combine here for the stream work SwiftUI has no answer for: debounced typeahead, combineLatest over several sources, retrying network composition.

questions.question: How do Combine and Swift Concurrency (async/await) interoperate?
questions.answer:
Combine and async/await interoperate in both directions, and Apple's direction of travel points from Combine toward async/await.

• Publisher → async — `.values` exposes an AsyncSequence; iterate it with `for await`.
• async → Publisher — wrap the call in a `Future`, or push results into a Subject from a `Task`.
• `assign(to: &$prop)` binds a publisher straight into a `@Published` property.
• `Task { @MainActor in ... }` inside a sink is the bridge into actor-isolated mutation.

Under Swift 6 strict concurrency the seams show: Combine predates Sendable and has no isolation model, so sink closures that hop isolation domains produce warnings or errors. The fix is normally to end the pipeline early and continue the work inside a Task.

Guideline: write new code with async/await, AsyncStream and Swift Async Algorithms. Reach for Combine when you are already inside a Combine code base, when you need `ObservableObject`/`@Published` interop, or when a UIKit-era API only vends a publisher.

questions.question: Which Combine mistakes silently break a pipeline, and how do you avoid them?
questions.answer:
Most Combine bugs come from a pipeline that was never retained, retained too strongly, or delivered on the wrong scheduler.

• Discarding the AnyCancellable — the subscription is torn down immediately and nothing ever fires. Always `.store(in: &bag)`.
• Strong capture of self in `sink` — a retain cycle; use `[weak self]`.
• Wrong scheduler for UI — UI mutation must land on `DispatchQueue.main` (or `RunLoop.main`) via `.receive(on:)`.
• Re-running expensive upstream work — without `.share()` or `.multicast()` every new subscriber replays the whole chain.
• Tearing down on the first error — most operators complete on failure; use `.catch` / `.replaceError` when the stream must survive.
• `.assign(to:on:)` retains its target — prefer `.assign(to: &$prop)`, which binds to a `@Published` without retaining.
• Unbounded demand — Combine is demand-driven, but `sink` requests unlimited. With a high-rate source add `.collect`, `.throttle`, or a custom subscriber.
• Sendable friction under Swift 6 — hop out of the pipeline with `Task { @MainActor in ... }` rather than mutating actor-isolated state inside a sink.

questions.question: What is the difference between val and var in Kotlin?
questions.answer:
`val` fixes the reference while `var` allows reassignment, and neither says anything about whether the object itself can change.

• val — read-only reference (like Java's `final`). The binding cannot be reassigned; the object behind it may still be mutable.
• var — mutable reference. Can be reassigned.

Idiomatic Kotlin defaults to val — IDE inspections suggest var → val whenever a variable is never reassigned. Writing `var` should be a deliberate decision, since immutability is a thread-safety and correctness win.

Both are statically typed; inference is the rule and explicit annotations are reserved for public API and ambiguous initializers. `const val` goes one step further: a compile-time constant, allowed only at top level or inside an `object`/`companion object`, inlined at every call site.

questions.question: How does null safety work in Kotlin?
questions.answer:
Nullability is part of the type in Kotlin: `String` can never hold null, `String?` can, and the compiler enforces the difference.

Safe operators:
• `?.` — safe call. Returns null when the receiver is null.
• `?:` — Elvis operator, supplies a default for null.
• `!!` — non-null assertion. Throws NullPointerException when null; treat every one as a bug waiting to happen.
• `?.let { ... }` — run the block only when non-null.
• `requireNotNull` / `checkNotNull` — fail fast with a message instead of a bare NPE.

When you interoperate with Java, types arrive as platform types (`String!`): Kotlin lets you use them either way and only fails at runtime, so annotate Java sources with @Nullable / @NonNull or convert at the boundary.

The K2 compiler, default since Kotlin 2.0, widened smart casts considerably — a null check now survives into more places, including a local `var` captured by a lambda and conditions combined with `||`. Less `!!` is needed than older tutorials suggest.

questions.question: Is Kotlin's `List` immutable? How do read-only and mutable collection types differ?
questions.answer:
Kotlin's `List` is read-only, not immutable — the interface simply has no mutators, while the object behind it may be a MutableList somebody else can still change.

• `List<T>` vs `MutableList<T>` (add/remove/set).
• `Set<T>` vs `MutableSet<T>`.
• `Map<K, V>` vs `MutableMap<K, V>`.

Factory functions:
• `listOf`, `setOf`, `mapOf` — read-only.
• `mutableListOf`, `mutableSetOf`, `mutableMapOf` — mutable.
• `emptyList()`, `emptyMap()` — empty read-only.

Under the hood these wrap JDK collections, and the read-only types are interfaces rather than copies. Passing a MutableList where a `List` is expected is allowed; the consumer just cannot mutate through that reference. For a real guarantee use `kotlinx.collections.immutable` (`PersistentList`, `ImmutableList`) or copy defensively — Compose in particular relies on immutable collection types to keep parameters comparable.

Functional helpers (map / filter / reduce / fold / groupBy / chunked / windowed / partition) make data wrangling concise, and `asSequence()` turns a long chain lazy so it stops allocating an intermediate list per step.

questions.question: Explain functions, lambdas, and higher-order functions in Kotlin.
questions.answer:
Kotlin functions are first-class values — you can pass them as arguments, return them, and store them in variables.

• Declaration: `fun name(...): T = body` (single-expression) or `fun name(...) { ... }` (block body).
• Default and named arguments — fewer overloads to write.
• Lambda: `{ a, b -> a + b }`, with an implicit `it` for a single parameter.
• Higher-order: a function that takes or returns a function (`(Int) -> String`, `() -> Unit`).
• Trailing-lambda convention: `list.forEach { println(it) }`.
• Function references: `::isEven`, `String::length`, `User::name`.
• `inline` copies the body into the call site at compile time, removing the lambda allocation and enabling non-local return.

Kotlin idiom leans heavily on lambdas — collections, coroutines, Compose and every DSL are built out of them.

questions.question: When is `if`/`when` an expression in Kotlin, and what does that require?
questions.answer:
In Kotlin control structures are expressions — they produce a value and can sit on the right-hand side of an assignment or be returned directly.

• `if/else` — as an expression both branches are required. The result type is the least upper bound of the branch types.
• `when` — matches values, types (`is X`), ranges and collections (`in`), or arbitrary predicates when written without a subject. As an expression it must be exhaustive, either by covering a sealed / enum / Boolean type or through `else`.
• `try` is an expression too — `val n = try { input.toInt() } catch (e: NumberFormatException) { 0 }`.
• A `when` STATEMENT over a sealed or enum subject must be exhaustive as well: that stopped being a warning and became an error in Kotlin 1.7.

Using them as expressions removes a lot of mutable state, because each branch produces the final value directly. Kotlin 2.1 added guard conditions, so a subject branch can carry an extra predicate: `is Cart if cart.isEmpty() -> ...`.

questions.question: What are smart casts in Kotlin and when do they work?
questions.answer:
A smart cast is the compiler narrowing a value's type after a runtime check, so you never write the cast yourself.

• After `if (x is Type)` the compiler treats `x` as `Type` inside the block.
• After `if (x != null)` it treats `x` as non-nullable.
• It works in `when` branches and after an early `return` in the opposite branch.

A smart cast applies only when the compiler can prove the value did not change between check and use:
• `val` properties — always.
• A `var` of a class — only when the class is not open (an override could change the getter) and the property has no custom getter.
• Local variables and function parameters — generally yes.
• A mutable property of another object — no, another thread could change it between the two reads. Capture it into a local first.

The K2 compiler, default since Kotlin 2.0, made this noticeably smarter: a local `var` captured by a lambda, a value narrowed by a `||` condition, and a check inside an inline lambda now all smart-cast where the old front end gave up. When it still cannot prove safety, use `as` (throws on mismatch) or `as?` (returns null).

questions.question: What are data classes in Kotlin and what does the compiler generate?
questions.answer:
A `data class` exists to hold data, and the compiler generates its equality, printing, copying and destructuring for you.

• `equals()` / `hashCode()` from the primary-constructor properties ONLY — a property declared in the class body is ignored by both.
• `toString()` like `User(id=1, name=Alice)`.
• `copy(...)` — a new instance with selected fields replaced.
• `componentN()` operators, which is what makes destructuring work.

Requirements: at least one primary-constructor parameter, and every one of them must be `val` or `var`. A data class cannot be `abstract`, `open`, `sealed` or `inner`, though it may extend a non-data class.

Two modern points. `data object` gives a singleton a readable `toString()` and a stable `equals`, which is why sealed hierarchies now write `data object Loading`. And a private constructor no longer leaks silently through `copy()`: since Kotlin 2.0.20 that combination is deprecated — opt in with `@ConsistentCopyVisibility` or stop using a data class there.

Two traps to name in an interview: `copy()` is shallow, so nested mutable objects stay shared, and structural equality over a mutable property will change an object's hashCode after it has been put in a HashSet.

questions.question: What are sealed classes / sealed interfaces in Kotlin?
questions.answer:
A sealed class/interface restricts who can extend it: only classes declared in the SAME module + same package (sealed class) or same module (sealed interface) can subclass.

This enables:
• Exhaustive `when` — no `else` branch needed; if you add a new subtype, the compiler errors at every existing `when`.
• Algebraic-data-type modeling — express finite alternatives like `Result`, screen state, parser tokens.
• Library API design — control extensibility while still using inheritance.

Sealed types are reference types; the JVM treats them as ordinary classes. Use `data class` or `data object` subclasses for value semantics.

questions.question: What is the difference between class, object, and companion object in Kotlin?
questions.answer:
`object` declares a singleton, `companion object` is a singleton bound to a class, and `class` is the ordinary instantiable declaration.

• `class` — instantiated with `Foo()`; every instance is separate.
• `object` — a named singleton. The compiler creates exactly one instance, initialized lazily and thread-safely on first access, reachable as `MyService.action()`.
• `companion object` — a singleton tied to an enclosing class, holding the static-like members Kotlin has no `static` keyword for: factories, constants, `operator invoke`. Reached through the class name (`User.create(...)`).

Objects can implement interfaces and extend one class, which is what makes them useful as stateless strategies, comparators and DI entry points. An anonymous `object : Listener { ... }` expression is Kotlin's version of a Java anonymous class, and unlike a named object it may capture surrounding state.

Two traps: a companion member is NOT a JVM static, so Java callers need `@JvmStatic`; and a top-level `object` lives for the whole process, which makes holding mutable state or an Android Context in one a classic leak. For genuine compile-time constants use `const val` at top level or inside an object.

questions.question: What are extension functions and properties in Kotlin?
questions.answer:
Extensions add functions or properties to existing types without modifying their source. Resolved STATICALLY — the compiler picks the extension based on the static type of the receiver.

• `fun String.titleCase(): String = ...` — extension function.
• `val String.firstLetter: Char get() = first()` — extension property (no backing field; computed only).
• Member functions win over extensions with the same signature on the same type.
• Extensions don't override virtual methods — they're static dispatch.

Idiomatic uses: utility helpers (`Date.toIsoString()`), domain DSLs, view-binding helpers in Android, ergonomic API on third-party types.

questions.question: What are scope functions (let, run, with, apply, also)?
questions.answer:
Scope functions run a lambda in the context of an object, and they differ on two axes: how the object is referenced (`it` vs `this`) and what the lambda returns (the object itself vs the lambda result).

• `let` — refer as `it`, returns lambda result. Common for null-safe transforms.
• `run` — refer as `this`, returns lambda result. For computing on an object.
• `with` — refer as `this`, returns lambda result. Like run, but as standalone function.
• `apply` — refer as `this`, returns the object. For configuring an object after construction.
• `also` — refer as `it`, returns the object. For side effects (logging, validation) without breaking a chain.

Guideline: pick the pair (`it`/`this`, value/object) that makes the call site cleanest. Don't nest scope functions deeply.

questions.question: Kotlin classes are final by default — how do `open class`, `abstract class` and `interface` differ?
questions.answer:
Kotlin makes every class final by default, so `open`, `abstract` and `interface` are three different ways of opting into extension.

• `class` — final. Neither the class nor its members can be extended or overridden unless marked `open`.
• `open class` — subclassable, but only members that are themselves `open` can be overridden, and each override must carry the `override` keyword (it is mandatory in Kotlin, unlike Java's optional `@Override`).
• `abstract class` — cannot be instantiated. It may hold state through constructor properties and mix abstract with concrete members. Single inheritance, and `abstract` already implies `open`.
• `interface` — no backing fields, therefore no stored state, but it may declare abstract members, default implementations and computed properties. A class can implement many.

Kotlin's bias toward final-by-default is deliberate: the author must opt into extensibility, which heads off fragile-base-class problems.

The Kotlin-specific spellings are worth naming: a single colon covers both `extends` and `implements` (`class Service : Repository(), Logger`), the superclass constructor is called right there in that clause, and `super<A>.greet()` disambiguates when two interfaces supply the same default implementation.

Choose an interface for a contract or capability, an abstract class when subtypes must share state, a data class for a value type, and `sealed` when the set of subtypes is closed and you want `when` to stay exhaustive.

questions.question: How do generics, variance, and `out`/`in` modifiers work in Kotlin?
questions.answer:
Kotlin declares variance at the declaration site: `out` marks a type parameter the class only produces, `in` one it only consumes.

• Invariant (the default) — `Box<Dog>` is unrelated to `Box<Animal>` even though Dog is an Animal.
• `out T` — covariant. A `Producer<out T>` only returns T, so a `Producer<Dog>` is usable as a `Producer<Animal>`.
• `in T` — contravariant. A `Consumer<in T>` only accepts T, so a `Consumer<Animal>` is usable as a `Consumer<Dog>`.

Use-site variance exists too: `Box<out Any>` in a parameter position is the equivalent of Java's `? extends Any` wildcard, and `*` is the star projection for when the argument genuinely does not matter.

Generics are erased on the JVM, so `is T` is normally impossible inside a generic function. `inline fun <reified T>` is the escape hatch — the compiler substitutes the concrete type at every call site, which is how `filterIsInstance<T>()` and most Kotlin JSON APIs get their signatures. Bounds (`<T : Comparable<T>>`) constrain what the parameter accepts.

questions.question: What are inline functions and reified type parameters in Kotlin?
questions.answer:
An `inline fun` is replaced at compile time with the body of the function copied into the call site. The lambda parameters are inlined too — no Function<...> object allocation, no extra invocation.

Why:
• Performance — avoid lambda allocation in hot loops.
• Non-local return — `return` inside an inline lambda returns from the ENCLOSING function.
• Reified generics — when a type parameter is `reified`, the compiler knows T at the call site and you can write `T::class`, `is T`, `as T`.

Downsides:
• Code bloat if overused — every call site copies the body.
• `noinline` opts out of inlining for specific lambda parameters; `crossinline` forbids non-local returns from a specific lambda.

questions.question: What are property delegates? Explain `by lazy`, `by Delegates.observable`, custom delegates.
questions.answer:
Property delegation hands a property's get and set to another object: `by` forwards every read and write to that object's `getValue` / `setValue`.

Built-in delegates:
• `lazy { ... }` — computed on first read; thread-safe by default, and `LazyThreadSafetyMode.NONE` drops the synchronization when you know the access is single-threaded.
• `Delegates.observable(initial) { prop, old, new -> ... }` — a callback after every set.
• `Delegates.vetoable(initial) { ... }` — the same, but the lambda can reject the change.
• `Delegates.notNull()` — the substitute for `lateinit` on primitive types, which `lateinit` does not support.
• `by map` — back a property with a Map, handy for dynamic schemas and deserialization.

Custom delegates are easy: implement the `getValue` / `setValue` operators, or the `ReadOnlyProperty` / `ReadWriteProperty` interfaces. Kotlin also supports `provideDelegate` if the delegate needs the property name at construction time.

Android is full of them — `by viewModels()`, `by activityViewModels()`, `by remember` in Compose. Note that the SharedPreferences-backed delegate below is the classic teaching example, but new Android code stores preferences in DataStore; the delegate shape is identical, only the suspending API differs.

questions.question: How do you write a type-safe DSL in Kotlin?
questions.answer:
A type-safe Kotlin DSL rests on three features: lambdas with receiver, extension functions and the `@DslMarker` annotation.

• Lambda with receiver — `block: A.() -> Unit` makes `this` an `A` inside the lambda, so A's members are in scope without a qualifier.
• Extension functions — add builder verbs to a type for the duration of the block without touching its source.
• `@DslMarker` — restricts which receivers are visible inside nested builders, so an inner block cannot accidentally call an outer scope's method.

The pattern is always the same: a top-level function takes a lambda with receiver, instantiates a builder, applies the lambda to it, and returns the built result. `apply` does the last two steps in one call.

Known DSLs to name: the Gradle Kotlin DSL, kotlinx.html, Compose itself (`Column { Text("...") }`), Ktor routing and the Exposed SQL DSL. Kotlin 2.2 added context parameters, replacing the experimental context receivers, as another way to make a scope available without threading a receiver through every signature.

questions.question: What are typealiases and when should you use them?
questions.answer:
`typealias` introduces a name for an existing type. It does NOT create a new type — it's purely a compile-time alias the compiler resolves to the underlying type.

Good uses:
• Shorten complex generic types: `typealias Cache = Map<String, ByteArray>`.
• Clarify intent: `typealias UserId = Long` reads better than passing raw Long around.
• Function-type aliases: `typealias Validator<T> = (T) -> Result<Unit>`.
• Deprecate old names while moving toward new ones.

Limitations:
• Not a wrapper — `UserId` and `Long` are the SAME type. The compiler does not enforce that you don't mix them.
• For real type-safety use a value class (inline class) or a wrapper data class.

questions.question: What are value classes (inline classes) in Kotlin?
questions.answer:
A value class wraps a single value that the compiler erases at runtime, replacing the wrapper with the underlying value wherever it can.

• Declared as `@JvmInline value class Email(val value: String)`; the `@JvmInline` annotation is required on the JVM target.
• Wraps exactly one property, and may carry an `init` block for validation plus its own functions and operators.
• You get language-level type safety with no allocation in most positions.
• The compiler still boxes when the wrapper appears as a generic argument, a nullable type or an interface implementation — `List<UserId>` really does hold boxed objects.

Idiomatic uses: domain primitives (UserId, Email, Money), units (Px, Dp, Hz), and any place a bare `Long` or `String` invites mixing two things up. Compare with `typealias`, which is only a name and gives no safety at all.

`@JvmInline value class` replaced the old `inline class` modifier, which was deprecated in Kotlin 1.5 and is no longer accepted by current compilers — you will only meet it in old code. Value classes with more than one property are still an experimental preview, not something to rely on.

questions.question: What are coroutines and how do they differ from threads?
questions.answer:
Coroutines are lightweight concurrency primitives that suspend without blocking the underlying thread. A `suspend` function can pause and resume; the underlying thread is free to run other coroutines while it waits.

Vs threads:
• Tens of thousands of coroutines easily co-exist on a small thread pool — threads cost megabytes of stack each.
• Suspension is cooperative; a coroutine only suspends at suspension points (`suspend fun`, `delay`, channel send/receive).
• Cancellation is cooperative (CancellationException propagates).
• Structured concurrency — coroutines are launched into a CoroutineScope, parent waits for children, cancellation cascades.
• Coroutines run on a CoroutineDispatcher (Default, IO, Main, Unconfined, custom).

Think of coroutines as Kotlin's answer to async/await + structured concurrency.

questions.question: What are CoroutineScope, Job, and structured concurrency?
questions.answer:
Structured concurrency means every coroutine has a parent that owns it, waits for it and can cancel it.

• CoroutineScope — defines lifetime plus context (a Job and a dispatcher). Everything launched inside becomes a child of its Job.
• Job — the lifecycle handle (New, Active, Completing, Cancelling, Cancelled, Completed) with parent and child links.
• Cancellation travels both ways — cancelling a parent cancels every child, and an uncaught child failure cancels the parent and its siblings unless the parent is a SupervisorJob.

In practice you never call `GlobalScope.launch`: it has no parent, so nothing cancels it and nothing waits for it, and the work outlives the screen that started it.

What to use instead:
• `viewModelScope` and `lifecycleScope` on Android, which cancel themselves at the right moment.
• `coroutineScope { }` inside a suspend function — it suspends until every child finishes and rethrows their failures.
• `supervisorScope { }` when one child's failure must not take down its siblings.
• A scope you construct with `CoroutineScope(SupervisorJob() + Dispatchers.IO)` and cancel yourself in the owner's teardown.

questions.question: Which dispatcher do you pick for CPU work, blocking I/O and UI updates?
questions.answer:
A CoroutineDispatcher decides which thread or thread pool a coroutine runs on.

• `Dispatchers.Default` — CPU-bound work (parsing, sorting, image math). A pool sized to the CPU count.
• `Dispatchers.IO` — blocking I/O (files, JDBC, blocking sockets). An elastic pool, 64 threads by default, which shares its threads with Default so a `withContext(IO)` hop is usually cheap.
• `Dispatchers.Main` — the Android or Swing UI thread; the only place you may touch views.
• `Dispatchers.Main.immediate` — Main without a re-dispatch when you are already on it, which removes a frame of latency for UI updates.
• `Dispatchers.Unconfined` — runs in the calling thread until the first suspension; for tests and advanced cases only.
• `Dispatchers.IO.limitedParallelism(n)` — a view on the IO pool capped at n threads. This is the modern way to serialize work, `n = 1` for a single SQLite writer, instead of allocating your own executor that you then have to close.

Switch with `withContext(Dispatchers.X) { ... }`, and remember that a properly written suspending library (Retrofit, Room, Ktor) already moves off the caller's thread, so wrapping its calls in `withContext(IO)` is noise.

Inject the dispatcher rather than hardcoding it, so a test can pass a `StandardTestDispatcher` from kotlinx-coroutines-test and control virtual time.

questions.question: What is Flow? How is it different from suspending functions or Channel?
questions.answer:
A `Flow<T>` is a cold asynchronous stream — like a `Sequence`, except its producer is allowed to suspend.

• Cold — nothing runs until `collect`, and every collector triggers a fresh execution of the builder.
• Backpressure-aware — `emit` suspends until the collector is ready, unless you insert `buffer()` or `conflate()`.
• Cancellable — cancelling the collecting coroutine stops the producer.
• Operators — `map`, `filter`, `transform`, `onEach`, `debounce`, `combine`, `flatMapLatest` / `flatMapConcat` / `flatMapMerge`, `retryWhen`, `catch`, `onCompletion`, `stateIn` / `shareIn`.

Against the alternatives:
• A `suspend fun` returns ONE value; a Flow delivers many over time.
• A `Channel` is hot and stateful: each value goes to exactly ONE consumer, and a value sent with no receiver waits in the buffer or is dropped. Use channels for work queues and hand-offs, flows for streams. `callbackFlow` is the right way to wrap a listener API, since it gives you a channel plus `awaitClose` for unregistering.

Exception transparency is the rule people get wrong: handle upstream failures with the `catch` operator, not a `try/catch` wrapped around `collect`, because operators are allowed to assume emissions never throw through them.

questions.question: What are StateFlow and SharedFlow? When to use which?
questions.answer:
StateFlow always holds a current value and replays it to every new collector, while SharedFlow is a configurable broadcast hub with no value of its own.

• StateFlow<T> — exactly one current value, always readable through `.value`, and conflated: a slow collector may miss intermediate updates but never the latest one. It also de-duplicates, so emitting a value equal to the current one notifies nobody.
• SharedFlow<T> — configurable `replay`, `extraBufferCapacity` and `onBufferOverflow` (SUSPEND, DROP_OLDEST, DROP_LATEST). No initial value, no conflation.

Which to use:
• StateFlow for UI state (a loading flag, a list, the current user) where a new collector must see the current snapshot. It is what replaced LiveData in modern Android.
• SharedFlow with `replay = 0` for one-shot events such as a snackbar or a navigation command. Be ready for the follow-up: a dropped event is invisible, which is why many teams model events as part of the state and have the UI acknowledge them instead.

Collect them lifecycle-aware or you keep work running behind a backgrounded screen: `collectAsStateWithLifecycle()` in Compose, and `repeatOnLifecycle(Lifecycle.State.STARTED) { flow.collect { } }` inside `lifecycleScope.launch` in a Fragment or Activity. Turn a cold repository flow into state with `stateIn(viewModelScope, SharingStarted.WhileSubscribed(5_000), initial)`, which keeps the upstream alive across a rotation but stops it once the screen is really gone.

questions.question: How do you handle exceptions and cancellation in coroutines?
questions.answer:
Cancellation and exception handling are two separate mechanisms, and `CancellationException` is the one you must never swallow.

Cancellation:
• It is cooperative — a coroutine only notices at a suspension point or when it checks `isActive`. A tight CPU loop with no suspension never cancels.
• `CancellationException` is normal control flow, not a failure, so it has to propagate. Raise it inside long computations with `currentCoroutineContext().ensureActive()`.
• `withContext(NonCancellable) { ... }` inside a `finally` is the sanctioned way to run cleanup that must complete after cancellation.
• A broad `catch (e: Exception)` around suspending code silently eats cancellation. Rethrow CancellationException first, or catch narrower types. `runCatching` has exactly the same trap.

Exceptions:
• With a regular Job the first child failure cancels the parent and every sibling.
• `SupervisorJob` and `supervisorScope` keep a failure isolated to the child that failed.
• `CoroutineExceptionHandler` catches what `launch` throws, and only in the root coroutine of a scope; it is ignored for `async`.
• `async` stores the failure in its Deferred and rethrows it from `await()` — but an `async` whose result is never awaited still cancels its parent scope.

questions.question: What is Jetpack Compose? How is it different from the View system?
questions.answer:
Jetpack Compose replaces the View system with `@Composable` functions that describe the UI for a given state.

The runtime calls those functions, builds a UI tree from what they emit, and calls them again when the state they read changes — that re-run is recomposition.

Differences vs the View system:
• Declarative — the UI is a function of state, not an imperative tree of mutable Views you keep in sync by hand.
• Kotlin only — no XML layouts, no findViewById, no view binding.
• Composition over inheritance — small functions instead of subclassing View.
• Animation, theming and accessibility (semantics) are first-class APIs rather than bolt-ons.
• Two-way interop — `AndroidView` hosts a View inside Compose and `ComposeView` hosts Compose inside an XML layout, so migration can be screen by screen.
• Material 3 components plus the `Modifier` chain replace styles, themes and drawable XML.

The setup detail interviewers do ask about: depend on the `androidx.compose:compose-bom` platform once and leave the individual compose artifacts version-less, so the whole set stays mutually compatible. Since Kotlin 2.0 the Compose compiler ships with Kotlin itself and is turned on by the `org.jetbrains.kotlin.plugin.compose` Gradle plugin — the old `composeOptions { kotlinCompilerExtensionVersion = ... }` block and its Kotlin-to-compiler version table are gone.

questions.question: What are Modifiers in Compose and how do they work?
questions.answer:
A `Modifier` is an ordered chain of decorations applied to a composable: size, padding, background, border, click handling, semantics.
