• Order matters, and it is the number one Modifier interview question. `.padding(16.dp).background(Red)` paints red around the padded box; `.background(Red).padding(16.dp)` paints red behind the content only and puts the padding outside it. `.clickable` before `.padding` makes the padding tappable; after it, it does not.
• Modifiers are immutable values, so pass them as parameters to make a composable reusable.
• Every reusable composable should take `modifier: Modifier = Modifier` as its first optional parameter and apply it FIRST in its own chain, so the caller's decorations sit on the outside.
• Hoisting a chain into a `val` or a `remember` lets Compose reuse it instead of rebuilding it on every recomposition.
• A modifier that only reads state in layout or draw (`Modifier.offset { }`, `graphicsLayer { }`, `drawBehind { }`) skips recomposition entirely.

For a custom modifier, `Modifier.then(...)` is enough to concatenate existing ones. Anything that needs its own state or coordinates should be a `Modifier.Node` implementation exposed through a `ModifierNodeElement`. `Modifier.composed { ... }` is the older factory and is discouraged: it forces an allocation at composition time and defeats the reuse the Node API was built for.

questions.question: What are the main layout containers in Compose?
questions.answer:
Compose has three basic layouts — Column stacks children vertically, Row horizontally, Box on the Z axis — plus lazy variants for long content.

• `Column` / `Row` — measure and place every child, so use them for a bounded number of items.
• `Box` — children overlap; `contentAlignment` sets the default and `Modifier.align` overrides it per child.
• `LazyColumn` / `LazyRow` — compose only the visible children. Mandatory for long or unbounded lists, and always pass a stable `key` in `items(...)`.
• `LazyVerticalGrid` / `LazyHorizontalGrid` with `GridCells.Fixed(n)` or `GridCells.Adaptive(minSize)`, plus `LazyVerticalStaggeredGrid` for uneven heights.
• `FlowRow` / `FlowColumn` — wrap children onto the next line when they run out of width; the idiomatic chip group.
• `ConstraintLayout` from `compose-constraintlayout` — only when a layout is genuinely relational. Nesting Rows and Columns is cheap in Compose because each child is measured exactly once, so the deep-hierarchy fear from the View system does not carry over.

`Modifier.weight` splits the leftover space inside a Row or Column, `Arrangement.spacedBy` gives even gaps more cleanly than padding on every child, and `Spacer` inserts a fixed gap. When none of the containers fit, `Layout` and `SubcomposeLayout` let you measure and place children yourself.

One rule to state explicitly: never put a `LazyColumn` inside a scrollable `Column` of the same direction — the infinite height constraint crashes or forces every item to compose.

questions.question: What is recomposition, and what decides whether Compose skips a composable?
questions.answer:
Recomposition is Compose re-running the composable functions whose inputs changed, to bring the UI back in line with state.

The runtime records which composable read which state object, so a write only re-runs the readers rather than the whole tree.

Key behaviours:
• A composable may run any number of times, in any order, and on any thread. It must be fast and free of side effects.
• Compose SKIPS a composable when all of its parameters compare equal to the previous call. Since strong skipping mode became the default (the Compose compiler shipped with Kotlin 2.0.20 and later), unstable parameters no longer block skipping — they are compared by instance identity instead — and lambdas are remembered automatically.
• Side effects belong in `LaunchedEffect`, `DisposableEffect` or `SideEffect`, never in the function body.
• Read state as low in the tree as you can: a value read only inside a leaf recomposes only that leaf.
• Compose runs three phases — composition, layout, draw. Deferring a read into a lambda (`Modifier.offset { }`, `graphicsLayer { }`, or taking `() -> String` instead of `String`) keeps a fast-changing value out of composition so only layout or draw re-runs.

The consequence of strong skipping is that `@Immutable` / `@Stable` annotations and immutable collections are now a refinement that makes comparisons cheap and correct, not a prerequisite for skipping at all.

questions.question: How does theming and Material 3 work in Compose?
questions.answer:
Material 3 theming in Compose is one composable — `MaterialTheme` — holding a color scheme, a typography set and shapes that every component reads through composition locals.

• `MaterialTheme(colorScheme, typography, shapes) { content }` is the root; components read `MaterialTheme.colorScheme`, `MaterialTheme.typography`, `MaterialTheme.shapes`.
• `lightColorScheme(...)` / `darkColorScheme(...)` build the schemes. Every role has a matching `onX` color for the content drawn on top of it — using them is what keeps contrast correct.
• `dynamicLightColorScheme(context)` / `dynamicDarkColorScheme(context)` derive the palette from the wallpaper on Android 12 and later; guard the call by SDK level and keep a static fallback.
• `Surface` applies the background and the matching content color, and `LocalContentColor` carries that down the tree.
• Custom tokens (spacing, elevation, brand colors) belong in your own `CompositionLocal` beside MaterialTheme rather than crammed into it.

Dark mode comes from `isSystemInDarkTheme()` choosing the scheme, with an in-app setting able to override it.

Worth naming for currency: the Material 3 Expressive APIs — `MaterialExpressiveTheme`, a motion scheme and a wider shape scale — ship in the same `material3` artifact behind an experimental opt-in. They are additive and opt-in, so an existing `MaterialTheme` does not change under you.

questions.question: How do you set up navigation in an Android app built with Jetpack Compose?
questions.answer:
Navigation Compose gives an Android app one `NavHost` that owns a back stack of composable destinations, driven by a `NavController`.

The pieces:
• `rememberNavController()` creates the controller that owns the back stack.
• `NavHost(navController, startDestination)` declares the graph.
• `composable<Route> { ... }` registers a destination.
• `navController.navigate(route)` pushes and `popBackStack()` pops; `navigate(route) { popUpTo(Home) { inclusive = true }; launchSingleTop = true }` controls what the stack looks like afterwards.
• Each destination is its own `ViewModelStoreOwner` and `SavedStateRegistryOwner`, so a `viewModel()` or `hiltViewModel()` obtained inside a destination is scoped to that back-stack entry and dies with it. This Android-specific behaviour is the part interviewers actually probe.

Type-safe routes are the current default: mark a route as a `@Serializable` data class or data object and use `composable<Profile>` with `backStackEntry.toRoute<Profile>()`, instead of `"profile/{id}"` strings and `navArgument`. String routes still compile, and they are what you will find in code written before that API landed.

Two follow-ups to be ready for: deep links, declared with `navDeepLink<Profile>(basePath = ...)` on the destination and matched by an intent filter in the manifest; and returning a result to the previous screen, which goes through `previousBackStackEntry.savedStateHandle` rather than a shared singleton.

Alternatives exist — Voyager, Decompose, Compose Destinations — and Google is building Navigation 3, where the app owns the back stack as an ordinary list of keys. Check its stability before adopting it; Navigation Compose is still the safe answer for an Android app today.

questions.question: What is `remember` and `rememberSaveable` in Compose?
questions.answer:
`remember` keeps a value across recompositions, and `rememberSaveable` additionally survives configuration changes and process death.

• `remember { ... }` stores the value in the composition, keyed by call-site position. It is lost when the composable leaves composition, when the Activity is recreated, or when the same call moves to a different position in the tree.
• `rememberSaveable { ... }` does the same and also writes through the saved-instance-state mechanism. The value must be Bundle-friendly (primitive, String, Parcelable) or come with a `Saver` — `listSaver` and `mapSaver` cover most custom types.
• Both take keys: `remember(userId) { ... }` recomputes when the key changes. Wrong keys are the usual source of stale state on screen.
• Use `remember` for derived or expensive objects (a formatter, a scroll connection) and `rememberSaveable` for anything the user typed or picked.

Neither is the place for state that outlives the screen. Anything loaded from a repository, or that must survive back-stack navigation, belongs in a ViewModel; `rememberSaveable` is for small UI state such as a text-field draft, an expanded flag or the selected tab.

questions.question: What is `mutableStateOf`, `mutableStateListOf`, `derivedStateOf`?
questions.answer:
`mutableStateOf` makes a value observable, `mutableStateListOf` does the same for a collection, and `derivedStateOf` caches a computation over other state.

• `mutableStateOf(value)` — reading `.value` (or through `by`) subscribes the enclosing composable; writing it invalidates every reader. Use `mutableIntStateOf`, `mutableLongStateOf` and friends for primitives to avoid autoboxing on every write.
• `mutableStateListOf<T>()` / `mutableStateMapOf<K, V>()` — observable collections whose mutations trigger recomposition. A plain `MutableList` held in a `mutableStateOf` does NOT: nothing notices `list.add(x)` because the reference never changed.
• `derivedStateOf { ... }` — recomputes when its inputs change but only notifies downstream readers when the RESULT changes. The classic case is turning a constantly moving scroll position into a rarely flipping boolean.

Wrap these in `remember` so they survive recomposition, and use `snapshotFlow { ... }` when a coroutine needs to observe Compose state as a Flow.

Do not reach for `derivedStateOf` on a cheap one-to-one mapping — it adds a snapshot object and an extra layer of bookkeeping for nothing. It earns its keep only when the input changes far more often than the output.

questions.question: What is state hoisting? Why is it the recommended pattern?
questions.answer:
State hoisting moves state OUT of a composable into its caller. The composable becomes stateless: it receives current state and a callback to change it.

Benefits:
• Reusability — the same composable can be plugged into different state owners.
• Testability — render with any input, verify the callback is invoked correctly.
• Single source of truth — the parent (often a ViewModel) owns the state; children render it.
• Easier preview — pass plain values without setting up a state holder.

Simplest hoisting: replace `var x by remember { ... }` inside a composable with `value: X` and `onValueChange: (X) -> Unit` parameters.

questions.question: How do you connect a ViewModel + StateFlow to Compose UI?
questions.answer:
The ViewModel owns the screen state as a `StateFlow<UiState>` and the composable reads it with `collectAsStateWithLifecycle()`.

• The ViewModel is the only thing that mutates that state, normally through a private `MutableStateFlow` plus `_state.update { it.copy(...) }`, exposing the read-only view with `asStateFlow()`.
• The screen collects with `collectAsStateWithLifecycle()` from `androidx.lifecycle:lifecycle-runtime-compose`, which stops collecting below STARTED. Plain `collectAsState()` keeps collecting behind a backgrounded screen and is the wrong default on Android.
• User actions travel back as method references (`onRefresh = vm::reload`), never by the composable mutating state itself.
• `viewModelScope` is cancelled when the ViewModel is cleared, so work started there dies with the screen.
• Derive state from a repository flow with `stateIn(viewModelScope, SharingStarted.WhileSubscribed(5_000), initial)`, so it survives a rotation but stops once the screen is really gone.

Keep the ViewModel out of the reusable composable: the screen-level composable takes it and passes plain values plus lambdas down to a stateless content composable, which is the one you preview and test.

One-shot effects (a snackbar, a navigation command) are the awkward part. Either model them as a field of the state that the UI acknowledges, or expose a `Channel`/`SharedFlow` consumed inside a `LaunchedEffect` — and be ready to say why a plain StateFlow is a bad fit for them.

questions.question: What are LaunchedEffect, DisposableEffect, SideEffect, and produceState?
questions.answer:
Compose effect handlers exist because a composable body may re-run at any moment, so a side effect needs to start, restart and clean up in step with composition.

• `LaunchedEffect(key1, ...) { ... }` — launches a coroutine when the composable enters composition, cancels and relaunches it when a key changes, cancels it on exit. For animations, a debounced search, or a load tied to an argument.
• `DisposableEffect(key1, ...) { ... onDispose { ... } }` — for anything that must be unregistered: listeners, sensors, BroadcastReceivers, LifecycleObservers.
• `SideEffect { ... }` — runs after every successful recomposition. For publishing Compose state into a non-Compose object such as an analytics client.
• `produceState(initialValue, key) { value = ... }` — a LaunchedEffect and a State in one helper, for turning a suspend call or a callback into observable state.
• `rememberCoroutineScope()` — a scope tied to the composition, for coroutines started from an event handler like `onClick`, where LaunchedEffect does not apply.
• `rememberUpdatedState(value)` — captures the latest value inside a long-lived effect you deliberately do not want to restart.
• `snapshotFlow { state }` — reads Compose state as a Flow inside an effect.

Never start a coroutine or mutate anything outside the composable from its body. Two recurring mistakes worth naming: `LaunchedEffect(Unit)` for an effect that actually depends on a parameter, which then runs with a stale value (that is what `rememberUpdatedState` fixes), and using `LaunchedEffect` for navigation, which re-fires whenever the composable re-enters composition.

questions.question: What causes excessive recomposition and how do you minimize it?
questions.answer:
Excessive recomposition comes from composables Compose cannot skip, and the fix is nearly always to make parameters comparable or to move the state read further down the tree.

Where it comes from:
• A composable the compiler marked non-skippable — the Compose compiler report says so explicitly, and it is the first thing to look at.
• Reading state too high in the tree, which invalidates the whole subtree. Push the read into the leaf that needs it, or defer it into a lambda so only layout or draw re-runs.
• Passing a whole state object down when the child needs one field of it.
• Unkeyed `LazyColumn` items — without `key = { it.id }` an insertion recomposes every row after it.
• Genuinely unstable parameters — a `MutableList`, or a class from a module built without the Compose compiler. Use `kotlinx.collections.immutable` or `@Immutable`.

What changed: with strong skipping mode on by default (the Compose compiler shipped with Kotlin 2.0.20 and later), composables with unstable parameters are still skippable, compared by instance identity, and lambdas are memoized automatically. Blanket advice to wrap every lambda in `remember { { ... } }` predates that and is now mostly noise.

How to measure: recomposition counts in the Layout Inspector, the Compose compiler metrics and reports for the skippable and restartable breakdown, and a Macrobenchmark trace for the frames that actually janked. Fix what the numbers point at, not what looks suspicious.

questions.question: In what order do the Activity lifecycle callbacks fire, and which one runs only once per instance?
questions.answer:
An Activity is the entry point for one screen, and the system drives it through a fixed sequence of callbacks.

• onCreate(savedInstanceState) — Activity created. Inflate UI, restore state. Called ONCE per Activity instance.
• onStart — Activity becomes visible.
• onResume — Activity in foreground, receiving input.
• onPause — losing focus (another Activity in front, multi-window). Pause animations, save anything ephemeral. Called BEFORE onStop and BEFORE the next Activity's onResume.
• onStop — no longer visible.
• onRestart — coming back from stopped (after onStop, before onStart).
• onDestroy — Activity being torn down. Last call. Configuration changes recreate the Activity.
• onSaveInstanceState(out) — pre-onStop hook to save UI state into a Bundle (rotation / process death recovery).

Fragments mirror this with their own callbacks (`onAttach → onCreate → onCreateView → onViewCreated → onStart → onResume → onPause → onStop → onDestroyView → onDestroy → onDetach`).

A Compose-first app still has exactly one Activity, so the lifecycle is where you scope flow collection with `repeatOnLifecycle(STARTED)` and where the process-death Bundle arrives.

questions.question: What is a Fragment? When do you use Fragments vs Activities?
questions.answer:
A Fragment is a reusable, self-contained piece of UI that lives inside an Activity (or another Fragment). Has its own lifecycle, view tree, and back stack support.

Use Fragments when:
• Multi-pane layouts (master/detail on tablet vs single-pane on phone) — swap fragments in/out.
• Multiple screens behind a single Activity — common with the `Navigation` library.
• Reusable UI components needing their own lifecycle hooks (e.g. a permissions flow).

A Compose-first app usually has no Fragments at all: one Activity hosts composable destinations. Fragments remain in View-based codebases and in mixed apps, where a Compose screen is hosted inside a Fragment through `ComposeView`.

Gotchas: Fragments have TWO lifecycles (the fragment and its view) — observe `viewLifecycleOwner` for view-bound state, `this` for fragment-bound state. Null out a view binding in `onDestroyView`, or the fragment keeps the whole destroyed view tree alive.

questions.question: What is an Intent? Explicit vs implicit, and how do you get a result back?
questions.answer:
An Intent is a message describing an operation to perform. Used to:
• Start an Activity.
• Start or bind a Service.
• Send a Broadcast.

Two flavors:
• Explicit — you name the exact component (`Intent(ctx, ProfileActivity::class.java)`). Used for in-app navigation.
• Implicit — you name an action (e.g. `Intent.ACTION_VIEW` plus a URI). The system picks an app that can handle it. Used for sharing, dialing, opening links.

Intents carry data in extras (a Bundle). Keep them small — an oversized extra throws `TransactionTooLargeException`, because the whole thing crosses a Binder transaction.

To get a result back, use the Activity Result API: `registerForActivityResult(contract) { result -> }` at construction time, then `launch(...)`. It replaces `startActivityForResult` / `onActivityResult`, both deprecated, and it survives process death and rotation because the callback is re-registered before the result is delivered.

One trap: since Android 11, package-visibility filtering means `resolveActivity` returns null for apps you haven't declared in `<queries>`, so it is not a reliable "can anyone handle this?" check. Catch `ActivityNotFoundException` around `startActivity` instead.

questions.question: How do you handle configuration changes (rotation) on Android?
questions.answer:
By default, configuration changes (rotation, locale, dark-mode flip, multi-window resize) trigger Activity destruction + recreation. Strategies to keep state:

• ViewModel — survives configuration changes; tied to the ViewModelStoreOwner (Activity / Fragment / NavBackStackEntry). Idiomatic place for screen state.
• `onSaveInstanceState(out: Bundle)` — small Bundle for transient UI state (selected tab, scroll, draft text). Used after process death too.
• `rememberSaveable` (Compose) — wraps the same mechanism for composables.
• `android:configChanges="orientation|screenSize"` — opts out of recreation. Use sparingly: you must handle layout updates manually and miss the recreation flow.
• Saved State Module (`SavedStateHandle` in ViewModel) — persists key/values that survive process death AND rotation.

questions.question: Which parts of an app have to be declared in AndroidManifest.xml rather than in code?
questions.answer:
The manifest is how an app tells the system what it contains, before any of its code runs.

It lives at `app/src/main/AndroidManifest.xml` and declares:

• Application-level attributes — name, theme, icon, backup rules.
• Components — `<activity>`, `<service>`, `<receiver>`, `<provider>`. A component that is not declared cannot be started at all.
• Intent filters — which intents each component handles (launcher, deep links, share targets). Anything with an intent filter needs an explicit `android:exported` value.
• Permissions — `<uses-permission>`; dangerous ones still need a runtime request.
• Hardware and software requirements — `<uses-feature>` (camera, NFC), which also drives Play Store device filtering.
• Network security config — cleartext policy, certificate pinning, debug-only trust anchors.

What does NOT belong here: `applicationId`, `minSdk`, `targetSdk` and `versionCode`/`versionName` come from the Gradle build file and are injected at build time.

Gradle merges the main manifest with build-variant and library manifests into one file; when a library adds a permission or a provider you did not expect, the merged result under `build/intermediates/merged_manifests/` and the merger report are where you find it.
questions.code_example:
<!-- AndroidManifest.xml — main pieces -->
<manifest xmlns:android="http://schemas.android.com/apk/res/android">

  <uses-permission android:name="android.permission.INTERNET" />
  <uses-permission android:name="android.permission.CAMERA" />
  <uses-feature android:name="android.hardware.camera" android:required="false" />

  <application
    android:name=".MyApp"
    android:allowBackup="true"
    android:icon="@mipmap/ic_launcher"
    android:roundIcon="@mipmap/ic_launcher_round"
    android:theme="@style/Theme.MyApp"
    android:networkSecurityConfig="@xml/network_security_config">

    <activity
      android:name=".HomeActivity"
      android:exported="true">
      <intent-filter>
        <action android:name="android.intent.action.MAIN" />
        <category android:name="android.intent.category.LAUNCHER" />
      </intent-filter>
    </activity>

    <!-- Deep link -->
    <activity android:name=".ProfileActivity" android:exported="true">
      <intent-filter android:autoVerify="true">
        <action android:name="android.intent.action.VIEW" />
        <category android:name="android.intent.category.DEFAULT" />
        <category android:name="android.intent.category.BROWSABLE" />
        <data android:scheme="https"
              android:host="example.com"
              android:pathPrefix="/u/" />
      </intent-filter>
    </activity>

    <service android:name=".SyncService" android:exported="false" />
    <receiver android:name=".BootReceiver" android:exported="true">
      <intent-filter><action android:name="android.intent.action.BOOT_COMPLETED"/></intent-filter>
    </receiver>

    <provider
      android:name="androidx.core.content.FileProvider"
      android:authorities="${applicationId}.fileprovider"
      android:exported="false"
      android:grantUriPermissions="true">
      <meta-data android:name="android.support.FILE_PROVIDER_PATHS" android:resource="@xml/file_paths"/>
    </provider>
  </application>
</manifest>

questions.question: How do runtime permissions work on Android?
questions.answer:
Android grades permissions by risk, and only the dangerous ones need a runtime request.

• Normal — granted at install time (internet, vibrate). Declaring them in the manifest is all it takes.
• Dangerous — privacy-sensitive (camera, location, contacts). Declared AND requested at runtime, and the user can revoke them later.
• Special — system-managed (overlay, exact alarms, all-files access). No in-app dialog exists; you send the user to a Settings toggle.

The request flow:

1. Declare the permission in the manifest.
2. Check with `ContextCompat.checkSelfPermission` — never assume a previous grant is still there.
3. If not granted, launch the Activity Result contract (`RequestPermission` or `RequestMultiplePermissions`). The old `requestPermissions` / `onRequestPermissionsResult` pair is deprecated.
4. If `shouldShowRequestPermissionRationale` is true, explain why before asking again.
5. On permanent denial the system dialog stops appearing and returns denied immediately, so the only remaining path is a deep link into app settings.

Recent changes worth knowing: POST_NOTIFICATIONS became a runtime permission in Android 13; Android 14 added partial photo access (`READ_MEDIA_VISUAL_USER_SELECTED`), so a granted media permission may cover only the photos the user picked. Best of all, the Photo Picker needs no permission at all — prefer it over asking for READ_MEDIA_IMAGES.

questions.question: Name the layers in Google's recommended Android architecture and what each one owns.
questions.answer:
Google's recommended architecture is a layered design with strictly unidirectional data flow.

• UI layer — Compose UI plus a ViewModel. Renders UI state, forwards user events. Owns no business logic.
• Domain layer (optional) — UseCase / Interactor classes that orchestrate a complex flow or combine several repositories. Skip it until a ViewModel starts doing real work.
• Data layer — one Repository per type of data, and it is the single source of truth for that data. The Repository hides its sources (RemoteDataSource over Retrofit, LocalDataSource over Room or DataStore) behind a domain-shaped API.

The rules that make it work: state flows down and events flow up; the screen exposes one `StateFlow<UiState>` collected with `collectAsStateWithLifecycle()`; the UI never mutates state, it calls the ViewModel; the ViewModel has no Android framework dependencies, so it unit-tests on the JVM; and data classes cross layer boundaries as domain models, not DTOs or entities.

The full guide is at developer.android.com/topic/architecture.

questions.question: What is the Repository pattern? Why use it on Android?
questions.answer:
A Repository is a single class that owns access to a domain entity, hiding WHERE the data comes from (network, DB, cache, in-memory).

Why:
• Single source of truth — UI talks to Repository, not directly to network.
• Offline-first becomes natural — Repository may serve from DB while refreshing from network.
• Testable — substitute a fake Repository to test ViewModels.
• Cross-cutting concerns (caching strategy, retry, mapping) live in one place, not duplicated across screens.

Best practice: Repository returns DOMAIN models (clean Kotlin types), never DTOs. Mappers convert wire/db rows ↔ domain at the boundary.

questions.question: What is unidirectional data flow (UDF) in Android UI?
questions.answer:
Unidirectional data flow means state travels down from the ViewModel and events travel back up from the UI.

• State flows DOWN — ViewModel → Composable / Fragment.
• Events flow UP — user actions → callbacks on the ViewModel.
• The UI never mutates state directly; it only asks for a change.

The resulting structure:

• `data class UiState(...)` — one immutable object that is the single source of truth for the screen.
• `StateFlow<UiState>` exposed by the ViewModel and collected with `collectAsStateWithLifecycle()`, so collection stops below STARTED.
• `fun onAction(action: UiAction)` (or individual methods) receives events.

Why it is worth the ceremony: there is exactly one place to look when the screen is wrong, the UI becomes a pure function of state so you can test it by handing it a state object, every action is loggable, and it matches Compose's rendering model — the same state always produces the same UI.

One-off events (navigate, show a snackbar) are the awkward case. Model them as a field in the state that the UI marks as consumed, or send them through a `Channel`; a `SharedFlow` with replay will re-fire them after a rotation.

questions.question: What is Clean Architecture? How does it map to Android?
questions.answer:
Clean Architecture splits code into concentric layers whose dependencies all point inward, toward pure business rules.

• Domain (innermost) — business rules and entities. Pure Kotlin. No Android, no networking, no DB.
• Use Cases / Interactors — orchestrate those rules for one specific operation.
• Adapters / data layer — map external data (DB rows, API payloads) to domain models.
• Frameworks (outermost) — Android, Retrofit, Room, everything replaceable.

The Dependency Rule is the whole idea: the domain never imports Android or Retrofit. The data layer implements interfaces the domain declares, and DI supplies the implementation at runtime, so dependencies point inward even though data flows both ways.

On Android this materializes as Gradle modules — `:domain`, `:data`, `:app`, or feature modules over `:core:domain` and `:core:data`. A pure-Kotlin domain module keeps its tests on the JVM (milliseconds, no emulator) and makes it a compile error to leak a framework type into business logic.

When it is worth it: medium and larger apps, several teams, long-lived products. For a small app it is ceremony — Google's recommended architecture is the same idea with three layers and far fewer classes.

questions.question: How would you split a large Android app into Gradle modules, and which module depends on which?
questions.answer:
A large app is normally split into one thin app module, one module per feature, and a set of shared core modules.

• `:app` — thin entry module that composes everything: nav graph, DI wiring, Application class.
• `:feature:*` — one per screen or flow: Compose UI, ViewModel, screen-specific state.
• `:core:domain` — pure Kotlin business types and use cases.
• `:core:data` — repository implementations, mappers, data sources.
• `:core:network` — Retrofit, interceptors, serialization config.
• `:core:database` — Room database and DAOs.
• `:core:designsystem` — colors, typography, shared composables.
• `:core:common` — small utilities (dates, formatting, dispatchers).

Dependency direction is the part interviewers actually probe: features depend on core modules and never on each other, `:app` is the only module that sees every feature, and cross-feature navigation goes through a route contract declared in a core module. A feature should compile against `:core:domain` interfaces, with `:app` binding the implementations.

What you gain: parallel compilation and far smaller incremental rebuilds, boundaries enforced by `internal` visibility instead of code review, per-module tests, and the ability to swap an implementation per build variant.

Share Gradle configuration through convention plugins in `build-logic` (a change in `buildSrc` invalidates the whole build cache), and declare versions once in a `libs.versions.toml` version catalog.

questions.question: What makes Android code hard to unit-test, and which patterns fix it?
questions.answer:
Android code becomes untestable when it reaches out for its dependencies instead of receiving them. Every pattern below follows from fixing that.

• Constructor injection — no static `getInstance()`, no framework singleton reached from business code.
• Wrap framework APIs behind interfaces — `Clock`, `Logger`, `LocaleProvider` — so a test can supply a deterministic version instead of the real clock or the real locale.
• Keep ViewModels free of Android imports: Kotlin types plus repository interfaces. Their tests then run on the JVM in milliseconds.
• Inject the dispatcher instead of hardcoding `Dispatchers.IO`, and use `kotlinx-coroutines-test` — `runTest`, `StandardTestDispatcher`, virtual time, `Dispatchers.setMain`.
• Prefer fakes over mocks for repositories: a fake keeps working as the interface evolves, while a mock encodes today's exact call sequence and breaks on every refactor.
• Compose UI: test a stateless content composable with `createComposeRule()` and a hand-built state object, addressing nodes by `onNodeWithText` / `onNodeWithTag`.
• Instrumented tests: `androidx.test.ext.junit` plus Hilt test rules; Robolectric when you want framework classes without a device.

Pitfalls: asserting on implementation details instead of observable behaviour, mocking types you do not own, driving everything through an Activity instead of testing ViewModel and UI separately, and tests that depend on real time or the real main dispatcher.

questions.question: What are Retrofit and OkHttp? How do they relate?
questions.answer:
OkHttp is the client that actually moves the bytes, and Retrofit is a typed API layer generated on top of it.

OkHttp owns the transport: connection pooling and reuse, redirects, gzip, HTTP/2, timeouts, the response cache, certificate pinning, and the interceptor chain.

Retrofit turns an annotated Kotlin interface into an implementation. It builds the request from the annotations, hands it to an OkHttp `Call`, and converts the response body into your type. Functions can be `suspend`, return `Response<T>` for access to status and headers, or return `Call<T>`.

How they fit together in practice:
• Use OkHttp on its own only for raw HTTP — streaming downloads, arbitrary URLs, WebSockets.
• Use Retrofit for a typed REST API; it removes essentially all request-building boilerplate.
• Add a converter to deserialize JSON — `kotlinx.serialization` is the default in Kotlin projects; Moshi and Gson still appear in older code.
• Add interceptors (logging, auth, retry) to the OkHttp client, not to Retrofit, and share one `OkHttpClient` across every API interface — it owns the connection pool and thread pool, so creating several wastes both.

If the networking code has to be multiplatform, Ktor client is the alternative — Retrofit and OkHttp are JVM/Android only.

questions.question: Application vs network interceptors in OkHttp — what is the difference, and what belongs in each?
questions.answer:
An OkHttp `Interceptor` takes a `Chain` and returns a `Response`, so it can observe, rewrite, retry or short-circuit any call.

• Application interceptors — run once per call, see the logical request and response, and do not run at all when the response is served from cache. They can short-circuit without touching the network. Almost everything belongs here.
• Network interceptors — run on every network round trip, including each redirect and retry, and see the wire-level request with its `Content-Length`, `Host` and encoding headers. Use them for low-level instrumentation and for rewriting cache headers.

Good things to put in an interceptor:
• Common headers — User-Agent, Accept-Language, API version, device id.
• Logging (`HttpLoggingInterceptor`, with `redactHeader("Authorization")`).
• Request signing (HMAC).
• A custom retry or circuit breaker for transient failures.
• Stubbed responses in debug builds.

Token refresh after a 401 is the one case that should NOT be an interceptor: use OkHttp's `Authenticator`. It is invoked only on an auth challenge, OkHttp retries the original request with whatever you return, and it stops automatically instead of spinning in a retry loop. Refresh under a mutex so ten parallel 401s trigger one refresh.

Keep each interceptor single-purpose, and remember they run in the order you add them.

questions.question: How do you handle errors and typed responses with Retrofit?
questions.answer:
Retrofit throws on a non-2xx response when a suspend function returns the body type directly, so something has to catch. The options:

• Throw and catch at one boundary — simplest. The Repository wraps every call and maps exceptions to a domain result type.
• Return `Response<T>` — status code, headers and error body without an exception; you inspect and decide.
• A sealed `NetworkResponse<Success, Error>` from a third-party call adapter — success and typed error arrive as data.
• Your own `CallAdapter.Factory` — every endpoint returns a Result-like sealed type directly.

The usual setup keeps the API interface throwing and maps exceptions once, in the Repository. Distinguish the three cases, because they need different handling:
• `IOException` — offline, DNS failure, timeout. Retryable, and the user should be told the network is the problem.
• `HttpException` — the server answered and said no. Read `code()` and parse `errorBody()` for the server's own error payload; 401 is not the same as 422.
• A serialization exception — the contract drifted. That is a bug, not something to retry.

Do not let `HttpException` reach the ViewModel: the UI layer should receive a domain error it knows how to render, otherwise error handling ends up duplicated in every screen.

questions.question: How do you cache HTTP responses on Android with OkHttp?
questions.answer:
OkHttp ships a built-in HTTP cache that respects standard `Cache-Control` headers. Configure it with `Cache(directory, maxSize)` and hand it to `OkHttpClient.Builder`; it stores GET responses only, and it is shared by every call made through that client.

Behavior follows the HTTP caching spec (RFC 9111):
• The server's `Cache-Control: max-age` is honored.
• `Cache-Control: no-store` disables caching for that response.
• Conditional revalidation with `ETag` / `Last-Modified` happens automatically — a 304 refreshes the stored entry without re-downloading the body, which is the biggest practical win.

When the server sends nothing useful, override the policy with interceptors:
• A network interceptor that rewrites the response `Cache-Control` on the way in.
• An application interceptor that rewrites the request to `only-if-cached` with a `maxStale` when there is no connectivity, so an offline read hits the cache instead of failing.

For a genuinely offline-first app, do not lean on the HTTP cache: it cannot be queried, it expires on its own schedule, and the OS can evict the whole cache directory at any time. Use Room as the source of truth and treat the network as a refresh source.

questions.question: How do you upload a file with Retrofit, and how do you report progress?
questions.answer:
Retrofit sends a multipart body when you mark the function `@Multipart` and pass each field as a `@Part`.

• `@Part` — a `RequestBody` for a scalar field, or a `MultipartBody.Part` when the server needs a filename.
• `@PartMap` — dynamic parts as `Map<String, RequestBody>`.
• `@Body RequestBody` — a raw single-stream upload with no multipart envelope, when the API takes the bytes directly.

Build bodies with the OkHttp extensions `File.asRequestBody(mediaType)` and `String.toRequestBody(...)`. The old static `RequestBody.create(...)` overloads are deprecated, and streaming from a `File` matters: reading the file into a ByteArray first is what makes large uploads OOM.

Progress: OkHttp gives no callback, so wrap the `RequestBody` in one that counts bytes as they are written to the sink. Throttle what you emit — `writeTo` fires per 8 KB segment, and updating a StateFlow that often will cost you more than the upload.

Reliability: an upload that must survive the user leaving the app belongs in a WorkManager `CoroutineWorker` with a network constraint, backoff and a foreground notification for long ones — not in `viewModelScope`, which dies with the screen. For very large files use a resumable protocol where the server tracks an offset, so a dropped connection does not restart from zero.

questions.question: Which real-time transport do you pick on Android — WebSocket, SSE or long-poll?
questions.answer:
WebSocket is full duplex, SSE is one-way from server to client, and long-poll is the fallback that costs the most battery.

• WebSocket — a single upgraded connection carrying frames both ways. `client.newWebSocket(request, listener)` in OkHttp. Pick it when the client also sends: chat, presence, collaborative editing. Interceptors still apply to the handshake request, so auth headers work as usual.
• Server-Sent Events — plain HTTP streaming, server to client only, with automatic reconnect and event ids in the protocol itself. The `okhttp-sse` artifact (`EventSources.createFactory(client)`) implements it. Simpler than a WebSocket and it survives proxies that mangle upgrades; ideal for feeds, notifications and progress.
• Long-poll — request, the server holds it open until there is data, respond, immediately re-request. Trivial to implement on the server, worst for battery and connection churn. A fallback, not a design.
• gRPC bidirectional streaming — strong typing and multiplexing when the backend already speaks it.

The part interviewers push on is lifecycle, not the transport. Close the socket when the app goes to background (a socket owned by `viewModelScope` dies with the screen; one that must outlive it belongs to a foreground service). Reconnect with exponential backoff plus jitter, or a thundering herd hits the server after every outage. Send heartbeats, because carrier NATs drop idle connections silently and you learn about it only on the next write. Expose the stream as a `callbackFlow` so collection is lifecycle-scoped and the socket closes when the collector goes away.

None of these deliver anything while the process is dead — that is what FCM is for.

questions.question: What persistence options are available on Android and when do you choose each?
questions.answer:
Pick the smallest tool that fits the shape of the data: key-value settings, structured rows, or files.

• DataStore (Preferences or Proto) — the default for settings and small key-value state. Reads through `Flow`, writes through a suspending transaction, no `commit()`-on-main footgun. Preferences keys are typed at the call site; Proto gives a real schema.
• SharedPreferences — the legacy key-value store, still present in most codebases. The first read blocks on disk and there is no type safety, so new code should use DataStore (with `SharedPreferencesMigration` to move existing values across once).
• Room — the SQLite layer for anything with structure, relations, queries, or more than a handful of rows. Compile-checked SQL, `Flow` queries that re-emit on change, migrations, FTS, Paging integration.
• Files — `context.filesDir` for app-private data, `context.cacheDir` for anything regenerable (the OS deletes it under storage pressure), `context.getExternalFilesDir(...)` for app-private files on shared storage.
• MediaStore and the Photo Picker — the only supported way to reach user-visible photos, video and audio under scoped storage. Direct paths into shared storage stopped working.
• Android Keystore — cryptographic keys, hardware-backed where the device supports it. Encrypt sensitive values with a Keystore key and store the ciphertext in one of the stores above.

Two sizing rules that get asked about: never put a large blob or a growing list in Preferences DataStore, because every commit rewrites and re-parses the whole file; and never keep tokens or personal data in plain SharedPreferences, which is readable on a rooted device and can end up in a cloud backup.

questions.question: What is Room? Show a basic Database, DAO, and migration.
questions.answer:
Room is a compile-time SQL layer over SQLite: you declare the schema and the queries, and it generates the implementation.

• Entities — `@Entity` classes that map to tables.
• DAOs — `@Dao` interfaces with `@Query`, `@Insert`, `@Upsert`, `@Update`, `@Delete`.
• Database — a `@Database` class extending `RoomDatabase`, listing entities, version and DAOs.

Room parses your SQL at build time, so a typo or a column you renamed fails the build instead of crashing a user. A DAO function can be `suspend` (one shot, moved off the main thread for you) or return `Flow<T>`, which re-emits whenever a write touches one of the tables the query reads.

Migrations are the part that goes wrong in production. Bump `version` and either supply a `Migration` with the SQL, or — with `exportSchema = true` — declare `@AutoMigration(from = 1, to = 2)` and let Room diff the exported schema JSON; only ambiguous changes such as a renamed column need a spec. Commit the exported schema JSON, or auto-migration and migration tests have nothing to compare against. `fallbackToDestructiveMigration` deletes user data, so it belongs in debug builds only.

Wire the compiler with KSP (`ksp("androidx.room:room-compiler")`); kapt is legacy and considerably slower. Room also supports Kotlin Multiplatform now, so the same entities and DAOs can be shared with iOS.

questions.question: What are TypeConverters in Room? When are they needed?
questions.answer:
Room natively understands only what SQLite stores: Int, Long, Float, Double, String and ByteArray. Anything else — `Date`, `UUID`, an enum, a value class, a list — needs a `@TypeConverter`: one function that maps your type down to a supported type, and a second one for the way back.

Rules:
• Each direction is its own `@TypeConverter` function, and both must be reachable by Room — a class registered with `@TypeConverters`, or an object.
• Register on the `@Database` class to cover everything, or on a single `@Entity` or field to keep the scope tight.
• Store enums by `name`, never by `ordinal` — reordering the constants would silently re-map every existing row.
• A converted column is opaque to SQL. You cannot filter, sort or index on a list serialized to JSON, so anything you need to query belongs in a real column, an `@Embedded` object, or a relation table.
• Converters are also the wrong place for large data: a serialized blob is read and parsed in full on every query that touches the row.

questions.question: Preferences DataStore vs Proto DataStore — what's the difference?
questions.answer:
Both DataStore flavors are async and transactional — the difference is whether a schema is enforced.

• Preferences DataStore — schemaless. Keys are typed at the call site (`stringPreferencesKey`, `booleanPreferencesKey`), the file itself is not, and a typo in a key name is a silent default value. Cheapest to adopt and the direct migration target for SharedPreferences. Best for a handful of unrelated values (theme, last screen, a flag).
• Proto DataStore — schemaful. You describe the data once, as a Protocol Buffers message or as any type with a `Serializer` (a `@Serializable` Kotlin class with kotlinx.serialization works and skips protoc entirely). Typed reads, real defaults, controlled schema evolution. Best for settings that belong together as one object.

Shared behavior: one file per DataStore, reads exposed as a `Flow` that re-emits after every write, writes through a suspending `edit { }` / `updateData { }` that is atomic — a crash mid-write cannot leave a half-written file, because it writes to a temp file and renames. Errors arrive in the Flow, so handle `IOException` with `catch` rather than letting it crash a collector.

One process-level rule: exactly one DataStore instance per file. The `by preferencesDataStore(...)` delegate enforces it; constructing a second one over the same file throws.

Neither is a database. Every commit rewrites and re-parses the whole file, so anything large or growing belongs in Room.

questions.question: How do you do offline-first sync between local DB and server?
questions.answer:
Offline-first means the UI reads from the local database and never waits on the network to render. The network is only a refresh source.

The pattern:

1. The UI collects a `Flow` from Room, so whatever is stored is on screen immediately, on the first frame, with no spinner.
2. A repository refreshes from the API on demand or on a schedule and writes the result into Room; the Flow re-emits and the UI updates itself.
3. A local write goes into Room straight away and is marked pending — a `dirty` flag or a row in an outbox table — so the change is visible before the server has heard about it.
4. A WorkManager worker drains the outbox with backoff under a network constraint, and clears the flag when the server confirms.
5. Conflicts are resolved by an explicit rule — server-authoritative timestamps, last-write-wins, or a field-level merge. Decide it per field; "we'll figure it out later" means data loss.

The details that separate a working sync from a broken one: generate ids on the client (UUID) so an optimistic row survives the server assigning its own; enqueue with a unique work name so a burst of edits does not queue a hundred workers; return `Result.retry()` for an `IOException` but `Result.failure()` for a 4xx, which will never succeed no matter how often you retry; keep a per-record `updatedAt` so a pull can tell which side is newer; and never let a failed sync surface as a blocking error — the user's data is already saved locally.

questions.question: How do you securely store secrets (tokens, keys) on Android?
questions.answer:
The only real secure store on the device is the Android Keystore; everything else is a wrapper around it.

• Android Keystore — generates and holds a key whose material never enters your process. You ask it to encrypt, decrypt or sign. Hardware-backed on most devices (TEE, or StrongBox where present), the key can require the user to authenticate first, and it can be configured to be invalidated when a new biometric is enrolled.
• Encrypt values yourself with a Keystore-backed AES/GCM key and store the ciphertext in DataStore, a file or a Room column. `androidx.security-crypto` (`EncryptedSharedPreferences`, `EncryptedFile`) used to do that wrapping for you, but that library is deprecated — treat existing usage as legacy and do not start new code with it.
• Never ship a secret inside the APK. Strings, BuildConfig fields, resources and native libraries are all trivially extracted; anything embedded in the binary is public. Have the server issue short-lived tokens instead, and attest the caller with Play Integrity if the endpoint needs to trust the client.

Practices interviewers look for: store tokens, never passwords; keep the access token in memory and only the refresh token at rest; gate genuinely sensitive actions with `BiometricPrompt`, using the `CryptoObject` form so authentication actually unlocks the key rather than just showing a dialog; exclude your data from auto-backup with `android:dataExtractionRules` so it does not leave the device in the clear; pin certificates (or use the network security config) for the auth endpoints; and remember R8 obfuscation is friction, not security.

questions.question: What is dependency injection and why use it on Android?
questions.answer:
Dependency injection (DI) means giving an object its collaborators from outside, rather than letting it construct or look them up itself.

Why it matters on Android:
• Testability — swap a real service for a fake in a unit test without touching the class under test.
• Explicit dependencies — the constructor signature is the complete list of what a class needs.
• Lifetime control — singleton vs per-screen vs per-feature is decided in one place instead of in scattered `getInstance()` calls.
• It removes the service-locator anti-pattern, where a class reaches into a global to find what it needs and nothing in its signature says so.

Approaches:
• Manual DI — plain constructor injection with a container built in `Application.onCreate`. Perfectly fine for a small app and worth knowing, because every framework is doing this for you.
• Hilt — Google's recommended framework, built on Dagger 2. Annotation-driven, generated at compile time, and it knows about Android lifecycles (`@HiltViewModel`, `@AndroidEntryPoint`).
• Dagger 2 — the full toolkit with manual components and subcomponents. More boilerplate; used where Hilt's fixed component tree is not enough.
• Koin — a runtime DSL with no code generation. Easy to start with, but a missing binding fails when the screen opens rather than when you build. `koin-annotations` adds KSP-generated modules and compile-time checks.
• kotlin-inject and Kodein — niche; kotlin-inject is the usual pick when the object graph has to be Kotlin Multiplatform.

questions.question: What is Hilt? How does it differ from Dagger 2?
questions.answer:
Hilt is Google's official DI library for Android, and it is Dagger 2 with the component tree already written for you.

• Entry points are annotations: `@HiltAndroidApp` on the Application, `@AndroidEntryPoint` on Activity/Fragment/Service, `@HiltViewModel` on ViewModels, `hiltViewModel()` in Compose.
• The component hierarchy is predefined and mapped to Android lifecycles — SingletonComponent, ActivityRetainedComponent, ActivityComponent, ViewModelComponent, FragmentComponent, ServiceComponent.
• `@InstallIn(...)` says which component a module belongs to, so a module is added by declaring it rather than by being listed in a component interface.
• You never write `Component` or `Subcomponent` interfaces, and you never hand-wire an Activity to its component.

Dagger 2 is still doing the work underneath, and Hilt does not hide it: `@Module`, `@Provides`, `@Binds`, `@Qualifier` and multibindings are all Dagger. If you need a custom component with a lifetime Android does not have, you drop to `@DefineComponent` or plain Dagger; most apps never do.

Setup is the `com.google.dagger.hilt.android` Gradle plugin plus `ksp("com.google.dagger:hilt-compiler")`. Hilt's processor runs under KSP now; kapt still works but is legacy, roughly doubles annotation-processing time and drags in the old compiler frontend.

Choosing: greenfield goes to Hilt. A large existing Dagger codebase can migrate gradually, since the two coexist in one build.

questions.question: What are scopes in Hilt and how do they map to component lifecycles?
questions.answer:
A Hilt scope pins a binding to the lifetime of one Android component, from the whole application down to a single ViewModel.

• `@Singleton` → SingletonComponent — one instance for the process.
• `@ActivityRetainedScoped` → ActivityRetainedComponent — survives configuration changes; the same lifetime as the ViewModelStore, so it lives from the first `onCreate` until the Activity really finishes.
• `@ActivityScoped` → ActivityComponent — one per Activity instance, so a rotation gives you a new one.
• `@FragmentScoped` → FragmentComponent.
• `@ViewModelScoped` → ViewModelComponent — one instance shared by the collaborators of a single `@HiltViewModel`, released when that ViewModel is cleared.
• `@ServiceScoped` → ServiceComponent.

An unscoped binding is created fresh at every injection point, and that is the correct default. Scope only what holds state that must be shared, or what is genuinely expensive to build.

Two things that bite in interviews. A scoped binding that holds an Activity `Context` outlives the Activity and leaks it — inject `@ApplicationContext` unless you truly need the Activity one. And a binding in a wider component cannot depend on one in a narrower component: a `@Singleton` cannot take an `@ActivityScoped` type, which is the usual cause of a "cannot be provided" build error.

questions.question: What are @Qualifier and multibinding in Dagger/Hilt?
questions.answer:
A `@Qualifier` tells Dagger which of several bindings of the same type you mean, and multibinding collects many bindings into one `Set` or `Map`.

Qualifiers — annotate both the binding and the injection point with the same annotation:
• Several `OkHttpClient` instances (authenticated vs plain).
• Dispatchers: `@IoDispatcher`, `@MainDispatcher`, `@DefaultDispatcher`. Injecting the dispatcher is what makes a class testable with a test dispatcher.
• Several Retrofit instances against different base URLs.
Prefer a real qualifier annotation over `@Named("io")` — a typo in a string is a runtime surprise, a typo in an annotation is a compile error.

Multibinding — contribute into a collection that Dagger assembles:
• `@IntoSet` adds the binding to `Set<T>`.
• `@IntoMap` with `@StringKey("...")` or `@ClassKey(...)` adds it to a `Map<K, V>`.
• Inject the collection as `Set<@JvmSuppressWildcards T>`, or Kotlin's variance turns it into `Set<? extends T>` and Dagger cannot match it.

Multibinding is what makes feature modules composable: each feature contributes its navigation routes, its settings entries or its initializers, and the app module gets the union without ever importing the features. `Map<Class<*>, Provider<ViewModel>>` is the same mechanism that Dagger-based ViewModel factories were built on before Hilt.

questions.question: How do you replace dependencies in tests with Hilt?
questions.answer:
Hilt provides the `@HiltAndroidTest` rule and `@TestInstallIn` / `@UninstallModules` to swap real bindings for fakes in instrumented tests.

For plain unit tests, do not involve Hilt at all — construct the ViewModel or Repository with fakes directly. That is faster, simpler, and it keeps the test independent of the DI graph.

For instrumented and Compose UI tests:
• Annotate the test class `@HiltAndroidTest` and add `HiltAndroidRule` as rule order 0, before the Compose rule, then call `hiltRule.inject()` in `@Before`.
• Replace a whole module with `@TestInstallIn(components = [...], replaces = [...])` in the test source set — the modern way; the replacement applies to every test that sees it.
• `@UninstallModules(NetworkModule::class)` on one test class removes a module for that class only, when you need a one-off.
• `@BindValue` on a test field binds that exact instance into the graph, which is the quickest way to hand a test its own fake and then assert on it afterwards.
• The whole app needs a test runner that creates `HiltTestApplication` (a custom `AndroidJUnitRunner`), or nothing is injected.

For Compose, host the screen in a `ComponentActivity` annotated `@AndroidEntryPoint` declared in the debug manifest, and drive it with `createAndroidComposeRule`.

questions.question: Hilt vs Koin — when to choose which?
questions.answer:
Hilt buys compile-time verification of the whole object graph; Koin buys a plain Kotlin DSL and no code generation.

Hilt:
• KSP code generation — a missing, duplicated or miscoped binding fails the build, never a user's phone.
• No reflection and no runtime lookup, so resolution costs nothing at startup.
• First-party integration with Jetpack: ViewModel, Navigation, Compose, WorkManager.
• More annotations to learn, and build time grows with the graph.

Koin:
• A module is just a Kotlin function; nothing to generate, nothing to wait for.
• Runtime resolution — a missing binding throws when the screen opens, not when you build. `verify()` and `koin-annotations` (KSP) recover some of that safety.
• Multiplatform: the same modules work in a shared KMP module, where Hilt cannot go at all.
• Lower barrier to entry, less ergonomic once you need real scoping across many modules.

Choosing:
• Android-only app, one team, greenfield → Hilt, the official path.
• Shared KMP module → Koin (or kotlin-inject); Hilt is Android-only.
• Large codebase with many feature modules → Hilt, for the build-time guarantees and multibinding.
• Prototype or learning project → Koin, for the lower ceremony.

Either way the classes themselves should take their dependencies through the constructor, which keeps the choice reversible.

questions.question: What is an ANR? How do you avoid them?
questions.answer:
An ANR fires when the main thread fails to respond in time — roughly five seconds for an input event.

The system raises one when:
• An input event has not been handled within about 5 seconds.
• A BroadcastReceiver has not returned within ~10s in the foreground or ~60s in the background.
• A service started with `startForegroundService` does not call `startForeground` within its timeout.
• `Service.onCreate` / `onStartCommand` or a ContentProvider call overruns.

Avoid them by never blocking the main thread:
• Move I/O, database work and heavy CPU off main with coroutines and `Dispatchers.IO` / `Default`.
• No `Thread.sleep`, no `runBlocking`, no `.get()` on a future on the main thread.
• Watch for the blocking calls that do not look blocking: synchronous IPC (`Binder.transact`), the first SharedPreferences read, a Room query accidentally left non-suspend, inflating a huge layout, decoding a bitmap during scroll.
• Turn on `StrictMode` in debug builds so disk and network on main fail loudly while you develop.
• Profile with a system trace (Perfetto, from the Android Studio profiler) and look at the worst frames, not the average.

Diagnose in production with Play Console Vitals, which gives the main-thread stack at the moment of the timeout, and read `ApplicationExitInfo` on the next launch to find out why the previous process died — it reports ANRs, crashes and low-memory kills with the trace attached.

questions.question: How do you find and fix memory leaks on Android?
questions.answer:
A leak on Android is almost always something long-lived holding on to a destroyed Activity, Fragment or View.

Where they come from:
• A static field or singleton holding a `Context` — pass `applicationContext` to anything that outlives a screen.
• Inner classes and lambdas capturing `this` — a delayed `Handler` callback, a listener, a Runnable.
• Listeners registered with a system service, an event bus or a third-party SDK and never unregistered.
• Fragments keeping a `View`, a view binding or an adapter past `onDestroyView` — the fragment outlives its view tree, so the binding must be nulled there.
• Coroutines in `GlobalScope`, or a `CoroutineScope` you created yourself and never cancelled.
• Large bitmaps and drawables cached in a static field.

Find them:
• LeakCanary in debug builds — it watches destroyed Activities, Fragments, ViewModels and Services, and when one stays reachable it prints the exact reference chain holding it.
• Android Studio's Memory Profiler — rotate a screen a few times, capture a heap dump, and look for more than one instance of the same Activity.
• `adb shell dumpsys meminfo <package>` for a quick size check, and Play Vitals for real-user OOM rates.

Fix by shortening lifetimes rather than sprinkling `WeakReference`: scope work to `viewModelScope` / `lifecycleScope`, unregister in the matching lifecycle callback, use `DisposableEffect` in Compose, and keep state in a ViewModel that is cleared for you.

questions.question: What is jank? How do you measure and fix dropped frames?
questions.answer:
Jank is a frame that misses its deadline, so the display shows the previous one again and the user sees a stutter.

The budget is one refresh interval — about 16.7ms at 60Hz, 8.3ms at 120Hz — shared between your main-thread work and the RenderThread.

Measure:
• While developing — a system trace (Perfetto) from the Android Studio profiler. Every frame is a slice on the frame timeline, janky ones are flagged, and you can see which call overran.
• In CI — Macrobenchmark with `FrameTimingMetric`, which reports P50/P90/P99 frame durations for a scripted journey, so a regression fails the build instead of shipping.
• In production — the `JankStats` library reports per-frame durations from real devices, tagged with the state you attach (which screen was on top).
• Quick check — `adb shell dumpsys gfxinfo <package> framestats`.

Common causes and fixes:
• Work on the main thread during scroll: image decoding, JSON parsing, disk reads. Move it off and prefetch before the row is visible.
• Compose — reading state too high in the tree so a whole screen recomposes; unstable parameters that defeat skipping; allocating in a composable. Defer reads into lambdas (`Modifier.offset { }`, `graphicsLayer`), hoist state no higher than it needs to go, give `LazyColumn` items a stable `key`, and check the recomposition counts in Layout Inspector.
• Views — deep hierarchies and overdraw. Flatten with ConstraintLayout, drop redundant backgrounds, and use `DiffUtil` with stable ids so RecyclerView rebinds only what changed.
• The first frames of a screen running interpreted instead of compiled — that is what a baseline profile fixes.

questions.question: What does R8 do to a release build, and what breaks when its keep rules are wrong?
questions.answer:
R8 shrinks, optimizes and obfuscates your code in a single pass over the bytecode when you build a release variant. It replaced ProGuard as the default years ago, so `minifyEnabled` today means R8.

What it does:
• Shrinking — walks the reference graph from the entry points named in the manifest and drops every class, method and field nothing reaches.
• Optimization — inlining, dead-code elimination, class merging, devirtualization, constant folding, all whole-program.
• Obfuscation — renames what survives to short names, which shrinks the DEX further and makes casual reverse-engineering harder.
• Resource shrinking (`shrinkResources`) — removes drawables and strings no surviving code references.

Full mode is the default in current AGP: R8 optimizes more aggressively and assumes less about reflection than the old ProGuard-compatibility mode, so a library that used to work may now need explicit keep rules.

What breaks is anything resolved by name at runtime — reflection, JNI lookups, `Class.forName`, Gson's field names, class names sent to analytics. Those survive only if a rule keeps them. Most libraries ship consumer rules and need nothing from you, so when a release build crashes and the debug build does not, a missing `-keep` is the first suspect. Keep rules are also the reason a release APK can be larger than it should be: `-keep class com.app.** { *; }` disables shrinking for your whole app.

Always test the release variant before shipping, and upload `mapping.txt` to Play or Crashlytics — without it every production stack trace reads `a.b.c`.

questions.question: What are baseline profiles and what do they buy you?
questions.answer:
A baseline profile lists the methods ART should compile ahead of time at install, instead of interpreting them on first run.

Without one, a fresh install runs your code interpreted and JIT-compiles it as it goes, so the first launch and the first scroll are the slowest the app will ever be. Google measures roughly 30% faster cold start and visibly smoother first scrolls on real apps.

How you get one:
• Add the `androidx.baselineprofile` Gradle plugin and a benchmark module.
• Write a `BaselineProfileRule` test that drives the critical journeys — launch, scroll the main list, open a detail screen.
• Run `./gradlew :app:generateBaselineProfile` on a rooted emulator or an unlocked device; the plugin writes the rules into the app module and AGP packages them into the APK or AAB.
• Verify with Macrobenchmark: measure `StartupTimingMetric` with `CompilationMode.None()` against `CompilationMode.Partial()` and compare, rather than trusting that it helped.

`includeInStartupProfile = true` additionally produces a startup profile, which lets AGP reorder the DEX so startup classes sit together and fewer pages are faulted in.

Two things to say if asked what it does not do: it changes nothing on a device that has already run the app for a while (ART's own profile takes over), and Play separately distributes a cloud profile aggregated from real users, which combines with yours. Regenerate it when the critical journeys change — a stale profile just precompiles code nobody runs.

questions.question: How do you optimize app startup time on Android?
questions.answer:
Cold start is the case that matters: the process, the Application object and the first Activity all have to be created before anything reaches the screen.

• Cold — no process exists. Everything is built from scratch.
• Warm — the process is alive, the Activity has to be recreated.
• Hot — the Activity is still in memory and is only brought forward.

Measure:
• Logcat prints `Displayed com.app/.MainActivity: +XXXms` for the first frame.
• `adb shell am start -W` reports `TotalTime` for one launch.
• Macrobenchmark with `StartupTimingMetric` gives time-to-initial-display and time-to-full-display across iterations, on a device you choose.
• Play Vitals and Firebase Performance give the real-user distribution, which is where slow devices show up.

Where the time actually goes:
• `Application.onCreate` initializing SDKs. Defer everything not needed for the first frame — the App Startup library, a lazy initializer, or work posted after the first frame.
• ContentProviders: every library that declares one is created before `Application.onCreate`, and you pay for it whether or not you use the library. App Startup exists to collapse them into a single provider.
• Your code running interpreted on first launch — ship a baseline profile.
• Blocking the first frame on data. Use `installSplashScreen()` with `setKeepOnScreenCondition` only while it is genuinely necessary, and call `reportFullyDrawn()` (or `ReportDrawn` in Compose) when real content is up, so the platform and Play measure time-to-full-display correctly instead of stopping at an empty skeleton.
• Layout work done twice — a deep view hierarchy, or a Compose screen that recomposes on every intermediate state during load.

A reasonable target: `Application.onCreate` well under 200ms, and the first meaningful frame under a second on a mid-range device.

questions.question: What is Kotlin Multiplatform (KMP) and what does it share between iOS and Android?
questions.answer:
KMP lets you write Kotlin once and compile it for Android, iOS, JVM, JS, Wasm and native desktop; it went Stable in 2023 and is a production choice, not a preview.

It is NOT 'write UI once' — what it shares is everything below the UI:

• Networking — Ktor Client.
• Serialization — kotlinx.serialization.
• Persistence — SQLDelight, Room (KMP support stable since Room 2.7 on Android, iOS, JVM and native), Realm KMP.
• Domain layer and business rules.
• ViewModels — the multiplatform lifecycle artifacts put `ViewModel` in commonMain.
• Coroutines and Flow.

UI stays native (SwiftUI / UIKit on iOS, Compose on Android) — or you share that too with Compose Multiplatform, which is a separate decision.

Gain: one place for business logic, so the two apps cannot quietly disagree about what a rule means. Cost: multi-target Gradle, iOS interop rough edges, and a library ecosystem that is smaller than the JVM one.

questions.question: What are expect/actual declarations in KMP?
questions.answer:
`expect`/`actual` is KMP's mechanism for platform-specific implementations of a shared API.

• In `commonMain` you write `expect class Foo` / `expect fun bar()` — declares the API with no body.
• In each platform source set (`androidMain`, `iosMain`, `jvmMain`) you provide `actual class Foo` / `actual fun bar()` with the platform implementation.
• The compiler ensures all expected declarations have an actual.

Use for things that genuinely need native APIs: file IO, secure storage, DateFormatter, Logger, UUID generation, BluetoothScanner. Don't expect/actual things that have a single common implementation.

Alternative pattern: define an interface in commonMain + provide platform implementations through DI; often cleaner than expect/actual.

questions.question: How does Swift consume KMP code, and where does the Objective-C bridge hurt?
questions.answer:
Kotlin/Native compiles the shared module into an Apple framework that Swift imports like any other module, and almost every pain point comes from the Objective-C bridge in between.

• Suspend functions surface as Swift `async` / `throws` — call them straight from async/await.
• `Flow` surfaces as an opaque Objective-C class, not an `AsyncSequence`. Bridge it with SKIE (Touchlab) or KMP-NativeCoroutines.
• Sealed hierarchies arrive as plain classes, so an exhaustive `switch` degrades into `case let x as ...` casts. SKIE regenerates them as real Swift enums.
• Generics survive but without variance, and Kotlin lambda types show up as awkward closure signatures.
• Package names are flattened into one namespace; resolve collisions with `@ObjCName` and keep internals out of Swift with `@HiddenFromObjC`.
• Value types map roughly: `Long` becomes `KotlinLong`, and `kotlinx-datetime` or decimal types have no natural Swift counterpart.

One thing to stop repeating: the freezing memory model is gone. The current model has been the default since Kotlin 1.7.20 and the legacy one was removed in 1.9.20, so `InvalidMutabilityException` is not a thing you will meet.

Where it is going: direct Swift export skips Objective-C and emits real Swift declarations. It is Alpha — fine for prototypes, not for shipping — and it does not cover coroutines yet, so SKIE or KMP-NativeCoroutines is still the practical answer today.

questions.question: Which libraries would you reach for in a KMP shared module for networking, persistence, DI and logging?
questions.answer:
The KMP ecosystem has converged on one fairly standard stack, and stepping outside it usually costs more than it saves.

• Networking — Ktor Client (Ktor 3.x is the current line) with a per-platform engine: OkHttp on Android, Darwin on iOS, Js on web. JSON through kotlinx.serialization.
• Persistence — SQLDelight 2.x for typed SQL generated from `.sq` files, or Room, whose KMP support went stable in Room 2.7. Key-value: `multiplatform-settings`, or the multiplatform build of DataStore.
• DI — Koin 4.x is the default. Kodein is the alternative, and plain constructor injection is genuinely viable in a shared module.
• Logging — Kermit (Touchlab), which routes to Logcat on Android and os_log on iOS.
• Date and time — `kotlinx-datetime`. Concurrency — `kotlinx-coroutines-core`. Both are official and safe bets.
• Crash and analytics — Sentry KMP, Firebase Crashlytics behind a KMP wrapper, RevenueCat KMP for purchases.
• Swift interop — SKIE and KMP-NativeCoroutines.

Selection rule: check that the library publishes klibs for every target you build, and that its version matches your Kotlin version. Compiler-plugin libraries (Compose, kotlinx-serialization, SQLDelight) break on a Kotlin mismatch far more often than ordinary JVM dependencies do.

questions.question: How high up the stack can KMP sharing reach — can ViewModels and navigation be shared, or do they stay native?
questions.answer:
The ViewModel class is genuinely multiplatform now, and navigation can be shared too — but only if the UI itself is Compose Multiplatform.

ViewModels:
• The multiplatform lifecycle artifacts put `ViewModel` and `viewModelScope` in commonMain. On Android you get the usual configuration-change retention; on iOS nothing retains it for you, so the screen owns the instance and must clear it on disappear.
• Expose `StateFlow<UiState>` plus one `onAction(action)` entry point. That pair is the whole contract native UI binds to, and it keeps platform code dumb.
• Predecessors you will still meet in older codebases: Decompose components, MOKO MVVM, or a hand-rolled class holding its own `CoroutineScope`.

Navigation:
• AndroidX Navigation Compose is published for every Compose Multiplatform target and is stable — same `NavHost`, type-safe routes and deep links as on Android. It needs Compose UI, so it is not an option when iOS is SwiftUI.
• Decompose stays the strongest choice when navigation must live in shared non-Compose code, or when you want component lifecycles and a back stack you can unit-test without a UI.
• Or keep navigation native on both sides and let shared ViewModels drive it. Most KMP-with-native-UI apps do exactly this, because navigation is where platform conventions matter most.

Binding: Compose collects with `collectAsStateWithLifecycle`; SwiftUI needs the `StateFlow` bridged to an `AsyncSequence` or an observable wrapper via SKIE or KMP-NativeCoroutines.

questions.question: Your team ships the same product on iOS and Android. How do you decide whether KMP is worth adopting?
questions.answer:
KMP pays off when a large, long-lived business-logic layer would otherwise be written twice, and it costs more than it saves almost everywhere else.

Good fits:
• Business-logic-heavy products on both platforms — banking, e-commerce, ride-hailing, content.
• Long-lived products where the two apps quietly drifting apart is a real and expensive risk.
• Teams comfortable with Gradle and Kotlin, with at least intermediate iOS ability on hand.
• Greenfield, or an existing app you can adopt one module at a time.

Bad fits:
• Short-lived apps. The multi-target build setup dominates a project measured in months.
• UI-dominated apps where shared logic would be a thin slice of the codebase.
• Teams with no iOS expertise — KMP removes none of the work of shipping a polished native iOS app.
• Shops already standardised on Flutter or React Native for cost reasons; KMP shares no UI by default.

Costs to budget: multi-target Gradle and framework packaging, slower iOS builds, the occasional Android-only library with no KMP equivalent, and iOS engineers learning Kotlin plus a second toolchain.

The honest pitch is 'shared business logic, native UI'. If what the business actually wants is 'write the app once', that is Compose Multiplatform or Flutter, not plain KMP.

questions.question: What is Compose Multiplatform and how does it relate to Jetpack Compose?
questions.answer:
Compose Multiplatform (CMP) is JetBrains' build of Jetpack Compose for non-Android targets — iOS, desktop on the JVM, and web on Wasm. The composable APIs you already know (Column, Row, Modifier, Material 3) are the same ones.

Relationship:
• Jetpack Compose is Google's Android runtime and UI toolkit.
• CMP is JetBrains' multiplatform build of the same source, tracking each Compose release.
• On Android, CMP simply delegates to Jetpack Compose — there is no second renderer.
• On iOS and desktop it draws with Skia onto a platform surface.

Maturity, which is the part people still get wrong:
• Android and desktop — production for years.
• iOS — Stable since Compose Multiplatform 1.8 in May 2025. The API surface is frozen, VoiceOver accessibility and type-safe navigation are in, and UIKit/SwiftUI interop works both directions. It is a supported production target, not an experiment.
• Web on Wasm — Beta. Usable, but expect churn and a large initial payload.

Gain: one UI codebase across platforms. Cost: the result looks like your design system everywhere, so anything that must feel platform-native still needs platform work.

questions.question: Where do images, strings and fonts live in a Compose Multiplatform project, and how do you reference them?
questions.answer:
CMP ships its own resource system that generates a typed `Res` object from files in your source sets — it uses neither Android's `R` class nor iOS asset catalogs.

Layout — a `composeResources/` directory in any source set (commonMain for shared assets, androidMain or iosMain to override per platform):
• `drawable/` — images and vector XML.
• `font/` — typefaces.
• `values/strings.xml` — strings in the Android XML format, with `values-ru/`, `values-de/` and other qualifier folders for locales, and plurals alongside them.
• `files/` — arbitrary raw bytes.

Access:
• In composition — `painterResource(Res.drawable.logo)`, `stringResource(Res.string.hello, name)`, `pluralStringResource(...)`, `Font(Res.font.sora_bold)`.
• Outside composition, as suspend functions — `getString(Res.string.hello)`, `Res.readBytes("files/config.json")`, and `Res.getUri(...)` when you have to hand a path to an interop view.
• The multiplatform resources API has been stable since Compose Multiplatform 1.7, so the common accessors no longer need an experimental opt-in.
