Everything is packed into each platform binary, so nothing gets copied per target. Large or remote imagery does not belong here — use Coil 3, which is multiplatform and can reuse the Ktor engine you already have.

questions.question: How do you embed a real native view (MapKit, AVPlayer, a WebView) inside a Compose Multiplatform screen?
questions.answer:
Every CMP target has an interop composable that hosts a real platform view inside the Compose tree, so 'we need MapKit here' is never a reason to hand a whole screen back to the platform.

• Android — `AndroidView { factory }` hosts any `View`; `AndroidExternalSurface` and `AndroidEmbeddedExternalSurface` are the camera and video paths.
• iOS — `UIKitView { factory }` for a `UIView`, `UIKitViewController { factory }` for a `UIViewController`, which is also how you embed SwiftUI by wrapping it in a `UIHostingController`. The current overloads take a `UIKitInteropProperties` argument for touch and accessibility behaviour, replacing the older standalone `interactive` and `accessibilityEnabled` flags.
• Desktop — `SwingPanel { factory }` for Swing and AWT components.
• Web — DOM interop is the least developed of the four; treat it as experimental.

The reverse direction matters just as much: `ComposeUIViewController { }` wraps a composable so UIKit or SwiftUI can present it. That is how CMP gets adopted in an existing native app, one screen at a time, rather than as a rewrite.

Keep the embedded view small and leaf-shaped. Layout, theming, navigation and back handling stay Compose's job; the moment the native view starts owning navigation you have two competing back stacks.

questions.question: Which navigation library do you use in Compose Multiplatform, and what must navigation handle on iOS and web that it does not on Android?
questions.answer:
AndroidX Navigation Compose is published for every Compose Multiplatform target now and is the default answer — the old advice to reach for a third-party library first is out of date.

Options:
• Navigation Compose, multiplatform build (`org.jetbrains.androidx.navigation:navigation-compose`) — the same `NavHost`, `composable(...)`, type-safe serializable routes and deep links as on Android. Stable alongside Compose Multiplatform 1.8.
• Navigation 3, the newer back-stack-as-state model, gained non-Android support in Compose Multiplatform 1.10 and is where the platform is heading. Still early for a large app.
• Decompose — component-based and independent of Compose, so it is the choice when navigation state must be shared with native UI or unit-tested without a UI at all.
• Voyager — lighter, screen-object API; fine for small apps, but it is now a third-party dependency where a first-party one exists.
• Native per platform — CMP screens wrapped in SwiftUI `NavigationStack` and Jetpack Navigation, driven by shared ViewModels.

What is genuinely different away from Android:
• There is no system back button on iOS. The interactive edge-swipe is a UIKit gesture, so a `NavHost` has to opt into predictive-back handling or the screen feels wrong.
• Deep links are declared once but wired three ways: an intent filter on Android, associated domains plus a URL callback on iOS, and the address bar on web.
• On web the browser back button and history stack are the navigation surface, and you have to keep them in sync with the nav back stack.
• Process death and saved-state restoration are an Android concern; iOS suspends instead, so `rememberSaveable` guarantees differ.

For a five-screen app any of these works. The platform differences above, not the API, are what actually costs time.

questions.question: CMP draws its own widgets on iOS instead of using UIKit. What does that cost, and when is it a reason not to use CMP?
questions.answer:
CMP does not wrap UIKit on iOS — it draws its own widgets with Skia onto a Metal surface, so the app looks like your Compose design system rather than like iOS.

Things that used to be real complaints and are now fixed, so do not repeat them in an interview:
• Accessibility — VoiceOver, AssistiveTouch and Full Keyboard Access are supported and part of the stable API surface.
• Text — native-feeling selection, the magnifier, and the system context menu.
• Interop and scrolling — UIKit-like scroll physics, and embedding works in both directions.

What still differs from a native app:
• Typography — Material 3 defaults look Material. San Francisco and Dynamic Type sizing are opt-in work you do yourself.
• Navigation chrome — large titles, sheet detents and the interactive edge-swipe back are Compose reimplementations, not UIKit's.
• Controls and gestures — pull-to-refresh, swipe-to-delete, pickers and date pickers behave slightly differently from the system ones users know.
• Anything OS-integrated — Live Activities, widgets, App Intents, share extensions, Handoff — is native code either way.

Reasons not to use CMP:
• 'Indistinguishable from native' is a hard product requirement, as in banking or premium consumer brands.
• The app is mostly platform integrations rather than screens.
• There is little logic to share, so you would pay the tooling cost for nothing.

Where it shines: brand-driven design systems that deliberately look identical on both platforms, internal tools, admin consoles, content apps with custom UI. The usual production answer is a mix — CMP for design-system screens, native for the ones that define how the app feels.

questions.question: What does adopting Compose Multiplatform actually cost you in tests, binary size and day-to-day tooling?
questions.answer:
Shared Compose UI tests really do run on every target, the iOS binary grows by roughly a Skia-sized framework, and the remaining tooling gap is the iOS build loop.

Testing:
• `runComposeUiTest` runs the same `onNodeWithText` and `performClick` assertions from `commonTest` on Android, desktop and iOS. It still needs an experimental test-API opt-in.
• Android keeps the familiar JUnit4 `createComposeRule` path as well.
• ViewModel and logic tests are plain JVM tests — fast, no emulator, no simulator. Push as much as possible down to that layer.

Binary size:
• An iOS framework carrying Compose UI adds roughly 10 to 15 MB compressed: Skia, the Kotlin runtime, bundled fonts. Heavier than hand-written Swift, much lighter than shipping the Flutter engine.
• Android pays almost nothing extra, because it is already Compose.
• Desktop distributions start around 30 MB because they bundle a JRE and the rendering engine.

Tooling:
• IntelliJ IDEA and Android Studio with the Kotlin Multiplatform plugin are the supported IDEs.
• `@Preview` works on common code in the IDE, and Compose Hot Reload has reached stable, so the desktop iteration loop is genuinely fast. Verifying the real iOS build still means Xcode.
• Debugging spans Kotlin and Objective-C frames; `lldb` works but symbol names are noisy.
• CI needs a macOS runner for anything iOS and a Linux runner for Android and desktop. They are priced very differently, and that difference shapes what you run per PR versus nightly.

The trade: fewer screens written twice, in exchange for a build you have to understand.

questions.question: How would you design an offline-first feed for a mobile app?
questions.answer:
Core principle: the UI reads from a LOCAL store and never blocks on network. The network is a refresh source.

Architecture:
• Persistent store — SQLite (Room / SQLDelight / Core Data) keyed by item id.
• Repository — exposes `Flow<List<Item>>` (or AsyncSequence on iOS) backed by the DB.
• Sync engine — background coroutine / WorkManager that pulls fresh data and writes to the DB.
• Pagination — keyset (cursor) pagination preferred over offset, for stable scrolling.
• Cache invalidation — TTL on rows + ETag/`If-None-Match` for conditional fetches.
• Conflict resolution — last-writer-wins or per-field merging. Always include server `updated_at` timestamps.

UI considerations:
• Show stale data with a 'last synced X ago' indicator.
• Pull-to-refresh triggers a sync; UI never loses scroll position.
• Optimistic local writes for user actions (like, save, delete) + outbox to retry server-side.

questions.question: Why does offset pagination break in a live feed, and what does the client half of cursor pagination look like?
questions.answer:
Offset pagination breaks the moment rows are inserted or deleted between two requests: the offset points at a position, the position shifts, and the user silently sees duplicates or misses items entirely.

• Keyset or cursor pagination (`?after_id=abc&limit=20`, or a compound cursor such as `?after_score=12,after_id=abc`) is stable across inserts because the cursor names a row rather than a position. Use it for anything that changes while the user reads it.
• Offset is still fine for static, sorted, rarely-changing data — an archive, or search results held stable for the session.

Client side:
• Persist pages into the local store and let the UI read from there. The network only appends, so a configuration change or process death does not refetch anything.
• Trigger the next fetch from scroll position rather than from the last row appearing — prefetch about five rows early and the spinner is rarely seen.
• Guard with a single in-flight flag. Without it a fast scroller fires four requests for the same cursor and you merge the same page repeatedly.
• De-duplicate by stable id when merging; an overlapping row from the server is legitimate, not a bug.
• Cap memory by trimming pages far off screen, keeping the cursor so back-scroll can refetch.

Libraries: AndroidX Paging publishes multiplatform artifacts now, so the Cash App fork is no longer the default choice for KMP. On iOS the hand-rolled equivalent is `onAppear` on a trailing row plus a coordinator that suppresses re-entrancy.

UX: a skeleton row beats a full-screen spinner, and new items arriving at the top should sit behind a 'new items' pill rather than jumping the scroll position.

questions.question: How would you design a chat / messaging feature?
questions.answer:
Chat is one of the hardest mobile features because it combines real-time, offline, attachments, and ordering.

Server transport:
• Long-lived WebSocket (or SSE) for real-time. Auth on connect; reconnect with exponential backoff.
• REST/GraphQL fallback for history fetch and message sending when offline.
• Message ids are server-assigned UUIDs; clients use a temporary `client_id` for optimistic display until server ack.

Client state:
• Local DB stores messages keyed by `id` + `client_id` + `chat_id`. Sort by `(created_at, id)`.
• Outbox: messages with `state in (sending, failed)` retry on connectivity restoration.
• De-dup by `client_id` when server's authoritative copy returns.

Ordering & merging:
• Use server `created_at` for display; tie-break by id.
• Compress duplicate writes (typing indicator at most once/second).
• Handle out-of-order arrival — render messages in created_at order and drop ones whose chat is no longer open.

Misc:
• Push notifications — payload contains chat id + message preview; tap routes to the chat.
• Read receipts — local mark on view, debounced upload to server.
• Attachments — separate upload pipeline with progress; message refers to media url once upload completes.

questions.question: How do you run feature flags in a large mobile app without ending up with hundreds of stale branches?
questions.answer:
A feature flag is a promise to delete code later, and the flags that ruin a codebase are the ones nobody ever removed.

Flag layers:
• Build-time constants — free at runtime, but frozen the moment the build ships.
• Remote config (Firebase Remote Config, LaunchDarkly, ConfigCat, GrowthBook, or your own endpoint) — flippable without a release, which is what makes a kill-switch possible at all.
• User-targeted — cohorts, percentage rollouts, experiment variants, resolved server-side so the client is never trusted to compute eligibility.

Keeping them under control:
• Every flag has an owner and an expiry date in a checked-in registry, and a CI lint fails the build when a flag outlives it.
• New flags default to off unless explicitly declared otherwise.
• Read flags through one typed API (`Flags.checkoutV2Enabled`), never a string key at the call site. That is what makes the registry enforceable and the flag greppable when it is time to delete it.
• Emit an exposure event where a flag actually changes behaviour, so analytics can attribute a metric movement to the variant instead of guessing.
• Test both branches in CI. The off branch is the one that silently rots.
• Schedule the deletion of the flag and the losing branch as work, not as good intentions.

Interaction with modularization:
• In a multi-module app a flag can decide which implementation the DI graph binds, so the dead path is a whole module you can delete rather than an `if` scattered through call sites.
• Keep a small set of kill-switches on critical paths — payments, sync, a risky third-party SDK — so a production incident is a config change rather than a release.

questions.question: How do you wire analytics, crash reporting and performance monitoring so you can swap vendors and keep PII out?
questions.answer:
Analytics, crash reporting and performance are three separate systems, and the usual mistake is letting three vendor SDKs spread through your call sites instead of hiding each behind one interface.

• Product analytics — a typed event API over a checked-in event registry, batched upload, offline buffering. Mixpanel, Amplitude, Segment, PostHog, Firebase Analytics.
• Crash reporting — Crashlytics, Sentry, Bugsnag. Wire the native handlers too (NDK on Android, the signal and exception handlers on iOS) or you only ever see the managed half of a crash. Note that Microsoft App Center has been retired, so anything still pointing at it needs migrating.
• Performance — Firebase Performance, Sentry Performance, Datadog RUM, or an OpenTelemetry mobile SDK. Track cold start, frame timing, screen time-to-interactive and network durations. On iOS, MetricKit gives you Apple's own aggregated numbers for free.

Design rules:
• One internal interface per concern with the vendor SDK behind it. Swapping providers then touches one file, and tests get a fake instead of a network call.
• Generate the typed event wrappers from a schema in JSON or YAML, so a renamed property is a compile error rather than a silently missing column.
• Buffer offline events with a hard cap and flush on reconnect; drop oldest rather than growing without bound.
• Sample expensive spans. Full tracing on every session is a billing surprise, not a feature.
• Never send PII. Use a stable anonymous id, respect the ATT decision on iOS, and keep the Play Data safety form and the App Store privacy labels matching what you actually send.
• Attach the release version and the active flag variants to every event, or you cannot tell a rollout regression from noise.

questions.question: Design a system that streams large amounts of data while being kind to the device.
questions.answer:
A high-rate stream on a phone is a budgeting exercise: memory, battery, CPU, network and the render loop each have a ceiling, and the design is mostly about deciding which one you are willing to hit first.

• Memory — never hold the whole dataset. Chunk it, page it, and release chunks behind the viewport.
• Battery — a long-lived WebSocket or gRPC stream costs far less than polling; suspend it when the app backgrounds instead of letting it run.
• CPU — parse off the main thread, and prefer a binary format (Protobuf, FlatBuffers) once payloads get large.
• Network — gzip or brotli both ways, and batch small uploads rather than sending each sample.
• Storage — batched transactions, append-only structures for hot writes; a transaction per sample will destroy throughput.
• Backpressure — the producer must respect the consumer's cadence. A coroutine `Flow` with `buffer(capacity, onBufferOverflow)` makes the drop policy explicit instead of accidental.

UI:
• Windowed rendering (`LazyColumn`, `RecyclerView`) so only visible rows exist as views.
• Throttle updates to the refresh rate at most; recomposing faster than the display refreshes is pure waste.
• Show derived statistics — mean, last value, a sparkline — rather than every frame of raw data.

Resilience:
• Reconnect with exponential backoff plus jitter, and resume from the last sequence number rather than restarting the stream.
• Persist progress periodically so a crash resumes cleanly instead of re-downloading everything.

questions.question: What is the OWASP Mobile Top 10 and what should every mobile dev know about it?
questions.answer:
The OWASP Mobile Top 10 names the ten risk categories that most often break real mobile apps, and the 2024 revision is the current one.

• M1 Improper Credential Usage — hardcoded API keys, secrets committed to source.
• M2 Inadequate Supply Chain Security — vulnerable or over-privileged third-party SDKs.
• M3 Insecure Authentication / Authorization — weak token storage, authorization decided on the client.
• M4 Insufficient Input/Output Validation — injection, and XSS inside WebViews.
• M5 Insecure Communication — missing TLS, weak ciphers, no pinning.
• M6 Inadequate Privacy Controls — collecting more PII than declared, no consent gate.
• M7 Insufficient Binary Protections — no obfuscation or integrity checks where the threat model needs them.
• M8 Security Misconfiguration — debug endpoints in production, components left exported.
• M9 Insecure Data Storage — secrets in plain SharedPreferences or UserDefaults. Note that Jetpack Security's `EncryptedSharedPreferences` is deprecated, so new Android code should encrypt with a Keystore-held key itself rather than reaching for that library.
• M10 Insufficient Cryptography — broken algorithms, home-grown constructions, reused nonces.

How to use it: treat it as a review checklist rather than trivia. Thread the categories through code review, run static analysis (MobSF, Detekt security rules, AppSweep), scan dependencies on every bump, and buy a penetration test for anything handling money or health data.

The interview version of this question is usually 'which of these have you actually hit' — having a concrete story about one beats reciting all ten.

questions.question: What does it take to make mobile API traffic hard to intercept and hard to replay?
questions.answer:
No single control protects mobile API traffic, so you layer transport security, token hygiene and server-side attestation on the assumption that every client-side control will eventually be patched out.

• TLS, non-negotiable. Disable cleartext on Android and ship no ATS exceptions on iOS; require TLS 1.2 or better and reject anything older.
• Certificate or SPKI pinning defeats a rogue or user-installed CA. Pin the SPKI hash rather than the leaf certificate, always ship a backup pin, and rotate before expiry — a pinning mistake bricks every installed copy at once and cannot be hotfixed.
• OAuth 2.0 or OIDC with PKCE, in a system browser tab. Never an embedded WebView, never a hand-rolled flow.
• Short-lived access tokens measured in minutes, refresh tokens in Keychain or Keystore, and refresh-token rotation so a stolen one becomes detectable.
• Device and app attestation — Play Integrity on Android, App Attest or DeviceCheck on iOS. It only means something when your server validates the token; a client-side check of the verdict is theatre. Play Integrity's standard request, where you prepare a token provider once and then request per call, is the one to use for anything called often; classic requests are slow and rate-limited.
• Replay protection on endpoints that move money or change credentials: a server-issued nonce plus request signing, with a short validity window.
• Rate limiting and anomaly detection server-side, because that is the one layer an attacker cannot patch.

Say the quiet part out loud in an interview: pinning and obfuscation raise the attacker's cost, they do not stop one. Anything you must genuinely enforce belongs on the server.

questions.question: Client-side root and jailbreak checks can be hooked out in minutes. What do you rely on instead, and what is a client-side check still worth?
questions.answer:
Treat the client's answer as a signal and the server's attestation verdict as the decision — a rooted device can lie about being rooted, so anything enforced only on the client is enforced nowhere.

Server-side attestation, which is what actually holds:
• Play Integrity (Android) returns device labels — `MEETS_BASIC_INTEGRITY`, `MEETS_DEVICE_INTEGRITY`, `MEETS_STRONG_INTEGRITY` for hardware-backed evaluation, and `MEETS_VIRTUAL_INTEGRITY` for emulators — plus separate app and account verdicts. Your backend validates the token and maps the labels to a trust level.
• App Attest and DeviceCheck (iOS) prove the request came from a genuine, unmodified build of your app on real hardware, with a Secure Enclave key bound to that install.

Client-side heuristics, worth having only as an extra signal:
• Android — an `su` binary on the path, BusyBox, Magisk artefacts, test-keys in the build fingerprint, `ro.debuggable` set in a release build. RootBeer bundles the usual set; Magisk's hiding modules defeat most of them.
• iOS — Cydia and apt paths present, writes succeeding outside the sandbox, a registered `cydia` URL scheme handler, unexpected dynamic libraries in the process. IOSSecuritySuite bundles these.
• Both — a debugger attached, or Frida and Objection hooks visible in the process.

On a cross-platform runtime the probe is never yours to make directly:
• Dart, JavaScript and Kotlin/Native see none of these signals — every check is native code reached through a plugin or a channel, so a plugin-free app cannot answer the question at all.
• The resulting boolean lands in a Dart snapshot or a JS bundle, which is cheaper to patch than native code. Ship obfuscated and re-decide server-side.
• Build-mode flags (`kDebugMode`, `__DEV__`) describe your build, not the device, and are not a root check.

What to do with the answer:
• Do not hard-block. Custom ROMs and developer devices are common false positives, and a hard block is the first thing an attacker patches out anyway.
• Degrade by risk instead: refuse to enrol biometrics, force step-up authentication, decline high-value payments, shorten session lifetime.
• Make the decision server-side and send it back as policy the client applies, so the branch an attacker wants to flip is not sitting in the binary.
• Do not name detection functions descriptively and do not tell the user which check fired — that is writing the attacker's changelog for them.

questions.question: Where does a private key actually live on Android and iOS, and how do you guarantee it cannot be extracted?
questions.answer:
The answer to 'where do I put the private key' is 'somewhere you cannot read it either' — both platforms generate the key inside hardware and only ever let you ask it to sign or decrypt.

Android, through the `AndroidKeyStore` provider:
• Generate with `KeyGenParameterSpec`; the key material never enters your process memory.
• StrongBox puts the key in a separate secure element, but throws when the device has no StrongBox, so always catch that and fall back to the TEE-backed key rather than crashing on cheap hardware.
• `setUserAuthenticationRequired(true)` gates use behind biometrics or the device credential, combined with `BiometricPrompt` and a `CryptoObject`.
• `setAttestationChallenge(...)` yields a certificate chain your server can verify. That is what turns 'I promise this key is hardware-backed' into something checkable.
• Enrolling a new biometric invalidates the key if you asked for that — treat the resulting exception as a re-enrolment trigger, not a crash.

iOS, through the Secure Enclave:
• P-256 keys only, for signing and key agreement. CryptoKit's `SecureEnclave.P256.Signing.PrivateKey` is the readable API; the Keychain equivalent sets `kSecAttrTokenID` to `kSecAttrTokenIDSecureEnclave`.
• `SecAccessControl` binds usage to `.biometryCurrentSet`, which invalidates when Face ID or Touch ID enrolment changes, or to `.userPresence` when you want the passcode to be an acceptable fallback.
• Pick the accessibility class deliberately — the `ThisDeviceOnly` variants stop an item riding a backup onto a different device.

Cross-cutting:
• AES-GCM for symmetric, ECDSA or Ed25519 for signatures, ECDH for agreement, HKDF for derivation. RSA only when a peer forces it, and never a construction of your own design.
• Never reuse a GCM nonce under the same key; store the IV next to the ciphertext.
• Design for rotation on day one: the server accepts several public keys per user during the overlap window, and you re-key on reinstall, on biometric change, and on a failed attestation.

questions.question: How do you keep sensitive content out of screenshots, screen recordings and the clipboard?
questions.answer:
You cannot stop someone photographing the screen, so the goal is narrower: keep secrets out of screenshots, out of the recents thumbnail, out of screen recordings, and out of a clipboard other apps can read.

Screenshots and recording:
• Android — `FLAG_SECURE` on the window blocks screenshots, blanks the surface in recordings, and hides the recents thumbnail. It is per-window, so dialogs and separately presented surfaces need it too.
• Android 14 added a screen-capture callback so you can react to a screenshot instead of only blocking it, and Android 15 added a way to hide just the recents thumbnail without the full `FLAG_SECURE` blackout.
• iOS has no equivalent of `FLAG_SECURE`. You observe the user-took-a-screenshot notification after the fact, watch `UIScreen.isCaptured` while a recording is running, and cover the window with a placeholder as the scene resigns active so the app-switcher snapshot shows nothing.

Clipboard:
• Do not auto-copy secrets. If a one-time code really must be copied, clear it on a timer.
• Android 13 and later — mark the clip with the sensitive-content flag so the system's clipboard preview does not render the value, and the OS clears the clipboard itself after a period. Android also toasts when another app reads the clipboard, so assume every read is observable.
• iOS — set an `expirationDate` on the pasteboard item, and keep it local to the device so it does not travel over Universal Clipboard.

Keyboard and text fields:
• Use the platform's secure input — `SecureTextField` in Compose, `isSecureTextEntry` in UIKit, `SecureField` in SwiftUI. It also excludes the field from recordings.
• Turn off suggestion learning on sensitive fields so secrets never enter the keyboard's personal dictionary.

questions.question: Before an app can ship, what privacy declarations and consent gates does each store require?
questions.answer:
Privacy is a shipping gate now rather than a policy document — both stores reject builds whose declarations do not match what the binary actually does.

Apple:
• App Tracking Transparency — request authorization before any SDK that tracks the user across apps or sites runs, and read the advertising identifier only when the status is authorized. Initialising an ad SDK before the prompt is a rejection, not a warning.
• Privacy nutrition labels in App Store Connect — which data types you collect and whether they are linked to identity.
• Privacy manifests (`PrivacyInfo.xcprivacy`), required since 2024. Declare tracking domains and an approved reason code for each required-reason API you touch, such as user defaults, file timestamps, or disk space. Third-party SDKs on Apple's list must ship their own manifest and a code signature, so an SDK that has not caught up becomes your submission problem.

Google:
• The Data safety form in Play Console — collected, shared, retained, encrypted in transit, deletable.
• The advertising ID needs its permission declared, and it vanishes when the user opts out, so never treat it as a stable identifier.
• Apps with accounts need an in-app account deletion path and a web deletion URL.

GDPR and its relatives:
• Establish a lawful basis, and gate non-essential SDK initialisation on consent. The SDK must not start before the user answers, which means the gate belongs in the startup path, not in a screen.
• Build the user-rights endpoints for real: access, export, deletion. Deletion has to reach the device too — local database, caches, Keychain and Keystore entries.
• Watch data residency for EU and UK users; some contracts require the data never to leave the region.

Engineering practice: keep an inventory of every SDK and what it sends on first launch, and re-audit on every version bump. An SDK update is an unreviewed change to your privacy posture.

questions.question: What does a typical mobile CI pipeline look like?
questions.answer:
A mobile pipeline is really two pipelines — a fast lane that must finish while the reviewer is still looking at the PR, and a slow lane that may take an hour — and most of the design work is deciding what belongs in which.

Fast lane, on every PR:
• Lint and static analysis — Detekt and ktlint on Android, SwiftLint and SwiftFormat on iOS, `dart analyze` for Flutter.
• Unit tests on the JVM or a simulator. No emulator, no signing, no uploads.

Slow lane, on main or nightly:
• Instrumented and UI tests on an emulator or simulator.
• Release builds, signed with material pulled from secrets.
• Artifact upload to TestFlight or Play internal testing for QA.
• Symbol upload (dSYMs, ProGuard mapping) so crash reports de-obfuscate.
• Staged rollout, driven by fastlane lanes or the store APIs.

Providers: GitHub Actions is the common default, with Bitrise and Codemagic as mobile-specialised options, plus CircleCI, Buildkite, and Xcode Cloud for iOS-only shops.

Rules that keep it healthy:
• Keep the PR build under about fifteen minutes, or people stop reading the results.
• Cache Gradle, SwiftPM and CocoaPods deliberately; an uncached mobile build is mostly downloading.
• Run everything you can on Linux runners. macOS runners cost several times more per minute, so reserve them for work that genuinely requires Xcode.
• Signing material never lives in the repository. It comes from encrypted secrets, is decoded at build time, and is never echoed into a log.
questions.code_example:
# .github/workflows/android.yml — the fast PR lane
name: Android CI
on:
  pull_request: { branches: [main] }
  push: { branches: [main] }
jobs:
  test:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v6
      - uses: actions/setup-java@v5
        with: { distribution: 'zulu', java-version: '17' }
      - uses: gradle/actions/setup-gradle@v6      # caches, and validates the wrapper
      - run: ./gradlew detekt lintDebug
      - run: ./gradlew testDebugUnitTest
      - uses: actions/upload-artifact@v6
        if: failure()
        with: { name: test-reports, path: '**/build/reports/' }

  instrumented:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest      # KVM on Linux is faster AND far cheaper than a macOS runner
    needs: test
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v6
      - name: Enable KVM
        run: |
          echo 'KERNEL=="kvm", GROUP="kvm", MODE="0666", OPTIONS+="static_node=kvm"' \
            | sudo tee /etc/udev/rules.d/99-kvm4all.rules
          sudo udevadm control --reload-rules && sudo udevadm trigger --name-match=kvm
      - uses: reactivecircus/android-emulator-runner@v2
        with:
          api-level: 36
          script: ./gradlew connectedDebugAndroidTest

# .github/workflows/ios.yml — macOS runners only where Xcode is unavoidable
# jobs:
#   test:
#     runs-on: macos-latest
#     steps:
#       - uses: actions/checkout@v6
#       - run: bundle exec fastlane scan --device "iPhone 17"

questions.question: What is Fastlane and what does it automate?
questions.answer:
Fastlane is a Ruby toolkit that turns the release ritual — build, sign, upload symbols, ship to a test track — into named lanes you run identically on a laptop and in CI.

Common automations:
• Build and sign — `build_app` (formerly `gym`) on iOS, the `gradle` action on Android.
• Code signing — `match` synchronises iOS certificates and provisioning profiles through a private, encrypted git repository (or S3, or Google Cloud Storage).
• Store authentication — `app_store_connect_api_key` loads an App Store Connect API key from an issuer id, key id and private key file. This is what CI should use; an Apple ID with an app-specific password is the legacy path and breaks on 2FA challenges.
• Beta distribution — `upload_to_testflight`, `firebase_app_distribution`, `upload_to_play_store` on the internal track.
• Production — `deliver` for the App Store, `supply` for Play, both scriptable including staged rollout percentages.
• Screenshots — `snapshot` drives UI tests across locales and devices, `frameit` decorates them, `deliver` uploads them.
• Symbols — `upload_symbols_to_crashlytics` and the Sentry plugin, so release crash reports are readable.

Why it survives: the same lane runs on a laptop and on CI, so 'works on my machine' becomes a testable claim. The alternative is a pile of bash that only one person understands, and that person is on holiday during the release.
questions.code_example:
# fastlane/Fastfile — Android
default_platform(:android)

platform :android do
  desc "Build and upload to Play internal testing"
  lane :internal do
    gradle(task: "clean bundleRelease")
    upload_to_play_store(
      track: "internal",
      release_status: "draft",
      aab: "app/build/outputs/bundle/release/app-release.aab",
      mapping_paths: ["app/build/outputs/mapping/release/mapping.txt"]
    )
  end
end

# fastlane/Fastfile — iOS
platform :ios do
  desc "Build and upload to TestFlight"
  lane :beta do
    setup_ci if is_ci                      # keychain the runner can actually use

    # API key, not an Apple ID: unattended, and immune to 2FA prompts
    api_key = app_store_connect_api_key(
      key_id: ENV["ASC_KEY_ID"],
      issuer_id: ENV["ASC_ISSUER_ID"],
      key_content: ENV["ASC_KEY_P8"]
    )

    match(type: "appstore", readonly: is_ci, api_key: api_key)
    increment_build_number(xcodeproj: "MyApp.xcodeproj")
    build_app(scheme: "MyApp", export_method: "app-store-connect")
    upload_to_testflight(api_key: api_key, skip_waiting_for_build_processing: true)
    upload_symbols_to_crashlytics(gsp_path: "./MyApp/GoogleService-Info.plist")
  end
end

# In CI
# bundle exec fastlane android internal
# bundle exec fastlane ios beta

questions.question: What does iOS code signing actually consist of, and how does CI get the certificates and profiles?
questions.answer:
iOS signing is four moving parts that all have to agree: a certificate identifying who built the binary, a provisioning profile binding an App ID to that certificate, entitlements compiled into the app, and a bundle identifier that already exists in App Store Connect.

Getting the material onto CI:
• `fastlane match` stores certificates and profiles in a private repository, encrypted with a passphrase. CI clones and installs them in read-only mode, so a runner can never regenerate and thereby revoke the whole team's certificates.
• Authenticate with an App Store Connect API key rather than an Apple ID — two-factor authentication makes password auth unusable unattended.
• Xcode Cloud, or Xcode's automatic signing, is a reasonable choice for a small team that does not need the pipeline reproducible anywhere else.

Distribution paths:
• TestFlight — up to 100 internal testers with no review, up to 10 000 external testers behind a lighter review.
• App Store — full review, then either an immediate release or a phased rollout.
• Ad hoc and enterprise in-house distribution still exist but are narrow and increasingly legacy.

Gotchas that actually bite:
• Regenerating a profile can silently drop capabilities such as push or App Groups, and entitlements in the binary must match the profile exactly. That mismatch is caught at upload processing, not at build time, so it fails after the slow part.
• Apple raises the minimum build SDK every year; the current cycle requires uploads built with Xcode 26 and the iOS 26 SDK. Check the deadline before planning a release freeze, and do not confuse the build SDK with your deployment target.
• An expired certificate does not break installed apps, only new builds — so the failure always turns up on a deadline.
questions.code_example:
# One-time setup, run by a human on a Mac
fastlane match init
fastlane match appstore              # creates or fetches cert + profile, encrypted into the repo

# CI: read-only, so a runner can never revoke the team's certificates
export MATCH_PASSWORD="${MATCH_PASSWORD}"
bundle exec fastlane match appstore --readonly

# Archive and export with explicit signing
xcodebuild -workspace MyApp.xcworkspace -scheme MyApp \
  -configuration Release -archivePath build/MyApp.xcarchive archive \
  CODE_SIGN_STYLE=Manual \
  PROVISIONING_PROFILE_SPECIFIER="match AppStore com.example.app" \
  CODE_SIGN_IDENTITY="Apple Distribution"

xcodebuild -exportArchive \
  -archivePath build/MyApp.xcarchive \
  -exportPath build \
  -exportOptionsPlist ExportOptions.plist

# Upload with an API key — no Apple ID, no 2FA prompt on a headless runner
bundle exec fastlane pilot upload --ipa build/MyApp.ipa

# ExportOptions.plist
# <key>method</key><string>app-store-connect</string>   <- 'app-store' is the old spelling
# <key>signingStyle</key><string>manual</string>
# <key>uploadSymbols</key><true/>

# Matchfile — note there is no username; auth comes from the API key
# git_url("git@github.com:org/certs.git")
# storage_mode("git")
# type("appstore")
# app_identifier(["com.example.app"])

# fastlane match nuke appstore    # revokes everything. Never from CI.

questions.question: How do you sign and ship an Android app?
questions.answer:
Android has two signing keys and the important one is not yours: you sign with an upload key, and Play App Signing re-signs the artifact with the app signing key that devices actually verify.

• Upload key — signs the AAB you upload. If you lose it, Play can reset it, which is the entire reason Play App Signing is worth using.
• App signing key — held by Google, used to sign the APKs delivered to devices.
• Build types: `debug` uses the shared debug keystore, `release` uses your keystore injected from CI secrets.
• The AAB is the required upload format. Play splits it per device by ABI, density and language, so what installs is never quite what you built — use `bundletool` when you need to reproduce a device's actual APK locally.

Distribution tracks:
• Internal testing — up to 100 testers, no review wait. This is where CI should push on every main-branch build.
• Closed and open testing — larger audiences, still reviewed.
• Production, with a staged rollout percentage you control and can halt.

Policy gates that block a release:
• Target API level, which Play raises annually. From 31 August 2026, new apps and updates must target Android 16 (API level 36), while existing apps need at least API level 35 to stay available to new users.
• A completed Data safety form and a privacy policy.
• 64-bit native libraries.
• An in-app account deletion path for apps with sign-in.

Keystore handling: base64 it into a CI secret, decode into the workspace at build time, delete it afterwards, and never echo the passwords into the log. Gradle will happily print them if you interpolate them into a task name.

questions.question: What are build flavors / variants and when do you use them?
questions.answer:
Flavors let you produce multiple APKs/AABs from one codebase, differing in package name, branding, endpoints, or features.

Android (Gradle):
• `productFlavors { free { ... }; paid { ... } }`
• Combined with `buildTypes { debug; release }` to give variants like `freeDebug`, `paidRelease`.
• Each flavor can override resources, manifests, source sets.

iOS (Xcode):
• Multiple targets — separate builds, separate Info.plist.
• Or schemes + xcconfig files — single target, different config files for dev / staging / prod.
• Asset catalogues + Info.plist substitution for branding.

Flutter:
• `--flavor` flag with `--dart-define` for compile-time constants.

Use flavors for:
• Dev / staging / prod with different API endpoints.
• White-label apps (same codebase, multiple branded apps).
• Free vs paid SKUs.
• Feature subsets per geography.

Keep flavor count small; each one multiplies your CI build matrix.

questions.question: How do you do a staged rollout and observe a release?
questions.answer:
Staged rollout = release to a small percent first, watch metrics, ramp.

Android (Play Console):
• Production → Releases → set rollout percentage (1%, 5%, 20%, 50%, 100%).
• Halt rollout if vitals drop. Resume when fixed (the affected version stays at the lower %).
• Internal app sharing — quick QA URLs.

iOS (App Store):
• Phased release for automatic updates: 1%, 2%, 5%, 10%, 20%, 50%, 100% over 7 days.
• Manual users get the app immediately.
• Pause / resume at any stage.
• Expedited review for critical fixes (use sparingly).

Observability during rollout:
• Crash-free users — Crashlytics / Sentry.
• ANR rate (Android) — Play Vitals.
• Frame rate / startup — Firebase Performance / MetricKit.
• Funnel + business metrics — Mixpanel / Amplitude.
• Server logs — error rate, latency.

Playbook: define KPIs and thresholds BEFORE shipping. Wire alerts (PagerDuty / Slack). Have a rollback plan: feature flags first, app pull-from-store as last resort.
questions.code_example:
# fastlane — staged Play rollout
lane :production_5pct do
  upload_to_play_store(
    track: "production",
    rollout: "0.05",                 # 5%
    aab: "app/build/outputs/bundle/release/app-release.aab"
  )
end

lane :production_50pct do
  upload_to_play_store(
    track: "production",
    rollout: "0.5",
    skip_upload_apk: true,            # already uploaded
    skip_upload_aab: true
  )
end

# Halting via Play Console UI is recommended — fastlane can change rollout but the UI is faster in incidents.

# iOS phased release — toggle in App Store Connect:
# 'Phased Release for Automatic Updates' = ON

# Observability dashboard — track these on a per-version basis:
# - crash-free users (target > 99.5%)
# - ANR rate (target < 0.5%)
# - p99 cold startup (target < 2s)
# - business KPI: signup conversion, checkout success rate

# Rollback decision tree
# 1. Crash spike from new code path -> flip feature flag OFF
# 2. Cannot mitigate via flag -> halt rollout, ship hotfix in next update
# 3. Severe regression -> Play 'halt rollout' / iOS 'pause phased release', expedited review
